chunk_text: Lesson-01: An Introduction to Parts of Speech. The different kinds of words used for different purposes in a sentence are called Parts of Speech. Example: Nancy is a brilliant student. Nancy / is / a / brilliant / student. Nancy names a person; is describes something; brilliant gives more information about student; student names Nancy. Lesson-02: Classification of Parts of Speech. In English Parts of Speech are of eight kinds: 1. Noun 2. Pronoun 3. Adjective 4. Verb 5. Adverb 6. Preposition 7. Conjunction 8. Interjection.

chunk_text: Noun: A noun is a word that names of a person, animal, place, thing or quality. Examples: The Padma is a big river. Dhaka is the capital of Bangladesh. Iron is a useful metal. The cow is a useful animal. January is the first month of the year. Forgiveness is a great virtue. Water has no colour. Pronoun: A word that is used instead of a noun is called Pronoun. Examples: Hasan is reading a book. It is very interesting. Students of this school are very disciplined. They all stay in the hostel. The officer asked soldiers to go to the field in the morning. But nobody was there. A pronoun is used to avoid repetition of a noun. Noun and Pronoun differences: an adjective and a determiner can sit before a noun, but a pronoun takes no adjective or determiner; a noun can take prefix and suffix, a pronoun cannot; the formation of a pronoun is fixed.

chunk_text: Adjectives: An adjective is a word that adds something (e.g. quality, quantity, condition or state, number etc.) to the meaning of a noun pronoun. Examples: Dhaka is a big city. He is a little boy. The girl is beautiful. The night is dark. It is a small town. It is a new pen. The garden is nice. It is a hot day. Adjectives are not affected by the number, gender or case of the noun, because the adjective is not controlled by the noun it modifies. Degrees: good - better - best. Verb: A verb is a word or phrase indicating an action, event or state. Examples: She teaches us English (action). The accident happened at night (event). He is in poor health (state). He eats rice (action). He goes to school (action). The book belongs to me (having). A verb is the most important part of a sentence; even a one-word sentence is formed with a verb only (Stop! Go.). A verb phrase may be formed with more than one word, even four words (may have been playing, would have been written).

chunk_text: Adverb: An adverb is a word that modifies a verb, an adjective, another adverb or a whole sentence by making its meaning more specific. Examples: Baby Nazneen sang sweetly (modifies verb 'sang'). Sayeed was rather quiet (modifies adjective 'quiet'). He works extremely slowly (modifies adverb 'slowly'). It takes quite a lot of courage to jump from a plane (modifies noun phrase). Nearly everybody was late (modifies pronoun). I am going for a jogging later (modifies a clause). Personally, I don't like it (modifies a sentence). Asking How? Where? When? How often? To what extent? about a verb gives an adverb. Adjective and Adverb differences: both work as modifiers; an adverb modifies all parts of speech except Interjection and expresses time or place, but an adjective modifies only nouns and never expresses time or place. Preposition: A preposition is a word that shows the relationship of a noun or pronoun to some other word in a sentence. Examples: I gave the pen to Sheena (preposition + noun). I gave it to her (preposition + pronoun). Sheena devotes her time to writing (preposition + gerund). He lives in Dhaka (place). I will meet you at 7 p.m. (time). You need to leave early in order to arrive on time (purpose). Object of Prepositions: prepositions generally take objects (noun, noun phrase, pronoun or gerund). Some prepositions take no object and work as adverbs; these are called Adverb particles (about, above, before, off, by, down, in, over, round, up). Examples: We drove round the city (preposition + object) / We drove round (adverb particle). I won't go out before lunch (preposition) / I have read this book before (adverb particle). List: at, in, on, to, with, for, by, after, about, among, before, upto, in spite of.

chunk_text: Conjunction: A conjunction is a word that joins words, phrases or sentences. Examples: Biplab or Sohel will help you. He is poor but honest. List: and, but, or, yet, either, neither, so, as, because, if, unless, whether, since, that, so that, in order that, until, before, after, as well as. Interjection: An interjection is a word or phrases that expresses emotion or exclamation. An interjection has no role in forming a sentence; it is used in a sentence to express sudden emotion even though it has no connection with the other words. Examples: Hello, Masud! How do you do? Hurrah! Today is a holiday. Oh! What a nice view. Fie! You are a liar. Bravo! You have done well. A Note of Exclamation (!) is placed after an interjection.

chunk_text: Lesson-01: What is Noun? A noun is a word that names a person, animal, place, thing or quality. There are seven kinds of noun: Proper, Common, Collective, Material, Abstract, Countable and Uncountable. The way to identify nouns: many nouns end in suffixes such as -tion, -sion, -ness, -ment, -ity, -ance, -ence, -hood, -ship, -dom, -age, -er, -or, -ist, -ism and -ty. Lesson-02: Classification of Noun. Concrete nouns name things that can be seen or touched; Abstract nouns name a quality, state or action that cannot be seen or touched. Concrete nouns are of four kinds: 1. Proper Noun (name of a particular person, place or thing, e.g. Dhaka, Nazrul, the Padma; written with a capital letter), 2. Common Noun (name common to every person, place or thing of the same class, e.g. boy, river, city), 3. Collective Noun (name of a group or collection, e.g. team, jury, flock, committee), 4. Material Noun (name of a material or substance, e.g. gold, iron, water, rice). A Noun of Multitude is a collective noun that denotes the members of a group taken separately (e.g. the jury were divided). Abstract Noun: names a quality (wisdom, beauty, cleverness), a state (poverty, sorrow, happiness) or an action (inspection, burglary, decision). Examples: Honesty is the best policy. Laughter is good for health. Always speak the truth. Remember: no article is generally used before an abstract noun, except when a particular quality of a person is meant: Charity is a great virtue. / The charity of Haji Muhammad Mohsin is known to all.

chunk_text: Lesson-03: Countable and Uncountable Nouns. Nouns are divided by countability into 1. Countable Noun [C] and 2. Uncountable Noun [U]. 1. Countable Noun: nouns that can be counted. A singular countable noun takes the article a or an (a book, an apple) and its plural takes -s or -es (two boys, many boxes, some mangoes). A countable noun expressing one idea is Singular number, expressing more than one is Plural number. Examples: The girl bought two pencils, an exercise-book, a ruler and two ball-pens. 2. Uncountable Noun: nouns that cannot be counted; no a or an is used before them and they have no plural. Examples: The lady bought ten kgs of rice, one kg of sugar, two litres of oil and two pineapples (rice, sugar, oil are uncountable; lady, kg, litre, pineapples are countable). Measure words are used before uncountable nouns: a piece of (news), two cups of (tea), a sheet of (paper), a stick of (chalk), a grain of (sugar), two kilograms of (sugar), a lot of (money). Some nouns are countable in one sense and uncountable in another: hair (uncountable) / hairs (countable); chicken as food (uncountable) / chickens as birds (countable); brick as material (uncountable) / bricks (countable); bus as a means of transport (uncountable) / buses (countable).

chunk_text: Lesson-04: Functions of Noun. A noun works in a sentence in six ways: 1. As the subject: Structure Subject (Noun) + verb + extension. Examples: Sheema is a good girl. The cow gives us milk. 2. As the object of a transitive verb: I eat a mango. He sees a bird. 3. As the complement of a linking or incomplete verb: Structure Subject + linking/incomplete verb + complement. Example: The girl is a dancer. 4. As the indirect object: Structure Subject + Verb + Indirect object + Direct object. Examples: Sheena gave me a book. She sent her friend a telex. 5. As the object of a preposition: Structure Preposition + Noun. Example: The cat is fond of milk. 6. As a noun in apposition: Mr. Rahman, a university teacher, teaches his students sincerely. Noun in apposition: when a noun or noun phrase placed after a subject noun or noun phrase points to that noun and is not the main part of the sentence, it is called a noun in apposition.

chunk_text: Lesson-05: Formation of Noun. From Adjective: 1. adjectives ending in ant or ent form nouns with -ce or -cy (absent - absence, obedient - obedience, patient - patience, assistant - assistance, decent - decency, urgent - urgency); 2. adjectives ending in ate or et form nouns with -cy (accurate - accuracy, private - privacy, secret - secrecy); 3. adjectives ending in ar or or form nouns with -ity (popular - popularity, similar - similarity, senior - seniority); 4. adjectives ending in le, al, il, ite form nouns with -ty or -ity (able - ability, noble - nobility, cruel - cruelty, brutal - brutality, casual - casualty, local - locality); 5. adjectives ending in ain, ane form nouns with -ty or -ity (certain - certainty, humane - humanity); 6. adjectives form nouns with -ness, -hood, -dom, -th (free - freedom, deep - deepness, false - falsehood, happy - happiness, kind - kindness, large - largeness). From Verb: 1. verbs ending in d form nouns with -tion or -sion (attend - attention, contend - contention, extend - extension, pretend - pretension); 2. verbs ending in de form nouns with -sion/-tion (accede - accession, allude - allusion, concede - concession, decide - decision, provide - provision, upgrade - upgradation); 3. verbs ending in se/ze form nouns with -sation (civilize - civilization, utilise - utilisation, realise - realisation, visualise - visualisation); 4. verbs ending in 'ume' form nouns with -ption (assume - assumption, consume - consumption, resume - resumption, presume - presumption); 5. verbs ending in tain form nouns with -tenance or -tention (detain - detention, retain - retention, maintain - maintenance, sustain - sustenance); 6. verbs ending in 'fy' form nouns with -fication or -faction (amplify - amplification, beautify - beautification, purify - purification, satisfy - satisfaction, notify - notification, gratify - gratification, verify - verification); 7. verbs ending in t/te form nouns with -tion/-tation (allocate - allocation, transport - transportation, locate - location); 8. verbs ending in ve/se/y form nouns with -al or -ial (approve - approval, propose - proposal, deny - denial, try - trial).

chunk_text: Lesson-06: Number. A countable noun has two forms: Singular and Plural. Singular form names one person, thing or idea (a man, a cat, a book); Plural form names two or more (men, books, pens, dogs, cows). Formation of Plural Number: 1. generally add -s (bird - birds, dog - dogs, book - books, cat - cats, girl - girls, hand - hands); 2. nouns ending in s, ss, sh, ch, z or x take -es (bus - buses, box - boxes, class - classes, dish - dishes, ass - asses, bench - benches, bush - bushes, match - matches, gas - gases; but if 'ch' is pronounced 'k', add only -s: stomach - stomachs, monarch - monarchs); 3. nouns ending in consonant + y change y to -ies (army - armies, lady - ladies, duty - duties, fly - flies, city - cities, spy - spies, baby - babies, pony - ponies; proper nouns ending in y take only -s: Henry - Henrys, Mary - Marys, Dolly - Dollys, Germany - Germanys; vowel + y takes only -s: boy - boys, key - keys, toy - toys, monkey - monkeys, day - days, play - plays; money - moneys or monies); 4. nouns ending in f or fe change f/fe to -ves (calf - calves, self - selves, leaf - leaves, wolf - wolves, wife - wives, knife - knives, thief - thieves, loaf - loaves, half - halves, shelf - shelves, life - lives; but ief, iff, oof, ulf take only -s: chief - chiefs, roof - roofs, cliff - cliffs, proof - proofs, grief - griefs, safe - safes, hoof - hoofs); 5. nouns ending in -o with a consonant before take -es (buffalo - buffaloes, echo - echoes, mango - mangoes, potato - potatoes, cargo - cargoes, hero - heroes, negro - negroes, volcano - volcanoes; vowel before -o takes only -s: bamboo - bamboos, cuckoo - cuckoos; but photo - photos, radio - radios, piano - pianos take only -s; some take both: banjo - banjos/banjoes, cargo - cargos/cargoes, halo - halos/haloes); 6. vowel change (man - men, foot - feet, mouse - mice, woman - women, goose - geese, louse - lice, tooth - teeth; German - Germans, not Germen); 7. add -en or -ren (ox - oxen, child - children); 8. compound nouns pluralize the main word (brother-in-law - brothers-in-law, passer-by - passers-by, man-servant - men-servants, step-brother - step-brothers, maid-servant - maid-servants, woman-servant - women-servants); 9. nouns ending in -ful take -s (armful - armfuls, cupful - cupfuls, mouthful - mouthfuls, spoonful - spoonfuls); 10. some compound nouns take -s at the end (book-shelf - book-shelves, book-case - book-cases, major-general - major-generals, poet-laureate - poet-laureates, forget-me-not - forget-me-nots, merry-go-round - merry-go-rounds); 11. some nouns have two plurals with different meanings (brother - brothers/brethren, cloth - cloths/clothes, beef - beefs/beeves, shot - shot/shots, dice - dices/dice, index - indexes/indices, penny - pennies/pence, fish - fishes/fish, sail - sail/sails, genius - genii/geniuses); 12. some nouns have two meanings in the singular and one in the plural (horse, word, foot, people, force, practice, light, issue, abuse); 13. some have one meaning in the singular and two in the plural (colour, spectacle, arm, effect, premise, quarter); 14. some have two meanings in the singular and three in the plural (letter, ground); 15. some have different meanings in singular and plural (advice - advices, sand - sands, iron - irons, corn - corns, good - goods, return - returns, air - airs, compass - compasses, content - contents); 16. nouns used only in the singular (furniture, scenery, information, poetry, machinery, expenditure, issue, bread); 17. nouns singular in form but plural in meaning, taking a plural verb (aristocracy, gentry, nobility, peasantry, cattle, poultry, majority, tenantry, perfumery, artillery, vermin, people, public, mankind, clergy, government); 18. nouns plural in form but singular in meaning, taking a singular verb (Mathematics, Physics, Politics, Economics, news, ethics, optics, innings, wages, gallows, athletics); Greek-origin subjects used as a subject name take a singular verb (Physics is my favourite subject) but as a special quality take a plural verb (His politics are not practical); 19. nouns always plural, taking a plural verb (alms, amends, mumps, measles, scissors, trousers, spectacles, environs, belongings, savings, earnings, surroundings, Aborigines, ashes, entrails, fetters, vitals); amends, mumps, measles, alms, tidings are also used in the singular; 20. nouns with the same singular and plural (deer, sheep, cannon, gross, pice, Apparatus, swine, species, innings, corps, salmon); 21. after a definite numeral adjective, dozen, brace, fathom, yoke, score, pair, hundred, thousand, head have no plural (two hundred taka, two pair of socks; but hundreds of people, thousands of dollars); 22. all fractions except half are plural (Two thirds of the work have been done); 23. 'More than one' is treated as singular (More than one boy was present; but More than two boys were present); 24. some pronouns change like nouns (I - We, Mine - Ours, You - You, This - These, Him - Them, My - Our, Me - Us, He/she/it - They, That - Those). Miscellaneous: Mister/Mr. - Messrs/Misters, Mrs./Madame - Mesdames, Mr. Zaman - Messers Zaman/Mr. Zamans, Mrs. Zaman - Mrs. Zamans, Miss Ruksana - Miss Ruksanas, Master Zaman - Master Zamans. Foreign Plural: Axis - Axes, Analysis - Analyses, Alumnus - Alumni, Appendix - Appendices, Criterion - Criteria, Datum - Data, Erratum - Errata, Focus - Foci, Formula - Formulae/Formulas, Genus - Genera, Hypothesis - Hypotheses, Hippopotamus - Hippopotamuses/Hippopotami, Locus - Loci/Locuses, Medium - Media, Basis - Bases, Crisis - Crises, Cherub - Cherubim/Cherubs, Bandit - Banditti/Bandits, Phenomenon - Phenomena, Parenthesis - Parentheses, Oasis - Oases, Referendum - Referenda, Radius - Radii/Radiuses, Seraph - Seraphim, Syllabus - Syllabi/Syllabuses, Thesis - Theses, Terminus - Termini/Terminuses, Vertex - Vertices.

chunk_text: Lesson-07: Gender. 'Gender' means sex or kind; its main work is to show male and female. A noun or pronoun that shows male, female, both male and female, or neither (lifeless things) has Gender. Classification of Gender: 1. Masculine Gender (male: Boy, Brother, Bull, Father, Husband), 2. Feminine Gender (female: Girl, Sister, Cow, Mother, Wife), 3. Common Gender (male or female: Friend, Person, Student, Teacher, Doctor, child), 4. Neuter Gender (lifeless things: Table, Chair, Bench, Gold, Flower, River, Rice). Remember: Masculine and Feminine can also be used as adjectives to describe a manly or womanly look (The girl standing in the room has masculine looks) - here they show quality, not gender. Forming Feminine from Masculine, generally in three ways: i. by a different word (boy - girl, bull - cow, cock - hen, dog - bitch, drake - duck, father - mother, fox - vixen, gander - goose, gentleman - lady, brother - sister, bridegroom - bride, buck - doe, bachelor - maid/spinster, bullock - heifer, boar - sow, horse - mare, husband - wife, man - woman, monk - nun, nephew - niece, ram - ewe, sir - madam, son - daughter, uncle - aunt, hero - heroine, lord - lady, king - queen, male - female, lad - lass, colt - filly, drone - bee, earl - countess, sloven - slut, tailor - seamstress, sheep - ewe, stag - hind, hart - roe, swain - nymph, widower - widow, wizard - witch); ii. by adding -ess to the masculine without change (author - authoress, giant - giantess, god - goddess, baron - baroness, host - hostess, heir - heiress, Jew - Jewess, lion - lioness, poet - poetess, prince - princess, patron - patroness, priest - priestess, shepherd - shepherdess, steward - stewardess); iii. by dropping the vowel of the last syllable and adding -ess (actor - actress, conductor - conductress, benefactor - benefactress, director - directress, doctor - doctress, enchanter - enchantress, hunter - huntress, inspector - inspectress, instructor - instructress, tiger - tigress, negro - negress, traitor - traitress, waiter - waitress, porter - portress). Note: very few (noun + ess) feminine forms exist in English; professional words are generally treated as Common Gender, so Authoress, poetess, directress, inspectress are not generally used: She is the director of this institute (not directress). She is an inspector of police (not inspectress). 4. Compound nouns change the masculine part to feminine - first part (boy-friend - girl-friend, bull-calf - cow-calf, buck-rabbit - doe-rabbit, brother-in-law - sister-in-law, son-in-law - daughter-in-law, he-goat - she-goat, billy-goat - nanny-goat, cock-sparrow - hen-sparrow, father-in-law - mother-in-law, man-servant - maid-servant) or second part (milkman - milkwoman, schoolmaster - schoolmistress, god-father - god-mother, pea-cock - pea-hen, grandfather - grandmother, fisherman - fisherwoman, gentleman - gentlewoman, washerman - washerwoman, landlord - landlady, step-brother - step-sister, foster-father - foster-mother). 6. Some irregular masculine and feminine pairs (bridegroom - bride, fox - vixen, hero - heroine, sultan - sultana). 7. Some irregular pairs (Duke - Duchess, Emperor - Empress, Governor - Governess, Mr. - Mrs., Master - Mistress, Abbot - Abotess). 8. Nouns and pronouns used as Common Gender: baby, cat, parent, we, cousin, friend, infant, student, fool, ruler, elephant, bird, I, you, orphan, pupil, spouse, citizen, monarch, sheep, fowl. 9. (a) In modern English, profession nouns ending in -man/-woman use -person and become Common Gender (businessman/businesswoman - businessperson, chairman/chairwoman - chairperson, newsman/newswoman - newsperson, salesman/saleswoman - salesperson, sportsman/sportswoman - sportsperson, spokesman/spokeswoman - spokesperson); (b) degree, title, qualification and decoration nouns are always Common Gender (BA, B.Sc, MA, M.com, LLB, Ph.D., D.Litt: He/She is an MA; He/She is Ph.D.; He/She is a B.Sc.); (c) caste, community, religion and nationality nouns are Common Gender (He/She is a Muslim/Hindu/Christian/Chinese); (d) nouns of strength, courage and chivalry, and sun, summer, thunder, winter are generally masculine; (e) nouns of beauty, grace, gentleness, sweetness, love and affection, and moon, earth, nature, hope, peace, ships, cars, railways, trains are generally feminine (The Titanic began her maiden voyage in 1912). Pronoun gender: He (masculine) - She (feminine); Him (masculine) - Her (feminine); His (masculine) - Her (feminine).

chunk_text: Lesson-08: The Case / Possessives. The relation of a noun or pronoun with other words in a sentence is called Case. Example: I gave her my book. 'I' does the work of the verb 'gave', so 'I' is in the Nominative Case. The work of 'gave' falls on 'book', so 'book' is in the Objective Case. 'my' shows the relation of possession with 'book', so 'my' is in the Possessive Case. Classification of Case: 1. Nominative case (subject: Raju plays cricket; asking 'who' or 'what' of the verb gives the Nominative case), 2. Objective case (object: Raju plays cricket - 'cricket' is the Objective case; asking 'what' or 'whom' of the verb gives it), 3. Vocative Case or Nominative of Address (addressing a noun: Meena, can you give me a pen? - 'Meena' is in the Vocative case), 4. Possessive case (ownership or relation: It is Raju's pen - 'Raju' with ('s) is in the Possessive case; generally formed by adding apostrophe + s ('s)). Formation of Possessive Case: the relation is shown in three ways - 's (Rafsan's school), s' (boys' school), of (founder of the school). Formation of Possessives: 1. living singular nouns take 's (Ankon's bicycle, Cat's paw, People's right to know, bird's nest; Manha's eyes are beautiful; That is Rubayet's diary); when several s-sounds come together, use only the apostrophe (I did that for conscience' sake; The Christians follow Jesus' teachings; We helped them promised not deprive him justice for justice' sake); 2. proper nouns ending in s take 's or only ' (Yeats's poems or Yeats' poems; Keats's poetry or Keats' poetry); 3. plural nouns ending in s take only ' (doctors' chamber, girls' school, boys' hostel, ladies' bag; She reads in a girls' school; Dogs' tails are hard to be straightened; Kawsar is in the officers' club; Students' representatives met the Headmaster; Lawyers' Association protested against the administrative initiative); 4. irregular plural nouns (no s) take 's (Children's Park, Women's Club; These are children's books; This is a men's club); 5. lifeless things use 'of' (The books of the publication, the auditorium of our school, the hands of a clock; The leg of the table is broken - not 'Table leg'); but personified lifeless things take 's (At the country's call, we fought together; Can you tell me the names of some Arab's heroes?; Everyone of us should abide by nature's laws; She was at death's door; God saved her from the premature death); 6. time, place, distance and weight take 's (His house is only at a stone's throw from mine; It is a day's journey from here to Dhaka; I need a week's leave to visit my native village; The product may be of a kilo's weight); 7. living nouns can also take 'of' before them (The trunk of the elephant is strong; The paw of the tiger is very powerful; The strength of the enemy is too much); 8. some phrases use 's (to heart's content, for truth's sake, for heaven's sake, for God's sake; For God's sake, tell me the truth; The man ate food to his heart's content); 9. rank or title takes 's (the PM's secretary, the MP's schedule, the SP's protocol); 10. compound nouns take 's on the last word (his father-in-law's car, the Government of Bangladesh's Act); 11. 's shows rank, dignity or title (the sun's rays, the moon's orbit, duty's call, truth's omnipotence; He couldn't deny his duty's call); 12. for joint possession only the second noun takes 's (Mr. Khan and Mrs. Khan's family), for separate possession both take 's (Mr. Zaman's and Mr. Huq's families); 13. to mean one of many, use apostrophe + s (A book of Jewel's - Jewel has many books, this is one of them; but A book of Jewel - one book of Jewel). Possessive of Pronoun and Adjective: the underlined words in the passage (Uncle Feroz drives our school bus; I reach my school in time; Nister, my friend, also goes with me; He is a brilliant student of our class; Today Nister's pencil box has been lost; So he has not completed his homework; As Nister is a friend of mine, I have lent him my pencil; Our class teacher is very serious about our homework) answer 'Whose?' - such words are called possessives. Person and case table: 1st person singular I - me - my/mine; plural we - us - our/ours; 2nd person singular/plural you - you - your/yours; 3rd person singular he/she/it - him/her/it - his/her/hers/its; plural they - them - their/theirs. Possessive Adjective vs Possessive Pronoun: My - Mine, His/her - His/hers, Our - Ours, Your - Yours, Its - (none), Their - Theirs. They have the same meaning but different use and position: a Possessive Adjective is used before a noun (This is my bicycle), a Possessive Pronoun is used after a verb or as subject (This bicycle is mine; This house is ours; Ours is a developing country). No apostrophe is used in Possessive Adjectives and Pronouns. Note the difference between 'its' (possessive) and 'it's' (It is). 'One' is a Possessive Pronoun; 'One's' is a Possessive Adjective.

chunk_text: Lesson-01 An Introduction to Pronoun (printed pp. 78-79). Everybody likes to hear varied words; the repeated use of the same noun sounds irritating, so the pronoun was added to English. 'Pro' means 'in place of', 'in favour of' or 'acting as', so pronouns sit in place of nouns or work like nouns. Examples: 'The last time I met Meena, I gave her a red rose' (her for Meena); 'Raju is impossible. I wish he would move away' (he for Raju). Without pronouns the repetition of the noun spoils the music of the sentences. Antecedent: a pronoun has no identity of its own; it takes its meaning from the word it stands for, and that word is the pronoun's antecedent (purbo-borti/anugami). Example: 'Shahed picked up his blazer and admired its buttons' - 'Shahed' is the antecedent of 'his' and 'blazer' is the antecedent of 'its'. Since pronouns are used in place of nouns, they can play the roles of nouns.

chunk_text: Lesson-02 Classification of Pronoun (printed pp. 79-84). Pronouns are divided into eight kinds by their use in a sentence: 1. Personal Pronoun, 2. Demonstrative Pronoun, 3. Relative Pronoun, 4. Interrogative Pronoun, 5. Indefinite Pronoun, 6. Distributive Pronoun, 7. Reflexive Pronoun, 8. Reciprocal Pronoun. Personal Pronoun: a pronoun that sits in place of a person or the name of a thing; three persons - First Person (I, we, me, us, my, our), Second Person (you, your, thou, thy, thee), Third Person (he, she, they, him, her, them, their, it, its). Forms vary by number, gender and case: First Person - Nominative I/We, Objective Me/Us, Possessive My, mine/Our, ours; Second Person - You/You, Your, Yours; Third Person - He/She/It/They, Him/Her/It/Them, His/Her/Its/Their, Theirs. Remember: my, our, his, your, her, their before a noun are Possessive Adjectives; mine, thine, hers, ours, theirs after a finite verb with no noun after them are Possessive Pronouns; 'his' can be both; 'its' is only a Possessive Adjective. Impersonal 'it': for a lifeless thing, a lower animal, a small child, referring to a previous thing, as a preparatory subject before 'to be', for emphasis before a noun or pronoun, as the subject of an impersonal verb (It rains), for weather or time, and for a collective noun. Uses: a personal pronoun agrees in number, person and gender with its noun; a collective noun takes a singular (neuter) pronoun and a noun of multitude a plural pronoun; two or more nouns joined by 'and' take a plural pronoun, but if each, every or no comes before them the pronoun is singular. Demonstrative Pronoun: this, these, that, those point to a person or thing; 'this/these' for near, 'that/those' for far; 'this' for the first of two nouns and 'that' for the second; 'that of/those of' in comparisons; 'such' and 'the same' also point back; when used before a noun they are Demonstrative Adjectives. Interrogative Pronoun: only five - who, whom, whose, what, which; 'who' only for persons, 'what' for things and professions, 'which' for persons and things with a choice among many, 'whom' as the object of a verb (modern English often uses 'who' as object), 'whose' for ownership or relation. Relative Pronoun: a pronoun that stands for a noun mentioned before, points to it, and joins two sentences like a conjunction (also called a conjunction pronoun). Indefinite Pronoun: one, some, any, somebody, others, everybody - they point to no definite person or thing; 'one' as subject takes 'one's' (not his/him), but after every/no or a phrase 'he, his, him' is used; 'one of' takes a plural noun but a singular verb; 'others' is used only for persons. Distributive Pronoun: each, either, neither, none - each refers to every one of two or more separately; either to any one of two; neither is the negative of either. Reflexive Pronoun: a personal pronoun + self/selves used as the object and referring back to the subject (myself, yourself, himself, herself, oneself, ourselves, yourselves, themselves); formed from a possessive adjective + -self or an object pronoun + -self. Emphatic Pronoun: the same -self form sitting after a noun or pronoun to lay stress on it ('I myself did it'), unlike the reflexive which is always used as object. Reciprocal Pronoun: each other and one another show a mutual relation; 'each other' for two persons, 'one another' for more than two.

chunk_text: Lesson-03 How to Identify Pronoun (printed p. 87). A table for recognising the kinds of pronoun: Personal Pronoun - sits in place of a person (I, we, you, he, she, it, they); Demonstrative Pronoun - points to a noun in a special way (this, that, these, those); Relative Pronoun - makes a relation between two sentences and sits inside the sentence (who, whose, which, whom, that); Interrogative Pronoun - used to ask a question, sits at the start of the sentence (who, whose, whom, which, what); Indefinite Pronoun - points to no definite person or thing (any, one, anyone, some, someone, anybody, somebody, nobody, many, everyone, all); Distributive Pronoun - points to each one of several persons or things of the same kind separately (each, every, either, neither); Reflexive Pronoun - formed by adding self or selves, subject and object being the same person (myself, ourselves, yourself, yourselves, himself, herself, themselves); Reciprocal Pronoun - shows a mutual relation among several persons or things (each other and one another).

chunk_text: Lesson-04 Person (printed pp. 87-88). In a sentence the words I, you, he, she, they, my, our are sometimes used as subject and sometimes as object to point to a noun or pronoun; these words are Person. The use of the verb depends on the person used in the sentence: I play, You play, He/She plays; I go, You go, He/She goes. Definition: the different subjects on which a verb depends in different sentences to perform its work are called Person. In English Person is of three kinds: 1. First Person (uttom purush), 2. Second Person (moddhyom purush), 3. Third Person (nam purush). Table: 1st person - I (singular), We (plural); 2nd person - You, You; 3rd person - He, She, It, They. 1. First Person: the person through which the speaker expresses himself or themselves - I, we, me, us, our, my, mine, ours (I go; We go; This is our home). 2. Second Person: the person to whom something is said in a sentence - You, your, thou, thee (You go; This is your book). 3. Third Person: the person about whom something is said - He, she, her, his, they, it, Rony, Sunny, Meena (He goes; She goes; Roney goes; They go). The four personal pronouns used as subject have three more forms: i. Object, ii. Possessive and iii. Double possessive. Table: 1st person singular - Subject I, Object Me, Possessive/Double possessive My-Mine; 1st person plural - We, Us, Our-Ours; 2nd person singular - You, You, Your-Yours; 2nd person plural - You, You, Your-Yours; 3rd person singular - He, Him, His; She, Her, Her-Hers; It, It, Its; 3rd person plural - They, Them, Their-Theirs.

chunk_text: Lesson-01: An Introduction to Interjection. Read the sentences and notice the words in bold: Wow, so big a cake! Alas! They have lost the game. Oops, I have got hurt! Omg, how could you do that! Oh! What a nice flower. The words in bold express sudden joy, sorrow, emotion, hatred, enthusiasm, wonder and similar sudden feelings; such words that express a sudden emotion are Interjections. Definition: the word used in a sentence to express the emotion of the mind is called an Interjection. In fact, even if a word or sound thrown into a sentence has no relation with the other words of the sentence, if it expresses the emotion of the mind it is called an Interjection. Remember: a Note of Exclamation (!) must sit after an Interjection. Interjection Phrase: when a phrase or group of words is used like an Interjection to express a sudden emotion or feeling, it is called an Interjection Phrase. Examples: For God's sake! For shame! Well done! Good gracious! Good heaven! Example: For God's sake, help me! For shame! How have you done it? Remember: an Interjection has no role in forming a sentence; it has no relation with the other Parts of Speech in the sentence. But when a Preposition or the conjunction 'that' is used after an Interjection, the Interjection works as a part of the sentence; then some part of the sentence or the whole sentence works as an Interjection. Example: Oh that I could be a poet! Other Parts of Speech also sometimes express emotion or feeling like an Interjection: 1. Noun: To live in such a big house! 2. Pronoun: What a girl! 3. Adjective: Fine! Wonderful! Excellent! 4. Verb: Had I the wings of a dove! 5. Adverb: How nice! 6. Conjunction: If I were the Prime Minister of Bangladesh!

chunk_text: Lesson-01: An Introduction to Suffix & Prefix. Suffix: a letter or a group of letters which is added to the end of a word and changes the meaning of the word or forms a new word. Look at the two sentences: Lots of people believe that God exists. Lots of people believe in the existence of God. Here 'exist' is a Verb and 'existence' is a Noun; the word 'existence' has two parts: 'exist' and '-ence'. In the language of Grammar 'exist' is the 'root word' and '-ence' is the 'suffix'; this Suffix joined to the end of the root word 'exist' has formed a noun word 'existence', although the '-ence' part has no separate meaning of its own. In this way, by adding Suffixes we can also form Verb, Adjective and Adverb. Examples: The system is being modernized (= made modern). I grew up in an industrial town (= a town where there are a lot of industries). The man is behaving strangely (= in a strange way). Prefix: a letter or a group of letters which is added to the beginning of a word and changes its meaning or forms a new word. Look at the two sentences: They're going to play the match on Wednesday. They're going to replay the match on Wednesday. Here 'play' is a root word and a Verb, and at its beginning 're-' is added to form another Verb 'replay'; this 're-' is a 'prefix'. A Prefix sits at the beginning of a word and changes its meaning; in the example above 'replay' means to play again. pre- = before, fix = add. Prefixes are letters added at the beginning of a word. Like Suffixes, Prefixes also form new meaningful words such as Noun, Adjective. There are different kinds of Prefixes, e.g. anti-, multi-, under-, dis-, non- etc. Points to Ponder Over: in Bangla a Prefix is called 'uposorgo' and a Suffix is called 'protyoy'. Generally, adding a Prefix changes the meaning of a word, and adding a Suffix changes the part of speech of a word.

chunk_text: Lesson-03: Formation of Words using Prefixes. List of Prefixes: each Prefix forms different Parts of Speech according to its general meaning. a- (in, on, up, from, without): away, ashore; ab- (bad, off away from): abuse, abnormal; al- (all): almighty, altogether; ante- (before, beside): antecedent, antemeridien (am); anti- (against): anti-aircraft, antibody, antibiotic, antidote; arch- (chief): arch-bishop, archfiend; auto- (self): autobiography, autocracy, automatic; be- (by): befriend, beside, belittle; bi- (two/twice): bicycle, bilingual, bilateral, bisect; by- (nearvia past): by-election, by-gone, by-product; co- (with): co-education, cooperate, co-curricular, co-education; counter- (against): counter-attack, counter part; de- (reversal): defame, defrost, deforestation, demerit, decompose; dis- (not): disadvantage, disagree, disappear, discourage, discredit; em- (to put into): embody, empower; en- (to put into, to make into): enable, enchant, enhance, enlarge, ensure; ex- (former): exanimate, ex-gratia, ex-wife, exclude, exhale; extra- (beyond): extracurricular, extraordinary; fore- (before): forecast, foretell; il- (not without): illegal, illegible, illiterate; im- (not): immortal, import, impend, impiety, impossible; in- (not): inability, inborn, injustice, inactive, independent, insufficient; inter- (between, amongst): interchange, interview, international; ir- (not): irregular, irrespective; mal- (bad): malnutrition, malpractice; mis- (bad, wrong): misbehave, misfire, mischief; mono- (single): monosyllable, monologue; multi- (many, much): multimillionaire, multinational, multistoreyed; non- (not): nonsense, nonviolence; out- (away, better): outbreak, outlet, outlook; over- (upper, excessive): overcast, overdose, overnight; pan- (all): pan-Islam, pantheism; post- (after): postgraduate, post-modern, postmeridian (pm), postwar; chunk_text: Primary Discussion on Idioms & Phrases. A Phrase or Idiom generally works as a single Parts of speech. chunk_text: Lesson-01: What are Modals? Modals or Modal auxiliaries are a special kind of auxiliary verb. Joined with a main (principal) verb they express the mood of the sentence: permission, possibility, certainty, necessity, ability, intention, opinion, advice, command, determination and so on. The auxiliary verb used to show the mood of an action is called a Modal Auxiliary Verb. Note: after a modal auxiliary the verb is in present (base) form, no -s or -es is added, and there is no '+ ing' form.

chunk_text: Lesson-03: Uses of Modal Auxiliaries. May/Might: 1. Permission (May I come in, Sir? You may come in; May I help you? He may stay here). 2. Possibility (She may come tomorrow; Tareq may get GPA-5; That might be our car; Might shows more uncertainty than May and is used in past conditional sentences: If I requested her, she might do the work). 3. Purpose (She studies hard so that she may do good in her exam; He tried/ practised hard so that he might get selected in the final squad). 4. Wishes/hopes (May Allah bless you; May Bangladesh win the match). 5. Supposition (They may be playing now; He might have gone). 6. Knowing information (I asked who he might be). Can: 1. Permission (Can I go to play? You can take my book; Can I take your pen? She can buy the dress). 2. Suggestion (I can give you a new book if you want). 3. Ability (He can swim well). 4. Perception verbs (I can see a bird; I can smell a flower; I can hear a sweet music). 5. Request (Can you help me?). 6. (a) General Possibility (You can ride bicycle safely in this road); (b) Occasional Possibility (A dog can be dangerous when it becomes mad). 7. Acquired knowledge/skill (I can drive a car; She can speak Japanese). Can has two negative forms: full 'cannot' (He cannot do this work) and contraction "can't" (Sorry, I can't help you). Could: 1. Permission (Could I write with your pen? Yes, you could). 2. Polite request (Could you help me in cooking food?). 3. Suggestion (You could discuss the problem with your parents). 4. Past ability (When I was in Dhaka, I could easily visit the zoo). 5. Result (He was so angry that he could not talk). 6. Present meaning in a conditional (Could he get another chance, if he missed this one). 7. Ability or opportunity in the past not used (I could have got GPA-5). Could also has two negative forms (He could not recognize me; Couldn't you stay here tonight?). Shall: generally used with First Person for future (I shall go there; We shall come here), but with 2nd and 3rd person singular to express a statement strongly (You shall have some nice toys; Jinnah said, 'Urdu alone shall be the state language of Pakistan'); negative shall not or shan't (I shall be very happy if you help me, shan't I? They shall not work here). Should: 1. Propriety/advice (We should love our country; You should read attentively). 2. Apprehension (He walks slowly lest he should stumble). 3. Supposition (He should have reached Dhaka by this time; It should be raining now). 4. Something that ought to have been done in the past (He could not win the game; He should have played tactfully). 5. Something that should be going on at present but is not (You should be studying now). 6. Something that should have been done in the past but was not (He should have apologized to her). 7. Purpose (The Caliph went out in disguise so that no one should recognize him). 8. Condition, possibility, expectation (If it should rain, they will not come; In case you should need something, please call me). Negative: should not or shouldn't (You should not run in the sun; I should correct my mistake, shouldn't I?). Will: 1. Future tense with Second and Third Person (You will suffer in the long run; He will play with us). 2. Firm determination or strong will with First Person (I will achieve it at any cost; I will watch the movie). 3. Request and supposition (Will you wait for me? I am sure he will help me). 4. Conditional sentence with If + Present Tense (If you work hard, you will be successful in life). Would: like Could, many uses: 1. Polite request (Would you write a letter for me please?). 2. Offer/invitation (Would you mind taking some food?). 3. Preference (I would like to have a glass of milk). 4. Determination (I would rather die than take bribe). 5. In the later part of an If + Past Indefinite sentence (If you watched the film, you would enjoy it). 6. If the If-clause is Past Perfect, the later part takes would have (If I had received her e-mail, I would have tried to reply). 7. Purpose (He worked hard so that he would shine in life). 8. A regular habitual action in the past (Hemon would often return house late). 9. Invitation (Would you like to go for a walk?). Must: 1. (numbered 2 in the book) Used as a modal auxiliary in Present, Past and Future tense for Obligation, Advice, Certainty (We must love our country; You must take some rest; He must be a gentleman; You must have gone there - past certainty). 2. Speculation, Determination and Logical conclusion (The giant must be dead now; We must do what we think right; You must be tired after a long walk). 3. Past certainty takes must have (You must have heard the name of Bangabandhu Sheikh Mujibur Rahman). 4. Negative form 'Must not' or "Mustn't" (We must obey our parents, mustn't we? We must not dishonour our elders). Ought to: 1. Basically the same use as Should; it can replace should, but ought to is better to express something more strongly and clearly (You ought to obey this rule; Russel ought to study harder). 2. Firm possibility, desirability (They ought to win the match; Shezan ought to visit his village). 3. Not used in Negative and Interrogative sentences; use should instead (You shouldn't (not oughtn't) run in the sun; What should we do? (not What ought to)). Structure: (a) Should + simple form of a verb (not 'to'); (b) Ought to + simple form of a verb (We should learn English; We ought to learn English). Used To: to express a past irregular or regular habit, used only in Past Tense (I used to take coffee; now I take tea; Mother used to read the Quran every morning). Need: used both as Principal and as Auxiliary verb; as Principal Verb it takes 's' with Third Person Singular and may take an infinitive (He needs to go there); as a Modal it always gives a negative meaning, takes no 's' and drops infinitive 'to' (He need not do this work). Dare: like Need, both Principal and Modal Auxiliary; as Modal Auxiliary it is used only in Negative and Interrogative sentences, expressing courage to do something or anger towards another, with no 's' after Dare (Dare he do it? No, he dare not do it; How dare you insult me?); as Principal Verb it means Challenge or courage: Sub + dare + object + full infinitive (to) + verb present form (He dares to play the game; subject is Third Person Singular so 's' is added to Dare); Dare has two past forms: Dared and Durst. Have To: Obligation and Advice (I have to do that work; You have to learn computer to get a good job); Must and Have to are nearly the same: when one feels the need to do something oneself, must is used; when someone tells one to do something, have to is used. Going to: to express a future wish or certainty (I am going to watch a film; The lion is going to kill the deer). Had Better: meaning it is better to do something (You had better leave this place; He had better change his decision).

chunk_text: Lesson-01: What is Verb? A verb is a word or phrase that expresses an action, an event or a state (She teaches us English -> action; The accident happened at night -> event; He eats rice -> action; He goes to school -> state). Verbs in bold express action, event or state. The underlined 'be' verbs (is, am, are, was, were, are being, has got, is getting, has been, have been) express no action but a state or condition: be verbs have present forms am/is/are, past forms was/were, and perfect forms have/ has/ had + been. Definition: verbs are words or phrases that express actions or conditions.

chunk_text: Lesson-02: Classification of Verbs. Two main kinds. 1. Finite verb (সমাপিকা ক্রিয়া): a verb that ends the statement of a sentence, expresses complete meaning, and changes form with the subject's number and person (go -> goes -> went; play -> plays -> played; do -> does -> did; have -> has -> had; The boy puts on fine clothes; They prepared the document). 2. Non-finite verb (অসমাপিকা ক্রিয়া): a verb whose form never changes with the subject's number or person (to go, going, gone, to play, playing, to do, to be done, tired, swimming); infinitives, gerunds and participles are non-finite verbs, also called Verbals (He came to see me: came is finite, to see is non-finite). Finite verbs split into Principal (Main) verb and Auxiliary (Helping) verb; Principal verbs split into Transitive and Intransitive. 3. Principal verb: expresses its meaning independently (Kazal reads a book; They play football; Nasima sings a song; The farmers work in the field). 4. Auxiliary verb: helps the principal verb express full meaning (He is reading a book; They will play football); also called Helping verb and Operators. There are 24 auxiliary verbs, split into Primary and Modal: Primary - to be (am, is, are / was, were), to do (do, does / did), to have (have, has / had); Modal - shall/should, will/would, can/could, may/might, ought to, must, need, dare, used to (no past form). Use of Primary Auxiliaries: 'to be' forms continuous/progressive tense and passive voice (I am writing a letter; He was running in the sun; The sum is being done; The crops have been cut; The new moon will be seen today) and can also be a principal verb (Rahim is a doctor; They are farmers); 'to have' forms perfect tense, passive voice and nominative absolute (We have played cricket; You had done it; It has been raining for two days) and can also be a principal verb (I have an umbrella); 'to do' forms interrogative sentences (Do you play football? Does he eat an orange? Did they come here?) and negative sentences before not (I do not like to go there; He does not drink tea; They did not do it). Modals show the mood of the action; they never take -s, -ed or -en, the principal verb after a modal is only in base/present form (He can do the work alone; Rahim may not come here today; We must abide by the rules and regulation of school), and modals modify the main verb's meaning. 5. Transitive verb: the action needs someone or something besides the subject (the action passes from the agent to something else). 6. Intransitive verb: the action needs no one besides the subject (the action stops with the agent). Characteristics: a transitive verb has an object; an intransitive verb has no object; an intransitive verb has a complement. Object: what is got by asking 'what' or 'whom' to a transitive verb; an object may be a noun (The man killed a tiger), a pronoun (I saw him), an infinitive (He wants to leave the place), a gerund (Stop writing), a noun phrase (Do you know how to do it?) or a noun clause (I do not know who comes next). Some verbs are used both transitively and intransitively (see, read, write, sink, grow, fly, boil). Transitive with double object: ask, tell, offer, buy, give, take, bring, lend, leave, write, promise, send, show, make, pay, refuse (Father gave me a shirt; The Headmaster teaches us English). Direct object answers 'what' (thing), Indirect object answers 'whom' (person); the indirect object usually comes first (Mr. Jalil taught you English; He gave me a book; I sent him money; She told me the fact), but if it comes after the direct object it takes 'to' or 'for' (She gave a flower to each of the guests). Cognate object: an intransitive verb sometimes takes an object whose meaning is contained in the verb (He slept a sound sleep; They fought a brave fight; Roudiya is singing a sweet song; He ran a race; We prayed an earnest prayer). Reflexive object: a reflexive pronoun as object (He sat himself down; They enjoyed themselves; She killed herself; I fanned myself last night). Retained object: in passive voice one of two active objects stays (I gave him a pen -> He was given a pen by me; Hira teaches us English -> English is taught us by Hira). Objects to the verbs of perception (see, notice, watch, hear, smell) take a bare infinitive without 'to' (Can you hear somebody go down the stairs? I hear him give a talk on forged note; I watched her go).

chunk_text: Lesson-03: Some Other Verbs. 1. Factitive Verb: a transitive verb that, even with an object, cannot express complete meaning without an extra word, called Objective complement (We elected him chairman; You made me nervous); also called Transitive verb of incomplete predication. 2. Quasi-Passive Verb: a transitive verb in active voice that gives a passive meaning (Honey tastes sweet; Rice sells dear). 3. Impersonal verb: a verb whose subject is impersonal 'it' (It rains; It snows; It hails; It dews in winter); the verbs have no doer of the action and 'it' is meaningless. 4. Reflexive verb: a verb whose object is a reflexive pronoun (He killed himself; She fans herself); subject and object are the same person. 5. Group verb or Prepositional verb: an intransitive verb that takes a preposition as an inseparable part and is used like a transitive verb (I look after my parents; He came of a good family; Don't smile at the poor; Look up the word in the dictionary). 6. Causative verb: a verb used transitively so that the action is done not directly by the subject but by another at its instigation (Birds fly in the sky -> They fly kites; He walks slowly -> Mother walks her baby; Jute grows here -> We grow jute here). Some verbs have separate causative forms: see->show, eat->feed, know->inform, rise->raise, drink->drench, sit->set, learn->teach, lie->lay, fall->fell, remember->remind. Some verbs have no separate causative form and work as causative themselves (The child can walk -> Mother walks the child; She boils water -> Water boils). 7. Cognate Verb: an intransitive verb that takes a noun of the same kind as its object and is used transitively (He ran a race; They fought a fight). 8. Copulative Verb: an intransitive verb that cannot complete the sentence's meaning without another word, called Subjective complement (She looks beautiful; The man seems tired); also called Intransitive verb of incomplete predication.

chunk_text: Unit-10 Contraction. A Contraction is a word or phrase in which one or more letters are dropped and an apostrophe (') is put in their place to shorten the word or phrase. In spoken English or informal writing we often use shortened forms like I'm, you're, etc., called 'Contraction' or short form. Usually one 'Noun' or 'Pronoun' joins one 'verb', or a 'verb' joins 'not' (Kamal is = Kamal's; He has = He's; Has not = hasn't). Contraction makes the language easier and smoother to write or speak. Usually a contraction is made with an auxiliary verb; 'be' and 'have' also make contractions even when they are not auxiliary verbs. When making a contraction, an apostrophe (') must sit where the dropped letter was (he has = he's - the apostrophe sits where 'ha' was dropped). In formal writing contractions should not be used. Common forms: Contractions with I, you, he, she, it, we, and they: 'm = am (I'm); 're = are (you're, we're, they're); 's = is and has (he's, she's, it's); 've = have (I've, you've, we've, they've); 'll = will (I'll, you'll, he'll, she'll, it'll, we'll, they'll); 'd = had and would (I'd, you'd, he'd, she'd, it'd, we'd, they'd). Contractions with auxiliary verb and not: the contraction for not is n't: aren't = are not (we aren't, you aren't); couldn't = could not; hasn't = has not; isn't = is not (she isn't, it isn't); shan't = shall not; wasn't = was not; won't = will not; can't = cannot; didn't = did not (I didn't, they didn't); haven't = have not; mustn't = must not; shouldn't = should not; weren't = were not; wouldn't = would not. be + negative has two contracted forms: 'She is not' becomes She isn't or She's not; but 'I am not' has only one contracted form: I'm not ('I'm n't' or 'I am n't' is wrong); likewise 'They are not' becomes 'They aren't' or They're not. After a noun, isn't/ aren't is the more common contraction; after a pronoun, 's/ 're is more common (The cakes aren't ready yet; She's not a friend of mine).

chunk_text: Other contractions. Contractions are also made with nouns, names, here, there and now and question words; they are not considered proper in formal writing (My sister's got married = My sister has got married; John'll be very happy = John will be very happy; Here's the coffee = Here is the coffee; There's your watch = There is your watch; Now's your chance = Now is your chance; Where's the milk? = Where is the milk?; What's happened? = What has happened?). No more than one contraction may be used in a sentence: He's not free. Or, He isn't free (Correct); He'sn't free. (Incorrect). Affirmative contractions may not be used at the end of a clause: A: I think we're lost. (Correct); B: Yes, I think we are. (I think we're. is Incorrect). So at the end of a clause we generally use a Negative contraction, and in Tag questions we use contractions: A: You've contacted Jan, haven't you? B: No, I haven't. In questions, the contracted form of am not is aren't: I'm getting a pay rise, aren't I? (Correct); amn't I? (Wrong).

chunk_text: Lesson-01: What is Conjugation of Verbs. A verb has three forms: i. Present or base form; ii. Past form; iii. Past Participle form. Changing a verb from its Present or Base form to its Past and Past Participle forms is called Conjugation of Verb. By the manner of this change verbs are divided into two kinds: 1. Regular Verb or Weak Verb; 2. Irregular Verb or Strong Verb.
ocr_confidence_note: Visual read of 150dpi render by worker; text verified against the page image.

chunk_text: Lesson-02: What are Regular and Irregular Verbs? 1. Regular verb / Weak verb: verbs whose Past and Past Participle forms are made by adding -d, -ed or -t at the end, e.g. kill - killed - killed; like - liked - liked; cook - cooked - cooked. Features of Regular Verb or Weak Verb: i. -d or -ed is added at the end to make the Past and Past Participle (call - called - called). ii. If the Present form ends in -d, the 'd' becomes 't' when making the Past and Past Participle (lend - lent - lent). 2. Irregular verb / Strong verb: verbs whose Past and Past Participle forms are made by changing the inner vowel or by adding -n, -en or -ne at the end, e.g. break - broke - broken; see - saw - seen; write - wrote - written.

chunk_text: Lesson-03: A List of Regular or Weak Verbs. Rule 1: add 'ed' to the Present form of most verbs to make the Past and Past Participle (abolish - abolished; accept - accepted; adapt - adapted; add - added; aim - aimed; allow - allowed; alter - altered; appear - appeared; appoint - appointed; ask - asked; attack - attacked; attract - attracted; avail - availed; boil - boiled; borrow - borrowed; cheer - cheered; clean - cleaned; climb - climbed; delay - delayed; discuss - discussed; dream - dreamed/ dreamt; end - ended; fail - failed; fill - filled; fix - fixed; flow - flowed; hang (to hang on a gallows) - hanged; help - helped; jump - jumped; kill - killed; laugh - laughed; load - loaded; lock - locked; look - looked; mend - mended; obey - obeyed; own - owned; paint - painted; pass - passed; play - played; pull - pulled; punish - punished; push - pushed; rain - rained; reach - reached; rear - reared; sew - sewed; sow - sowed; stay - stayed; thank - thanked; wait - waited; walk - walked; wash - washed; work - worked). Rule 2: if the root verb ends in 'e', add only 'd' to make the Past and Past Participle (abuse - abused; advise - advised; agree - agreed; arrive - arrived; arrange - arranged; believe - believed; behave - behaved; charge - charged; close - closed; compare - compared; complete - completed; dare - dared; dance - danced; die - died; divide - divided; gaze - gazed; hate - hated; hope - hoped; live - lived; lie (to tell a lie) - lied; loose - loosed; love - loved; move - moved; place - placed; hear - heard; manage - managed; prepare - prepared; preserve - preserved; refuse - refused; receive - received; rescue - rescued; smile - smiled; tremble - trembled; expose - exposed; notice - noticed). Rule 3: change the spelling inside the verb and add 'd' to make the Past and Past Participle (flee - fled; have - had; sell - sold; tell - told). Rule 4: if a verb ends in one Consonant preceded by one Vowel, double the Consonant and add '-ed' (beg - begged; cancel - cancelled; drop - dropped; hop - hopped; emit - emitted; nod - nodded; pat - patted; plan - planned; refer - referred; rub - rubbed; stop - stopped; travel - travelled; quarrel - quarrelled; pen - penned; nip - nipped). Rule 5: if the root verb ends in 'y' preceded by a consonant, change 'y' to 'i' and then add 'ed/ d' (bury - buried; carry - carried; cry - cried; dry - dried; envy - envied; fry - fried; ferry - ferried; try - tried; hurry - hurried; marry - married; lay - laid; pay - paid; say - said). Exception: if 'y' is preceded by a vowel, add only 'ed' (annoy - annoyed; enjoy - enjoyed). Rule 6: some verbs change a little and add 't' at the end to make the Past and Past Participle (bend - bent; build - built; burn - burnt/ burned (Past participle burnt); buy - bought; catch - caught; deal - dealt; dream - dreamt; dwell - dwelt; feel - felt; keep - kept; kneel - knelt; learn - learned/ learnt; leave - left; lend - lent; lose - lost; mean - meant; seek - sought; send - sent; sleep - slept; smell - smelt; spell - spelt; sweep - swept; teach - taught; think - thought; weep - wept).

Rule 1: change the inner Vowel of the root verb to make the Past and Past Participle (abide - abode; arise - arose - arisen; awake - awoke - awaken; be (am, is, are) - was, were - been; bear (to carry) - bore - borne; bear (to give birth) - bore - born; become - became - become; begin - began - begun; behold - beheld; bid (to command) - bade - bidden/ bid; bite - bit - bitten/ bit; bind - bound; bleed - bled; breed - bred; blow - blew - blown; break - broke - broken; chide - chid - chidden/ chid; choose - chose - chosen; cling - clung; come - came - come; creep - crept; dig - dug; do - did - done; draw - drew - drawn; drink - drank - drunk; drive - drove - driven; eat - ate - eaten; fall - fell - fallen; feed - fed; fight - fought; find - found; fly - flew - flown; forbid - forbade - forbidden; spit - spat; forgive - forgave - forgiven; forget - forgot - forgotten; forsake - forsook - forsaken; freeze - froze - frozen; get - got - got/ gotten; give - gave - given; go - went - gone; grow - grew - grown; hang (to hang up) - hung; hide - hid - hidden/ hid; hold - held; know - knew - known; lie (to lie down) - lay - lain; make - made; meet - met; mistake - mistook - mistaken; ride - rode - ridden; ring - rang - rung; rise - rose - risen; see - saw - seen; sit - sat; sing - sang - sung; sink - sank - sunk; shrink - shrank - shrunk; spring - sprang - sprung; spin - spun; speak - spoke - spoken; shake - shook - shaken; shine - shone; shoot - shot - shot (the printed table gives 'slew/ slain' for shoot, which are the forms of 'slay'; the correct forms shot/ shot are used here); smite - smote; stand - stood; steal - stole - stolen; stick - stuck; strike - struck; strive - strove - striven; swear - swore - sworn; swim - swam - swum; take - took - taken; tear - tore - torn; throw - threw - thrown; tread - trod - trodden; wake - woke - waken; wear - wore - worn; weave - wove - woven; win - won; write - wrote - written; withhold - withheld; withdraw - withdrew - withdrawn). chunk_text: Lesson-01: What is Subject-Verb Agreement? There is a close relation between a Subject and a Verb. The Verb is used according to the nature of the Subject. Generally if the Subject is Singular the Verb will be Singular; again if the Subject is Plural the Verb will be Plural. Besides this there are some different rules for certain differences of the Subject. This is Subject-Verb Agreement.
ocr_confidence_note: Visual read of 150dpi render by worker; text verified against the page image.

chunk_text: Lesson-02: Rules on Subject-Verb Agreement. 1. If the Subject of a sentence is 'plural' the verb will be 'plural'; if the Subject is 'singular' the verb will be 'singular' (The boys are swimming in the pond; He is running; Kamal enjoys the party; Many students are there). 2. If more than one Singular subject is joined by 'and' and they mean separate persons or things, the Verb will be plural; but if they mean the same person or thing the Verb will be 'Singular' (Rony and Jony are two friends - Plural; The Principal and Secretary of the college is coming - Singular; The Principal and the Secretary of the college are coming - Plural). Note: if each Subject joined by 'And', i.e. each Noun, has 'the' before it, they mean different persons or things. 3. If more than one singular subject joined by 'And' means one person, thing or a combined idea, the Verb takes the Singular form (Slow and steady wins the race; Bread and Butter is my favourite breakfast). 4. If each, any, everyone, everybody, everything, anybody, anyone, none of (the), every, no, more than one, each of (the), one of (the), nobody, no one, nothing, anything, somebody, someone, either of (the), neither of (the) etc. is used as subject in a sentence, the verb will be singular (Each boy and girl has got a prize; None of them knows the matter; One of them is going there; Neither of the two boys is present). 5. If two Subjects are joined by as well as, with, along with, in addition to, including, together with, accompanied by etc., the verb sits according to the first subject (Meena as well as her friends sings well; The teachers along with their students are busy). 6. In a sentence joined by Either .... or, or Neither .... or, or or/ nor, the verb sits according to the Subject after or or nor: if the Subject after or/ nor is singular the Verb is singular, and if the subject is plural the verb is plural (Either Raju or his friend is present; Neither he nor his brothers are present). 7. To mean all of one class, if 'the' sits before an adjective the verb is plural; but to mean all of one class, if 'the' sits before a noun the verb is singular (The rich are not always happy - Plural; The cow is a useful animal - Singular). 8. Even if the Subject looks plural, if it means a definite amount, length or distance the verb will be singular (Fifty kilometres is a long distance; Sixty cents of it is in pennies). Note: if it means a number the Verb is plural (Three-fourths of the crowd are male). 9. aristocracy, people, public, peasantry, cattle, mankind, poultry etc. nouns look singular but a plural verb sits after them (People are gossiping in the field; The peasantry in Bangladesh are poor). 10. In a sentence joined by Introductory 'there', the Verb sits according to the following Subject/ noun/ pronoun: if the Subject/ noun after the Verb is singular the verb is singular; if the Subject/ noun is plural the verb is plural (There is a playground in front of our college; There are two high schools in our area). 11. In a sentence with many a/ an the Singular form of the verb sits; but after Many the Subject is plural (Many a man ruins his career through laziness; Many an honest man comes to meet you almost everyday). 12. If a Collective Noun is used as a single unit it is taken as singular and a singular verb is used after it (Our class has won the competition; The flock of sheep is in the field). But if the members of this noun do not work together and hold different opinions, it is plural and a plural verb is used after it (The jury were arguing among themselves; The committee are divided in their opinions). 13. Some words look plural but mean singular; they take a singular verb (Physics is a difficult subject; Measles has weakened him). Again some words are always plural and take a plural verb (His wages are very high; My spectacles are broken). Again some nouns look singular but mean plural; they take a plural verb (People are waiting to see him; Cattle are grazing in the field). 14. After One-third, one-fifth + of + noun the verb is singular, but after two-thirds, two-fifths + of + noun the verb is plural (One-third of the book is already finished; Two-thirds of the spectators are cheering our team). 15. If a Relative Pronoun is the subject, the verb follows the number and person of the preceding Noun or pronoun (It is I who am guilty; These are the things that have been stolen from the house). 16. When a plural noun refers to a proper noun (the name of a book, the name of a country) and means one united unit, it takes a singular verb (Gulliver's Travels is a famous satire; The Philippines is a group of islands).

chunk_text: Lesson-01: Use of Tenses. 1. Universal truth, general truth, daily habit, custom, practice, historical event description etc. take Present Indefinite tense; if the Subject is 3rd person singular number, 's' or 'es' joins the root verb (I read the Holy Quran everyday; We celebrate our Victory Day; Honey tastes sweet; The sun rises in the east; The moon gives us light at night). Structure: Subject + root verb's present form + extension. 2. If a Sentence has always, daily, regularly, normally, generally, frequently, very often, often, really, always, sometimes, once, usually, and time words like every day/ week/ month/ year/ (season) summer/ night/ morning/ afternoon etc. and no past hint or sign, the sentence is Present Indefinite Tense (I water the plant regularly; Jerry sees his mother every summer; Rony usually takes his lunch at 2 p.m.; Very often, he comes to meet me). 3. If a future time or moment is mentioned or fixed for some work or event, the sentence is Present Indefinite Tense (He goes to London next week; Our college closes on Monday next). 4. If a sentence has past-indicating words or phrases like a few days ago, ago, formerly, last, last century, last decade, last week/ month/ year/ night, long ago, long before, long since, once, once upon a time, the day before yesterday, the previous day, the year before, then, yesterday etc., the sentence is past indefinite tense (I saw a nice bird yesterday; He invited me last week; Once upon a time, there lived a poor boy named Robi). 5. If a sentence has It is time, It is high time, I fancy etc. connective or introductory clause, the verb after the following subject takes the past form (It is high time we took steps to remove illiteracy; I fancy, I turned a little pale observing the situation). 6. In a sentence expressing an impossible wish or desire, after If + subject (Subject + wish, would that etc. after Subject) if there is 'be' verb it becomes were, if verb 'to have' it becomes had, and if Principal verb it takes its past form (I wish I sang; If I were a millionaire; I wish I had the wings of a dove). 7. To mean a past habit the verb takes Past Indefinite Tense; for a regular past habit 'used to' sits after the Subject, for an irregular past habit 'would' sits (He used to play football before his marriage; I used to swim in the pond when I was at home; I would meet my uncle very often; We would go to cinema). 8. If one work or event happens while another work or event is going on in the past, the Verb takes Past Tense (He saw me when I was going there; While she was walking on the street she saw a handsome boy; When he was sleeping, the phone rang). 9. If two works or events in the past happened almost together, with As soon as, when, while, as etc. the Past Indefinite Tense is used (When they danced on the stage, we sang a melancholy; As soon as he reached the station, the train left; As the dog lay close to him, it found comfort there). 10. If a sentence begins with I'm sure, I suppose, I doubt, I hope, I wonder, I think, probably, certainly, surely etc., its later part is Future indefinite tense (I'm sure he will pass the examination; Certainly, Bangladesh will achieve economic independence). 11. To say something will happen in future, or to guess or predict the future, Future Indefinite Tense is used; after the Subject shall be or will be sits (Sakhina will be happy oneday; The guest will be here by 4 p.m.; Nasir will be a good teacher oneday; We will be/ shall be industrious). 12. If a sentence has tomorrow, Next + time word like Next month, next week, next day, next year, etc. or coming + time word like coming year, coming decades, coming century, etc. or any future day, date, month or year mentioned, the sentence is Future Indefinite Tense (I shall leave for Dhaka tomorrow; We shall visit the National Park next week; Our final examination will begin tomorrow). 13. If some work or event is going on or happening in the present, the sentence is Present continuous tense; the sentence generally has gradually, frequently, slowly, rapidly, now, at present, at this moment, day by day etc. (Boys are playing cricket in the field now; He is reading the book at this moment; At present, he is doing the sums; Day by day, we are losing our national resources). 14. If a sentence has 'go' verb before an Infinitive, the sentence is present continuous tense (The managing director is going to open a new branch; He is going to start a new business). 15. To describe a temporary work or event the verb takes present continuous tense; the work or event started earlier, is still going on and may continue for some days/ time in future (Kamal is reading a novel; He is staying with his uncle in Chattogram). 16. If some work or event was going on or happening in the past, the verb takes Past continuous tense; the sentence may have then, at that moment etc. (Then I was writing a letter; At that time, I was sleeping in my room; Then they were gossiping under a tree; At that moment, they were quarrelling). 17. If a sentence has just, just now, ever, never, yet, not yet, still, already, lately, recently etc., the sentence is present perfect tense; have/ has is followed by the mentioned words (You have seen her recently; I just - (have) my breakfast now. Ans. I have just had my breakfast). 18. If a time is mentioned for completing some work but it is not yet finished, the Verb takes Present Perfect tense; the sentence generally has today, this week/ month/ year/ season (Rupa has passed the JSC Exam this year; Today we have visited the National Museum; He has met her today). 19. If some work started at some time in the past and is still going on till the present time or is not yet finished, the verb takes Present Perfect continuous or Present Perfect tense; to show Point of time or when the work started Since sits, and to show Period of time or how long the work has been going on for sits (We have been reading at Hajigonj Model School for two years; She has been ill since last week; I have been here for twelve years). 20. If the Principal clause of a sentence joined by time conjunctions After, as, as soon as, because, before, since, till, until, when etc. is Present Indefinite/ Future Indefinite/ Imperative sentence, the other Clause takes Present Perfect Tense (He will inform me when he has reached home; Don't come until I have finished my meal). 21. If 'since' or 'for' is used as a preposition in a sentence and the work is understood to continue till the present time, the sentence is present perfect tense/ present perfect continuous tense; for 'be' verb have been/ has been sits, but for a root 'verb' have been/ has been + v + ing sits (It has been raining since morning; She has been living here for 5 years). 22. After Since 'phrase of time' or Since 'clause of time' the following clause is always in present perfect tense (Since then I have not taken any cigarette - Since 'phrase of time'; Since she came, we have been happy - Since 'clause of time'). 23. If some definite work will be completed within some definite time in future, future perfect tense is used (He will have reached home by 6 pm; I shall have learnt my lesson by the night; We will have completed the work by Monday).

chunk_text: Lesson-02: Use of Non-finite (Infinitive, Gerund, Participle). 24. If two verbs are used one after another in a sentence, the later verb takes -ing (I saw him doing the job; I saw the girl dancing). 25. If a sentence has be + used to, confess to, get used to, look forward to, object to, with a view to, would you mind etc., the following verb takes -ing (The man prayed to God with a view to getting relief; Would you mind opening the window?). 26. If a sentence has listen, feel, watch, see, hear, notice etc., the following verb takes -ing (I heard him singing a song; I saw the boy swimming). 27. If a sentence has remain, mind, feel, help, keep, like etc., the following verb takes -ing (I cannot help going there; He would not mind coming here). 28. After some Prepositional phrases (like in stead of, in spite of, despite, because of, capable of, fond of, insisted on, on account of, prevent from, succeed in, think of etc.) the verb takes -ing (He is not capable of doing this; He insisted on my going there). 29. After some verbs (like love, prefer, continue, begin, like, dislike, hate, start, stop, try etc.) both (v + ing) and infinitive (to + verb) may sit (We started to talk; Or, We started talking). 30. After ask, attend, beg, begin, claim, consent, decide, demand, deserve, expect, fail, forget, hesitate, hope, afford, agree, appear, arrange, intend, learn, manage, mean, need, offer, plan, prepare, pretend, promise, refuse, regret, seem, tend, threaten, wait, want etc. verbs, to + verb's Present form sits (I don't want to buy a car). 31. In a Simple sentence, if the verb after the root verb expresses a purpose, that verb becomes an infinitive, i.e. 'to' sits before the verb's present form (He tried to do this work). 32. To form Perfect tense, after have, has, had the root verb's past participle form sits (The sailor had sailed away to the U.K.). 33. To form Passive voice, after the auxiliary verb the root verb's past participle sits (Rice is eaten by us). 34. If have, has, had, get, got etc. are used as causative verb, the verb after the Object used after them becomes Past participle (I had my hair cut). 35. After Having, to be, must be, can be, could be, should be, would be etc. the following verb becomes Past participle (I went outside having finished my work). 36. If a Simple sentence has two verbs and the first verb is admit, avoid, consider, delay, deny, finish, imagine, stop etc., the later one takes -ing (He avoided facing me; She stopped going there). If the first verb is afford, agree, aim, forget, hope, manage, offer, plan, refuse, threaten etc., the later one becomes infinitive (I forgot to give you the sheet; The chairman managed to hold a meeting). 37. When the Subject does not do the work itself but gets it done by someone else, have, has, had etc. work as causative verb; then if the complement after the causative verb is a non-living word, the verb takes past participle form, and if it is a living word, the verb takes Present form (I am having my house painted; He had the servant buy the food). 38. After causative verb got, if the complement is non-living, past participle sits, and if living, Infinitive sits (The writer got his book published; He got her to come here).
