chunk_text: Lesson-03: Use of Clauses. 39. If the clause before Since is present indefinite or present perfect tense, the following clause becomes Past indefinite form. Structure: Present indefinite/ Present perfect + since + Past indefinite (Two years have passed since he went there). 40. If the clause before Since is Past indefinite tense, the following clause may be either Past indefinite/ Past perfect (It was many years since I saw/ had seen you). 41. If the clause before Before is past perfect tense, the following clause becomes Past indefinite tense. Structure: Past perfect + before + past indefinite (We had reached the station before the train started). 42. If the clause before After is Past indefinite tense, the following clause becomes past perfect tense. Structure: Past indefinite + after + past perfect (We reached the station after the train had started). 43. If the clause before As if/ As though is present indefinite tense, the following clause becomes Past indefinite tense. Structure: Present indefinite + as if/ as though + Past indefinite (He talks as if he were a millionaire). 44. If the clause before As if/ As though is Past indefinite tense, the following clause becomes Past perfect tense. Structure: Past indefinite + as if/ as though + past perfect (He talked as though he had not known it). 45. If the Principal clause of a sentence joined by when, after, before, that, until, since, as, because, as soon as, as though, than etc. is Present or Future indefinite tense, the Sub-ordinate clause becomes Present perfect tense. Structure: Present/ Future indefinite + connecting word + present perfect. Or, Connecting word + Present perfect + Present/ Future indefinite tense (I shall go to the station after the train has arrived; When you have worked hard you will be successful in the examination). 46. If one verb of a sentence joined by time conjunctions when, while, before, after, that, than, since, as, because, as though, as if, till, until etc. is Past indefinite tense, the other becomes Past perfect tense. Structure: i. Past indefinite + connecting word + past perfect. Or, ii. Past perfect + connecting word + past indefinite (It was long since I had seen you last; Meena had been at the orphanage since she was five; Everyone said that he had killed the snake; You arrived after he had left; The doctor had come before the patient died). 47. If one clause of a sentence joined by Till or Until is present, future or imperative, the other becomes Simple present tense. Structure: Future/ Present/ Imperative + till/ until + present indefinite (Wait till I come back). 48. In Indirect Speech, if the Reporting verb is Past tense and the Reported speech has next day/week/ month/year etc., would or should sits before the verb and the verb takes base form (I told the salesman that I would pay him the next day). 49. In a Lest-joined sentence, after lest the subject that sits is followed by should/might and the verb takes base form (Walk fast lest you should miss the train; He took an umbrella with him lest it might rain).

chunk_text: Lesson-04: Use of Conditional Sentences. 50. If the If/ Unless joined clause is present indefinite tense, the other clause becomes Future indefinite tense/ Imperative sentence or Subject + can/ may + verb may sit. Structure: If/ Unless + present indefinite +, + Future indefinite. Or, Imperative sentence or Subj. + can/ may + verb (If you come here, you will get the pen; If he walks fast, he may get the train). 51. If the If/ Unless joined clause is past indefinite tense, the other clause becomes past conditional. Structure: If/ Unless + past indefinite +, + conditional. Or, Past conditional + if/ Unless + past indefinite. Past conditional = Subject + should/ would/ could/ might + verb's present form + extn. (If I had a computer, I could type it myself). 52. If the If joined clause is Past perfect tense, the following clause becomes perfect conditional. Structure: If + past perfect +, + perfect conditional. Or, Perfect conditional + if + past perfect. Perfect conditional = Subject + would/ should/ could/ might + have + verb's past participle + extn. (If he had told me before, I would have brought a car for him; If I were rich, I would have helped the poor). 53. Had + subject + been/ root verb's past participle + extension +, + perfect conditional (Had you helped him, he would have passed the examination). 54. In a sentence joined by No sooner .... than, Scarcely .... when, Hardly .... when/ before etc. correlatives, before than, when, when/ before generally past perfect tense sits and after it past indefinite tense sits; No sooner/ Scarcely/ Hardly etc. sit first in the sentence and after them had + subject + verb's Past participle sits. Structure: No sooner/ Scarcely/ Hardly + had + subject + verb's past participle + than/ when/ before + subject + verb's past form + extension (No sooner had the thief seen the police than he fled away; Hardly had we reached home when/ before the rain stopped).

chunk_text: Lesson-05: Miscellaneous Use. 55. news, gallows, physics, mathematics, politics, wages etc. words look plural but the verb is singular (Physics is my favourite subject; Ill news runs apace; Politics is the art of conucting state affairs). 56. In a sentence with now, at the moment, currently etc. words or phrases, the root verb after be- takes -ing (I am reading a book now; At the moment, they are playing). 57. If a sentence has do, does or did, the root verb's Present form always sits (He does not go to school; We did not get it). 58. After all Modal auxiliary verbs like can, could, may, might, must, should, would etc. the verb's Present form sits (A student should learn his lessons regularly). 59. After Let the verb's present form always sits (Let him do this). 60. After had better, had rather, would better/ rather/ sooner, need, must etc. the verb's Present form sits; in this case 'to' does not sit before the verb (You had better leave this place). 61. After Lest the subject used after it is followed by should and the root verb's Present form is used (He worked hard lest he should fail in the examination). 62. If a sentence's principal clause is past tense and the other clause has tomorrow, the next day/ month/ year/ week, the following day/ week/ month/ year, the day after tomorrow etc. words/ phrases, then after the Subject of that sentence would/ should sits and the root verb's present form is used (He said that he would do this). 63. If one of two subjects joined by And has no/ not, the verb follows the subject before not (I, not my sister, have broken the plate). 64. After More than one a singular verb sits, but after More than two/three a plural verb sits (More than one boy has copied in the exam; More than five people were involved in the robbery).

chunk_text: Lesson-01 What is Adjective? (printed p. 90). Adjectives are words that describe nouns. Examples: Dhaka is a big city; He is a little boy; The girl is beautiful. Big, little and beautiful are adjectives because they describe a noun's fault, quality, state or number - they tell what the noun (city, boy, girl) is like. An adjective gives extra information about a noun or pronoun, usually about: Quality - a nice day, a beautiful girl; Size - a tall tree, a big car, a small boy; Age - a young man, an old house; Temperature - a cool morning, a hot day; Shape - a round table, a square room; Colour - black eyes, gray hair, a white dress; Origin - a Swiss watch, a Chinese phone. Definition: a word that expresses a noun or pronoun's fault, quality, state, number, quantity etc. is called an Adjective. An adverb of degree (intensifier) such as too or very can sit before an adjective: She is too tired; The rose is a very beautiful flower. Adjectives have Comparative and Superlative degrees. They are not affected by the number, gender or case of the sentence, because they are not controlled by the noun or pronoun they modify.

chunk_text: Lesson-02 How to Identify Adjective (printed pp. 90-91). The main part of a word is called the root. Adjectives are formed by adding certain suffixes to the end of a root or word, and an adjective can be recognised by these suffixes: -able/ -ible - acceptable, favourable, horrible; -al - accidental, casual, emotional; -an/ -n - American, European, Indian; -ary/ -ory - momentary, reformatory; -atic/ -tic/ -ative - talkative, fantastic, fanatic, problematic; -en - bounden, golden, silken; -ern/ -ery - Eastern, Southern, Silvery; -ese - Chinese, Japanese; -ful - dutiful, useful, careful; -ial/ -ic/ -ical - partial, atomic, lyrical; -ish - bookish, childish, foolish, selfish; -ive - abusive, submissive; -less - artless, needless, hopeless; -ly - yearly, brotherly, cowardly; -ous - dangerous, famous, prosperous; -some - burdensome, troublesome; -t (-ant/ -ent) - absent, eminent, innocent, tolerant; -tial - essential, influential, substantial; -worthy - noteworthy, blameworthy; -y - airy, bloody, cloudy, hilly.

chunk_text: Lesson-03 Position of Adjective (printed p. 91). 1. Before a Noun: an adjective usually sits before a noun; this is its attributive use and such an adjective is called a pre-modifier. Examples: Meena is a good girl; He is a wise man. 2. After a noun: in some cases adjectives sit after a noun; this is its predicative use and such an adjective is called a post-modifier. (i) When more than one adjective qualifies one noun: The boys, thin and smart, brilliant and wise are invited to the party. (ii) When an adjective shows a number through a phrase: I want a boy ten years old. (iii) In poetry: Hearing which your blood will be cold. (iv) When an adjective shows a title: Omar the great was a just ruler. 3. After an Adverb: an adjective can also sit after an adverb. Structure: The rose is a very beautiful flower; It is a very hot day.

chunk_text: Lesson-04 Classification of Adjective (printed pp. 91-93) and KEY POINTS (p. 93). Adjectives are mainly of four kinds: 1. Adjective of Quality or Descriptive Adjective, 2. Adjective of Quantity or Quantitative Adjective, 3. Adjective of Number or Numeral Adjective, 4. Pronominal Adjective. 1. Adjective of Quality: shows a noun's fault, quality or state - He is a good boy; Rahim is dull; The woman is old; The farmer is poor. 2. Adjective of Quantity: shows the quantity of a noun - I have got some money; Give me some milk; There is little water in his glass; He has enough time to walk. Note: some adjectives show both Quality and Quantity - Bradman was a great cricketer (Quality); We pay the language martyrs great respect (Quantity). 3. Adjective of Number/ Numeral Adjective: shows a noun's definite number, place or order - I have five cars; He is the first boy in the class. Three kinds: Cardinal Numeral Adjective (One, two, three, four, etc.), Ordinal Numeral Adjective (First, second, third, etc.), Multiplicative Numeral Adjective (Single, double, triple, etc.). 4. Pronominal Adjective: when a pronoun sits before a noun and is used as an adjective - Some boys are playing; Every boy was given a prize; She likes this picture. Four kinds: (a) Demonstrative Adjective - pronouns that point to a noun in a special way: this, that, these, those (This girl is intelligent; These cars are new; Those mangoes are tasty). (b) Distributive Adjective - adjectives that show each of several persons or things separately: every, each, either, neither (They each have their own car; Every student in the class is capable of passing the exam; You can park on either side of the street). (c) Interrogative Adjective - adjectives used to question a noun or pronoun: what, which, whose (What vegetable do you like most? Which book do you need? Whose car is this?). (d) Possessive Adjective - adjectives showing ownership or relation: my, our, your, her, their, its (Here is our house; This is her bag). KEY POINTS: i. A Pronominal Adjective and a Pronoun may look alike, but a pronoun does the work of a noun while a pronominal adjective does the work of an adjective - His room is clean (Adjective); Ours is the best house in this area (Pronoun). ii. Proper Adjective: adjectives formed from a Proper Noun, especially from the names of geographical places (continents, countries, states); they show origin or source and begin with a Capital letter - a Japanese camera (Japan gives Japanese); Bangladesh gives Bangladeshi, Portugal gives Portuguese, China gives Chinese, America gives American, Canada gives Canadian, India gives Indian.

chunk_text: Lesson-01: An Introduction to Comparison of Adjectives & Adverbs. Mahin is a tall boy. Safin is taller than Mahin. Raiyan is the tallest of the three. Mahin bought a big basket. Safin bought a basket bigger than that of Mahin. Raiyan bought the biggest basket of the shop. The underlined words indicate three kinds of Adjective: tall (Positive) - taller (Comparative) - tallest (Superlative); big (Positive) - bigger (Comparative) - biggest (Superlative). So to show comparison among different persons, animals or things, the different forms of Adjective and Adverb are called Degrees of Adjectives or Adverbs. This is also called Comparison of Adjectives or Adverbs. To show this comparison, Adjective or Adverb has three forms: 1. Positive Degree, 2. Comparative Degree and 3. Superlative Degree. 1. Positive Degree: if an Adjective/ Adverb expresses a quality in the ordinary way without comparison, it is Positive Degree. Azad is a good boy. It is a tall tree. 2. Comparative Degree: when an Adjective or Adverb shows comparison of quality between two, it is Comparative Degree. Abul is taller than Karim. Rina is more intelligent than Sheela. 3. Superlative Degree: when an Adjective/ Adverb shows comparison of quality among more than two, i.e. among many, it is Superlative Degree. Hasan is the best boy in the class. Mr Jamal is the wisest man in the village.

chunk_text: Lesson-02: Comparison of Adjectives - rules 1-6 (forming Comparative and Superlative Degree from Positive form). 1. For most one-Syllable Adjectives, Comparative is formed by adding -er and Superlative by adding -est at the end. black - blacker - blackest; bold - bolder - boldest; bright - brighter - brightest; cheap - cheaper - cheapest; clean - cleaner - cleanest; clever - cleverer - cleverest; cold - colder - coldest; dear - dearer - dearest; deep - deeper - deepest; fair - fairer - fairest; great - greater - greatest; hard - harder - hardest; high - higher - highest; kind - kinder - kindest; light - lighter - lightest; low - lower - lowest; long - longer - longest; new - newer - newest; old - older - oldest; poor - poorer - poorest; quick - quicker - quickest; rich - richer - richest; short - shorter - shortest; small - smaller - smallest; soft - softer - softest; tall - taller - tallest. 2. For Adjectives ending in e, -r is added for Comparative and -st for Superlative Degree. able - abler - ablest; brave - braver - bravest; close - closer - closest; fine - finer - finest; large - larger - largest; nice - nicer - nicest; noble - nobler - noblest; ripe - riper - ripest; white - whiter - whitest; wide - wider - widest; wise - wiser - wisest. 3. If the Positive form of an Adjective ends in y and there is a Consonant before y, y is dropped and -ier is added for Comparative Degree and -iest for Superlative Degree. busy - busier - busiest; dry - drier - driest; easy - easier - easiest; happy - happier - happiest; healthy - healthier - healthiest; heavy - heavier - heaviest; holy - holier - holiest; hungry - hungrier - hungriest; greedy - greedier - greediest; lazy - lazier - laziest; lovely - lovelier - loveliest; merry - merrier - merriest; ready - readier - readiest; ugly - uglier - ugliest; tiny - tinier - tiniest; wealthy - wealthier - wealthiest. 4. If the Positive Degree has y and there is a Vowel before it, -er is added for Comparative Degree and -est for Superlative Degree. gay - gayer - gayest; gray - grayer - grayest. 5. If the Positive Degree Adjective ends in a single Consonant and there is a single Vowel before it, the final Consonant is doubled and then -er is added for Comparative and -est for Superlative Degree. big - bigger - biggest; fat - fatter - fattest; fit - fitter - fittest; hot - hotter - hottest; red - redder - reddest; sad - sadder - saddest; thin - thinner - thinnest. 6. But if the Adjective ends in two Consonants or there are two vowels before the final Consonant, -er and -est are added as usual for Comparative and Superlative Degree. broad - broader - broadest; thick - thicker - thickest.

chunk_text: Lesson-02: Comparison of Adjectives - rules 7-10. 7. For Adjectives of two or more Syllables and Adjectives with -ful, more or most is placed before to show increase and less or least to show decrease, forming Comparative and Superlative Degree respectively. active - more active / less active - most active / least active; beautiful - more beautiful / less beautiful - most beautiful / least beautiful; dutiful - more dutiful / less dutiful - most dutiful / least dutiful; careful - more careful / less careful - most careful / least careful; comfortable - more comfortable / less comfortable - most comfortable / least comfortable; dangerous - more dangerous / less dangerous - most dangerous / least dangerous; difficult - more difficult / less difficult - most difficult / least difficult; hopeful - more hopeful / less hopeful - most hopeful / least hopeful; honest - more honest / less honest - most honest / least honest; important - more important / less important - most important / least important; industrious - more industrious / less industrious - most industrious / least industrious; useful - more useful / less useful - most useful / least useful. 8. Some Adjectives and Adverbs have no fixed rule for forming Comparative and Superlative form. bad - worse - worst; far - farther - farthest; fore - former - foremost; good/ Well - better - best; hind - hinder - hind most; in - Inner - in most/ innermost; little - less/ lesser - least; many/ Much - more - most; near - nearer - nearest/ next; out - utter/ outer - utmost; up - upper - upmost/ uppermost. 9. Some Adjectives have no comparison because their meanings cannot be intensified: annual, blind, circular, dead, complete, dead, earthen, false, golden, monthly, perfect, right, round, superior, square, wrong, unique, etc. 10. Latin Comparative: some Adjectives much used in English have been taken from Latin into English. These Adjectives are called Latin Comparative. Features of Latin comparatives: (a) There are twelve Latin Comparatives in total: prior, anterior, major, minor, interior, superior, junior, exterior, inferior, senior, posterior, ulterior. (b) Of these, senior, junior, prior, anterior, inferior, posterior, superior - these seven are used in sentences as Comparative Degree. They end in '-or'. (c) major, minor, exterior, interior, ulterior - these five are used in sentences as Positive Degree. (d) Even when Latin Comparatives are used in a sentence as Comparative Degree, 'than' does not sit after them, 'to' sits. 'more' does not sit before them. I am senior to him. He is junior to me.

chunk_text: Lesson-03 Note: comparison usage. i. After Comparative Degree 'than' sits. Karim is better than Rahim. Karim is more intelligent than Rahim. ii. Before Superlative Degree 'the' sits and before those among whom comparison is made 'of' sits. He is the best of all the boys. Karim is the wisest of all in this village. iii. To show comparison of one animal or thing of the same class with many animals or things, after Comparative Degree's 'than', 'any other' or 'all other' sits. The elephant is larger than any other animal or all other animals. iv. To show comparison of qualities of the same person or thing, i.e. the degree of two Adjectives, 'more' sits before the first Adjective, sometimes 'er' is not added. The boy is more strong than tall.

chunk_text: Lesson-01: An Introduction to Adverb. An adverb tells us more about a verb. An adverb describes or modifies the verb in some way. Many adverbs end with the suffix 'ly', but not all. Adverbs often tell us how something happens. The underlined words are called Adverb. This kind of word usually modifies the verb, but it often modifies Adjective, Noun, Pronoun, Preposition, Conjunction, another Adverb and even a Phrase or a whole Sentence. Verb: Birds fly swiftly. ('fly' verb is modified by 'swiftly' adverb). Adjective: He is a very good boy. ('very' adverb modifies 'good' adjective). Adverb: She plays badminton quite well. ('quite' adverb modifies 'well' adverb). Preposition: The crow flew just over our head. ('just' adverb modifies 'over' preposition). Conjunction: He came simply because he loved us. ('simply' adverb modifies 'because' conjunction). Noun Phrase: He is undoubtedly a man of letters. ('undoubtedly' adverb modifies 'a man of letters' noun phrase). Pronoun: This book is actually his. ('actually' adverb modifies 'his' pronoun). Sentence: Really, he is an honest man. ('really' adverb modifies 'he is an honest man' sentence).

chunk_text: Lesson-02: Classification of Adverbs. Adverbs are mainly of three kinds by use. 1. Simple or Independent Adverb: simple adverbs modify only a word or sentence. By meaning Simple Adverb is divided into eight parts. (a) Adverb of Time: these Adverbs indicate the time of the verb's work. after, ago, already, always, before, daily, early, ever, formerly, immediately, instantly, lest, never, now, often, presently, since, sometimes, soon, then, today, tomorrow, when, which, yesterday, etc. They answer the question 'when?'. She will come late. (Adverb). (b) Adverb of Place: these Adverbs indicate the place of the verb. above, after, anywhere, below, down, everywhere, far, here, in, inside, near, neither, nowhere, out, outside, There, thither, up, etc. They answer the question 'where?'. She goes home. (c) Adverb of Manner or Quality: these Adverbs indicate how the verb is done. aloud, badly, certainly, gently, hardly, highly, justly, probably, quickly, silently, slowly, so, thus, well, wisely, etc. They answer the question 'How?'. The boy walks slowly. (d) Adverb of Quantity (Degree and Manner): these Adverbs indicate the degree, quantity and number of the verb. almost, enough, extremely, fully, half, hardly, how, least, little, more, much, once, quite, so, too, twice, very, wholly, etc. They answer the question 'How?'. He is extremely hungry. (e) Adverb of Cause and Effect: these Adverbs indicate the cause of the verb's work and its result. accordingly, as, because, consequently, hence, so, therefore, wherefore, Why, yet, etc. I do not know why he has done it. (f) Adverb of Order: these Adverbs indicate the order of the verb's work. first, second, third, last, secondly, lastly, etc. Secondly, we have to call a meeting. (g) Adverb of Affirmation and Negation: these Adverbs are used to give an affirmative or negative answer to a question. certainly, indeed, no, not, perhaps, possibly, probably, really, surely, truly, Yes, etc. Really, he is an honest man. (affir). No, he did not go there. (neg.). (h) Adverb of Frequency: they indicate how many times the verb's work is done. always, generally, often, once, rarely, sometimes, usually, etc. Take this medicine thrice a day. 2. Relative or Conjunctive Adverb: these Adverbs join two Clauses. When, where, why, how, while, etc. I know the place where he lives. 3. Interrogative Adverb: when an Adverb is used to ask a question, it is called Interrogative Adverb. These again can indicate place, time, quantity, etc. (a) When did he go? (time) (b) Where did he go? (place) (c) How did he go? (manner) (d) How are you now? (state/ condition) (e) How much did he buy? (quantity) (f) How often did he come? (frequency) (g) Why did he go? (cause).

chunk_text: Lesson-03: Some Other Adverbs. 1. Genitive adverbs: the adverb formed from a Possessive noun is called Genitive adverb. He came here once (= of one time) in his life. Note: Genitive = of + noun. 2. Prepositional adverb: the adverbs formed by adding a preposition before a Noun or Adjective are called Prepositional adverb. He keeps away from school. Structure: preposition + noun. on (= a) + way = away; in + deed = indeed; of (= o) + clock = o'clock; to + day = today. 3. Adverbial particles: the words/ prepositions used in a sentence as adverb and preposition are called Adverbial particles. When these words take an object, they work as preposition. But when they take no object, they work as Adverb particle. (a) We drove round the city. (round + object = preposition). We drove round. (no object = adverb particle). (b) We went up. (adverb). We went up the hill. (preposition). Well-known words used as Preposition or Adverb particle: about, above, across, after, along, around, before, behind, below, beneath, beyond, by, down, in, inside, near, off, on, opposite, outside, over, past, round, through, under, underneath, up, without, etc. 4. Compound Adverb: the adverbs formed with two or more words are called Compound Adverb. other + wise = otherwise; some + times = sometimes; no + where = nowhere; up + stairs = upstairs. 5. Sentence Adverb: the adverb which modifies a complete sentence is called Sentence Adverb. These adverbs are: certainly, consequently, fortunately, however, indeed, luckily, moreover, obviously, perhaps, surely, therefore, thus, yet, etc. These adverbs are used to express an opinion or viewpoint. They usually sit at the beginning of the sentence and a comma is used after them. Fortunately, the baby was saved. Obviously, she is innocent.

chunk_text: Lesson-04: Position of Adverbs. 1. Adverb usually sits after an intransitive verb. i. He lives there. ii. He died early. Exceptions: Adverb of time (always, seldom, never, ever, other, sometimes, frequently, etc.) sits after 'be verb' and before other verbs. Structure: be + adverb, ii. adverb + verb. i. He frequently told me this. (adv. + verb). ii. I am often busy. (be verb + adv.). 2. Adverb usually sits after the object. Structure: object + adverb. i. I did it quickly. ii. You have done the work badly. 3. Adverb sometimes sits between the auxiliary verb and the principal verb. Structure: Auxiliary Verb + adverb + principal verb. i. I shall never go there. ii. He has carefully examined the case. 4. Adverb sits before the Adjective. Structure: adverb + adjective. i. I am very happy. (Adverb + Adjective). ii. I am rather sorry for you. (Adverb + Adjective).

chunk_text: Lesson-05: Formation of Adverbs. 1. Generally most Adverbs are formed by adding '-ly' to an Adjective. actual + ly = actually; bad = badly; beautiful = beautifully; brave = bravely; careless = carelessly; certain = certainly; clear = clearly; definite = definitely; great = greatly; honest = honestly; hopeful = hopefully; hopeless = hopelessly; kind = kindly; local = locally; loud = loudly; partial = partially; quick = quickly; quiet = quietly; real = really; sad = sadly; slow = slowly; soft = softly; sound = soundly; strong = strongly; sudden = suddenly; sure = surely; urgent = urgently. 2. If an Adjective ends in 'le', 'e' is replaced by 'y' to form the Adverb. double + y = doubly; horrible = horribly; possible = possibly; single = singly; suitable = suitably; terrible = terribly. 3. If an Adjective ends in 'll', only 'y' is added to form the Adverb. full + y = fully; dull = dully. 4. If an Adjective ends in 'e', 'e' is replaced by 'ly' to form the Adverb. due + ly = duly; true = truly; undue = unduly. 5. If an Adjective ends in 'y', 'y' is replaced by 'ily' to form the Adverb. easy + ily = easily; happy = happily; heavy = heavily; lazy = lazily; lucky = luckily; noisy = noisily; ready = readily; satisfactory = satisfactorily. 6. If an Adjective ends in 'ic', 'ally' is added at the end to form the Adverb. automatic + ally = automatically; economic = economically; tragic = tragically. 7. Some Adverbs are formed from some Adjectives in a completely new way. good - well (He played well.); bad - worse (The situation is getting worse.). 8. Some Adverbs like here, hither, hence, etc. take some prepositions and form new Adverbs. henceforth, henceforward, hereafter, hereby, herefrom, herein, hereupon, herewith, hitherto, etc. 9. One Qualifying Adjective and one Noun/ adjective/ verb join to form some Adverbs. meantime, meanwhile, midday, midnight, midway, sometime, yesterday, etc. 10. One preposition and one noun join to form some Adverbs. abroad, ahead, along, aloud, asleep, away, etc. (away = on + way). 11. Sometimes two adverbs join by 'and' and sit together and work as Adverb. again and again (= I forbade him again and again.); far and near (= His reputation has spread far and near.). Adverbs with two Forms: close - closely; clear - clearly; deep - deeply; dear - dearly; easy - easily; high - highly; loud - loudly; near - nearly; fine - finely; pretty - prettily; tight - tightly. Examples: I want to deal with him direct. -> He came to me directly for help. I closed the door tight. -> She closed her lips tightly. He speaks very loud. -> He sings very loudly.

chunk_text: Lesson-03: Comparison of Adverbs. Like Adjectives, Adverbs also have Comparison of Degrees. 1. Some Adverbs take -er for Comparative and -est for Superlative. fast - faster - fastest; hard - harder - hardest; quick - quicker - quickest; soon - sooner - soonest. 2. Adverbs ending in -ly take 'more' before for comparative and 'most' before for Superlative. easily - more easily - most easily; clearly - more clearly - most clearly; loudly - more loudly - most loudly; quickly - more quickly - most quickly; swiftly - more swiftly - most swiftly; rapidly - more rapidly - most rapidly; wisely - more wisely - most wisely. 3. Some Adverbs' Comparative and Superlative are not formed by any fixed rule. well - better - best; far - farther, further - farthest, furthest; badly - worse - worst; much - more - most; little - less - least.

chunk_text: Lesson-01: An Introduction to Preposition. Read the passage and notice the italic words: Jarif and Jawad live at 'Chadgao Abashik Elaka' in Chattogram. They wake up early in the morning. They go to bed early at night. They go to school regularly. Jarif needs a bag of books for his new class. Jawad needs a bag for his new school. They go to school by school bus. The italic words naturally sit before a noun or noun-equivalent and establish a relation between the preceding subject and the following noun. All such words are called Preposition. 'at' shows the relation between 'Chadgao Abashik Elaka' and 'Jarif and Jawad'; 'in' between 'the morning' and 'they'; 'to' and 'at' between 'bed'/'night' and 'they'; 'to' between 'they' and 'school'. Definition: A preposition is a relating word. Ball-and-box diagrams: without a preposition the sentences 'The ball is ___ the box' are meaningless because there is no relation between the ball and the box; with a preposition the relation is established: The ball is in the box. The ball is under the box. The ball is above the box. The ball is behind the box. The ball is in front of the box.

chunk_text: Lesson-02: Kinds of Preposition. By structure and function a Preposition is divided into six kinds: 1. Simple Preposition; 2. Double Preposition; 3. Compound Preposition; 4. Phrase Preposition; 5. Participle Preposition; 6. Disguised Preposition. 1. Simple Preposition: generally formed by one basic word: at, on, by, for, from, with, after, of, off, etc. 2. Double Preposition: when two Simple Prepositions join together and are used like one Preposition: up + on = upon, up + to = upto, with + in = within, in + to = into, out + of = out of, etc. 3. Compound Preposition: when a Simple Preposition joins before a Noun, Adjective or Adverb: on + by + out = about, by + fore = before, on + cross = across, by + yond = beyond. Note: 'on' becomes 'a' and 'by' becomes 'be'. 4. Phrase Preposition: when two or more words together are used like one Preposition: on account of, in front of, instead of, etc. 5. Participle Preposition: when a Present Participle (verb + ing) or Past Participle is used like a Preposition: Regarding, considering, barring, touching, etc. 6. Disguised Preposition: sometimes 'a' is used instead of 'on' and 'o' instead of 'of': He went a hunting. (on hunting) The morning begins with 7 o'clock. (of clock) etc. Notes: i. Detached Preposition: some Prepositions are used in a sentence detached from their Prepositional objective, mostly with Interrogative Pronoun, Adverb (where, what) and Relative Pronoun: What class do you read in? What are you looking for? Where do you come from? ii. Special Preposition: 'Than' and 'but' are conjunctions, but sometimes they work like a preposition in a sentence: None but Allah can help us. It needs less than fifty taka for this purpose. iii. Some words are sometimes used both as Adverb and Preposition: March on. (Adverb) Keep it on the table. (Preposition) May I come in? (Adverb) He is in the library. (Preposition)

chunk_text: Lesson-03: Position of Prepositions. 1. Before Noun/Pronoun: Preposition generally sits before a noun or pronoun: at home, about him, on the table, etc. 2. At the end of a Sentence: Preposition can often sit at the end of a sentence. (a) Wh-questions: Structure: Wh-word + verb + subject + preposition (?): What is the box for? Where does she come from? Whom are you talking to? (b) Relative clause: the Preposition before a Relative Pronoun often changes its position and sits at the end of the Relative clause: The house in which I live is small. The house I live in is small. Note: in this kind of Relative clause the Relative Pronoun (which, whom, etc.) is dropped. (c) Exclamations: in expressing emotion the preposition sits at the end of the sentence: What a world we live in! What a fellow to travel with! (d) Passive sentence: Preposition sits at the end of the sentence: Such a situation can't even be thought of. Who was this poem composed by? Note: Preposition generally sits before a noun or pronoun. But in modern English the use of Preposition at the end of a Sentence is considered a very natural matter.

chunk_text: Lesson-04: Important Prepositions & Their Uses (entries 1-7). 1 About: (i) about a person or thing - Tell me all about this. There is something strange about him. (ii) to describe the purpose of something - Movies are all about making money these days. What was all about that? (iii) around a place, here and there - We wandered about the town for an hour or so. He looked about the room. (iv) approximate time - Mother gets up at about 5 a.m. 2 Above: (i) higher place or state than a person or thing - The water came above our knees. We were flying above the clouds. (ii) more than a number, value, weight, temperature or age - Inflation is above 6%. Temperatures have been above average. (iii) more important or honourable than a person or thing - I rate her above most other players of her age. Man is true above all. (iv) above the normal state, beyond suspicion - He cannot tell a lie because his honesty is above suspicion. 3 Across: (i) from one end of something to the other - He walked across the field. I drew a line across the page. (ii) on the other end of something - There is a bank right across the street. You will have it across the river. (iii) over a part of the body - He hit him across the face. It's too tight across the back. (iv) in every part of a place, group, people etc. - His family is scattered across the country. This view is common across all sections of the community. 4 After: (i) later or after something - We shall leave after lunch. They arrived shortly after 5. After an hour I went home. (ii) repeatedly or in succession - Day after day she began to become mad. I have told you time after time not to do that. (iii) behind someone - Shut the door after you. He ran after her with the book. (iv) after something in importance or order - Your name comes after mine in the list. He is the tallest, after Richard. (v) in search of something, especially with phrasal verb - Some politicians always run after money. 5 Against: (i) to express disagreement, opposition or against a person or thing - This is the fight against terrorism. We were rowing against the current. (ii) not in favour of a person or thing, unfavourable - The evidence is against him. Her age is against her. (iii) in contact with or beside a person or thing - Put the piano there, against the wall. The rain beat against the windows. (iv) to prevent something happening or to reduce harm from something - They took precautions against fire. Are we insured against theft? (v) to compare two things - You must weigh the benefits against the cost. Check your receipts against the statement. 6 Along: (i) from one end to the other or towards the other end of something - She walked along this road. You will find his office just along the corridor. 7 Amid/ Amidst: (i) in the midst of strong feelings like joy or sorrow - He finished his speech amidst tremendous applause. The firm collapsed amidst allegations of fraud. (ii) in the middle of a place surrounded on all sides - My house is amidst a large flower garden.

chunk_text: Lesson-04: Important Prepositions & Their Uses (entries 8-14). 8 Among/ Amongst: (i) surrounded by or in the middle of a person or thing - They strolled among the crowd. I found the letter among his papers. (ii) happening or included among a group of people or things - A British woman was among the survivors. He was among the last to leave. (iii) in dividing or sharing - The prizes have been distributed among the winners. They divided the money up among the children. 9 Around/ Round: (i) on all sides - He travelled around/ round the world. The earth moves round the sun. (ii) on the other end of something - Our house is round the next village. There she is coming round the corner. (iii) all around a person or thing - She put her arms round him. He had a scarf round his neck. 10 At: (i) a relatively small place - We live at Panjia in Keshabpur. I met him at the hospital. How many people were at the airport? I live at my village. (ii) a person's workplace, school or place of prayer - He has been at the bank more than anyone else. He was at the ford. We shouldn't discuss worldly affairs at the mosque. (iii) the exact point of time - Our office started at 8 a.m. At that time I was still a student. We shall go to picnic at the end of the month. What do you do at the weekend? (iv) the age at which something is done - Both of my parents left school at 16. I went to school at the age of 5. (v) towards a person or thing, aim or purpose - The dacoit pointed a gun at me. She looks at the water hyacinths. The naughty boys threw stones at the frogs. (vi) distance from something - Who can read a book at fifty metres? (vii) speed, rate, price etc. - He is driving at 90 km/h. The noise disturbs me at five minute intervals. Polybags do not decompose at any rate. Rice sells at 35 taka a Kilo. (viii) skill or lack of skill in a particular work, i.e. standard, with adjective - He is good at English. He is hopeless at managing people. (ix) a relatively big place can take 'at' while travelling - We had to change our bus at Dhaka. The plane stops at London. (x) before general words expressing a holiday - What does your family do at Christmas/ Eid? (Not at Christmas Day/ Eid Day) 11 Away: (i) distance of a place or idea or time - The beach is a mile away. Christmas is still months away. (ii) a different place or direction - Go away now. Put your toys away. (iii) absent - There were ten children away yesterday. Sorry, he is away. (iv) after a verb to show doing something continuously or with much energy - She was still writing away furiously when the bell rang. They were soon chatting away like old friends. (v) 'until completely gone' - The water boiled away. The music faded away. (vi) after use, thrown away - Thrown away polybags are recycled to make new things. 12 Before: (i) earlier than a person or thing or event - The year before last he won a gold medal and the year before that he won a silver. He arrived before me. She has lived there since before the war. (ii) in front of a person or thing - They knelt before the throne. He arrived before the judge. (iii) ahead of another person or thing in order - Your name is before mine on the list. He puts his work before everything. 13 Behind: (i) at the back of or hidden by a person or thing - Who is the girl standing behind Nasima? Stay close behind me. The sun disappeared behind the clouds. The man is behind the curtain. (ii) less progress than another person or thing - He is behind the rest of the class in reading. We are behind schedule. (iii) the role of a person or thing in doing or happening something - What's behind that happy smile? He was the man behind the plan to build a new hospital. 14 Below: (i) a lower level or limit than a person or thing - He dived below the surface of the water. Please do not write below this line. Skirts should be worn below the knee. (ii) less amount or value than a person or thing - The temperatures remained below freezing all day. Her work was well below average for the class. (iii) lower rank or less important than a person or thing - A police sergeant is below an inspector. There are two places below Chelsea in the table.

chunk_text: Lesson-04: Important Prepositions & Their Uses (entries 15-22). 15 Beside: (i) beside a person or thing - He sat beside her all night. There is a mill beside a stream. 16 Besides: (i) in addition to or besides a person or thing - We have lots of things in common besides music. Besides working as a doctor, he also writes novels in his spare time. 17 Between: (i) in the middle of two or more things, objects or people - Q comes between P and R in the English alphabet. I sat down between John and Diana. Switzerland lies between France, Germany, Austria and Italy. (ii) in the time between two days or years - It is cheaper between 6 p.m. and 8 a.m. Many changes took place between the two World Wars. (iii) relation between two - There is a link between unemployment and crime. There is a close relationship between Karim and Rahim. (iv) sharing between two persons or things - We drank a bottle of wine between us. This is just between you and me. 18 Beyond: (i) before a fixed time - It won't go on beyond midnight. I know what I shall be doing for the next three weeks but I haven't thought beyond that. (ii) more than something - Our success was far beyond what we thought possible. She has got nothing beyond her state pension. (iii) not possible - The bicycle was beyond repair. The situation is beyond our control. (iv) out of reach - The handle was just beyond my reach. The exercise was beyond the abilities of most of my class mates. 19 By: (i) means of travel or vehicle - I am going to Dhaka by bus. (ii) as agent - We have a modern dictionary by A.T Dev. (iii) a part of a person's body or dress - I seized him by the collar. She caught her by the hair. I pulled him by the ear. (iv) means or way of doing something (By + gerund) - Salma earns a lot by singing folk song. Children amuse themselves by watching cartoons. (v) money, wages or payment and means of communication - He gets his salary by cheque. She always contacts him by letter. (vi) unit of measurement (price, rate etc.) - We buy banana by the dozen. They are paid wages by the week. We buy milk by the liter. (vii) cause or source of an achievement, gain or event - We achieved our independence by supreme sacrifice. He has gained success by hard labours. They didn't send you the message by mistake. (viii) amount or measure (extent) - He is senior to me by 3 years. They won the game by 3 goals. Bangladesh won the match by 7 runs. (ix) profession - She lives by her stitch. He lived by his pen. (x) according to - It is 5 o'clock by my watch. (xi) beside - He came and sat by me. (xii) birth, marital status, profession etc. - I am a Bangladeshi by birth. He is a lawyer by profession. She is an Italian by marriage. (xiii) before the exact time - I shall finish my work by 11 p.m. 20 Down: (i) from a high place to a low place - The stone rolled down the hill. Tears rolled down her face. Her hair hung down her back to her waist. (ii) along or in the direction of - He lives just down the street. Go down the road till you reach the traffic lights. 21 During: (i) often confused with since and for; During is naturally used with a noun to show time, from start to end - During our vacation, we visited many relatives across the country. During the summer, we do not have to study. (ii) during or in is used when something happens at a stage of a fixed period - We'll be on holiday during/ in July. The old road is sometimes closed during/ in winter. (iii) during is used throughout a time - We need fewer workers during long weekends. There were no classes during the whole of May. 22 For: (i) for someone's use - There is a letter for you. It is a book for children. (ii) to help a person or thing - What can I do for you? Can you translate this letter for me? (iii) to do a work on behalf of someone as a representative - I am speaking for everyone in this department. He presented the matter in the Parliament for the countrymen. (iv) purpose or aim of getting something - He came to me for advice. For more information, call this number. (v) price or value of something - Copies are available for two dollars each. (vi) destination of a vehicle or programme - Is this bus for Chicago? She knew she was destined for a great future. (vii) duration of time - I am going away for a few days. That's all the news for now. (viii) cause (because of) - They are dancing for joy. Cumilla is famous for hospitality. (ix) abbreviation of something - What does SOS stand for? (x) liking or taste etc. - He has a taste for classical music.

chunk_text: Lesson-04: Important Prepositions & Their Uses (entries 23-29). 23 From: (i) place of departure or journey - From Dhaka I will be flying to London. The procession is from the university campus to Shahbag. (ii) time of journey/ from a time - I am on leave from 10 May. She lived in Dhaka from 1990-1995. (iii) place of birth or origin/ source - Jenet Green is from Britain. This is a gift from my brother. He cited a quotation from the Holy Quran. (iv) distance between two places or ideas - It is more than two kilometres from here to the top of the hill. The bus stop is just a kilometre from my home. (v) lower limit of number, price, weight etc. - Apples are available from 90 to 100 taka. Here are the boys from 12 years to 15 years. (vi) natural cause of something - He is suffering from fever. (vii) remedy, protection or defence - He saved the child from kidnappers. Masks reduce risk from swine flu. (viii) material; the material changes in this case - Most Ayurvedic medicines are made from herbs. Butter is made from milk. 24 In: (i) a place or region within boundaries, generally big city, town, state, province, country, continent, world or globe - They are working in the fields. He lives in Dhaka. (ii) volume or capacity of a container - We saw a hungry tiger in the cage. There is a little water in this pond. The meaning of words is given in a dictionary. (iii) profession - My brother is in the airforce. I am in business. (iv) state or position - I see, you are in trouble. He is in good/ poor health. Runa is in the canteen. (v) dress or colour - Today Tisha is in shorts/ tights. I am in jeans today. They are all in black/ red. (vi) before the name of a month, season or year, century and historical period - Summer time begins in May. Dickens died in 1870. The house was built in 19th century. Jazz first became popular in the 1920s. (vii) medium (language/ instrument) - He is writing the answers in ink. Every year many students fail in English. (viii) means of travel, especially if the means is modified by article, adjective or adjective clause, then 'in' is used instead of 'by' - We set out in a small boat. The president came in a red car. We went there in a car which was from Japan. (ix) a special inborn quality of a person - The genius in her is still alive. The poet in her impressed us. The mother in her rose. We saw a friend in the pet dog. (x) part of a whole - There are seven days in a week. There are sixty four districts in Bangladesh. (xi) before a period of time, something happens or ends (within) - I'll be back in an hour. We are leaving home in a few hours. They said they'd finish the work in two or three days. (xii) subject (about) - What are you thinking in this matter? Bangladesh is rich in mineral resources. (xiii) before some Phrase and Idiom like the long run, black and white, lieu of, stead of, association with etc. 'in' is used as appropriate preposition - The sinners suffer in the long run. You should submit it in black and white. Note: in the night ('during a specific night') vs at night ('during any night') 25 Into: (i) movement from outside to inside - The candidate waved and shook hands as he walked into the room. (ii) change of form - Water turns into vapour at 100 deg C. Translate the passage into English. (iii) change of state (especially mental state) - He burst into tears. She flew into rage. 26 Of: (i) relation or ownership - All the furniture of this family will be sold very soon. Is he a cousin of yours? (ii) quality - He is a man of letters. This work is of the highest calibre. (iii) part of something - The key of this lock is missing. The nib of this pen is broken. (iv) part of a whole, especially a member of an institution or organisation, with rank - Roni is a member of the language club. Karim is a teacher of this school. (v) source or origin - The poem of Nazrul is very instigating. Our syllabus is not designed considering the needs of our students. (vi) cause - They died of cholera. She is proud of her noble birth. (vii) about a subject (about) - He is a teacher of English. The result of our annual examination has not been published yet. (viii) with a unit of measurement, the measured thing - We need five kilos of rice. Please give me a sheet of paper. (ix) a fixed person or thing with distance or direction - My office is within two km of my house. The Bay of Bengal is to the south of Bangladesh. (x) age - Jerry was a boy of 4. (xi) material, but the material does not change its form - This is a house of stone. This window is made of glass. (Glass is made from sand) (xii) after some Adjectives like proud, afraid, careful, aware, conscious etc. 'of' is used as Appropriate preposition - Children are afraid of snakes. She is proud of her blue blood. 27 Off: (i) distance of place or time - I fell off the ladder. Scientists are still a long way off finding a cure. We are getting right off the subject. (ii) away from a road or room - We live off the main street. There is a bathroom off the main bedroom. (iii) away from work or duty - He has had ten days off college. I have got three days off firm. (iv) removal of something - You need to take the top off the bottle first. I want about an inch off the back of my hair. (v) what someone usually eats or uses but is not liking now - I am off alcohol for a week. He is finally off drugs. 28 On: (i) contact with a surface or touch - The book is on the table. Why do you have a hat on your head? (ii) near a place - There is a shopping mall on the main road. There is a vast plantation on either side of the road. (iii) at this exact time or a fixed time in the past, travelling - He is on the train for Chattogram. We are on the first plane journey to London. I was on plane last morning. (iv) possession or having something - I have no money on me at the moment. (v) by electronic or musical instrument - I spoke to her on the telephone/ mobile. He played on the guitar. (vi) support (living) with something - We have to live on a small pension. The cow lives on grass. (vii) present or past fixed-time professional work - He was on tour last Sunday. They are on holiday today. I am on official work now. (viii) cause or result (especially in the past) - We congratulated on his brilliant success. The driver stopped the bus on my request. (ix) in the direction of movement, target or subject; no fixed direction (like east, west) is mentioned - You can see the museum on the right. He pulled a dagger on the passer-by. There is a focus on eradicating corruption everywhere in the society. (x) member of an institution - He is on the management committee. I am on the staff of the school. (xi) about a subject (about) - Write an essay on jute. (xii) a fixed day or part of a fixed day and before a date - I'll see you on Sunday. We enjoy much on the weekend. The meeting is on Monday morning. The exam is on May 30th. (xiii) a place or near a place as preposition - Our life on earth is very short. We have a town on the coast. (xiv) before a special day or occasion - I'll be there on your birthday. 29 Over: (i) above a person or thing - She put a blanket over the sleeping child. He wore an overcoat over his shirt. She put her hand over her mouth to stop herself from screaming. (ii) higher position without touching a person or thing - They held a large umbrella over her. There was a lamp hanging over the table. (iii) from one end of something to the other - There is a bridge over the river. They ran over the grass. They had a wonderful view over the park. (iv) on the other side of something - He lives over the road. They reside over the canal. (v) falling from a place - The car had topped over the cliff. He didn't dare to look over the edge. (vi) all or most of something - Snow is falling all over the country. They have travelled all over the world. (vii) more than a fixed time, amount, cost etc. - She stayed in Lagos for over a month. He is over sixty. (viii) under someone's control - She has only the domination over her. He ruled over a great Empire. (ix) during a time - We are over the worst of the recession. It took her ages to get over her illness. (x) to express opinion about something - This is the argument over money. There is no disagreement over the best way to proceed. (xi) by means of something - We heard it over the radio. She wouldn't tell me over the phone.

chunk_text: Lesson-04: Important Prepositions & Their Uses (entries 30-40). 30 Through: (i) something that starts from outside a thing, enters it and leaves it - We travelled through Gazipur on the way to Dhaka. They walked home through the park. 31 Till: (i) generally 'up to' - We are open till 6 O'clock. They do the work till evening. 32 To: (i) direction generally - He went to Dhaka. They have gone to Chattogram. (ii) reaching a fixed state - The vegetables were cooked to perfection. He tore the letter to pieces. His expression changed from amazement to joy. (iii) a limit or end or duration of time - I would say he was 25 to 30 years old. I like all kinds of music from opera to reggae. We only work from Monday to Friday. I watched the programme from the beginning to the end. (iv) a person or thing receiving something - He gave it to his sister. Our teachers cannot make the lessons interesting to the students. I am deeply grateful to my parents. Who did she address the letter to? (v) two things joined together - Attach this rope to the front of the car. Connect this to that. (vi) relation of one person or thing with another - She was married to an Italian. This is the key to the door. That is the solution to this problem. (vii) fixed direction or relation - We have many duties to our parents. It was a threat to world peace. She made a reference to her recent book. (viii) the second part of a comparison or ratio - I prefer walking to climbing. We won by six goals to three. The industry today is nothing to what it once was. (ix) in honour of a person or thing - This is the monument to the soldiers who died in the war. Let's drink to Julia and her new job. (x) purpose or intention - I set out to buy food. I am going to tell you a story. She was determined to do well. His aim was to become President. (xi) result of something - She managed to escape. It was too hot to go out. He couldn't get close enough to see. 33 Toward(s): (i) direction, towards - The student was crossing the road and walking towards Dhaka College. She had her back towards me. (ii) for the purpose of achieving something - This is a first step towards Political Union. (iii) about or concerning - His attitude towards the government policy is positive. He was warm and tender towards her. (iv) near in time - He will come towards the end of the year/ March. (v) to help someone achieve something - The money will go towards a new school building. 34 Under: (i) below something - The book is under the table. (ii) under the influence of something - Shahjalal was arrested for driving under the influence of alcohol. Shirin believes that she is under the influence of a magic spell played by Shahjalal. (iii) lower in rank - I have to work under DGM of the company. (iv) below a fixed age limit - This book is not meant for those under eighteen. (v) under a state - The road is under construction. Your case is under consideration. (vi) according to (according to) - Under the rules, you can't get bonus. 35 Until: (i) generally 'up to' - He continued working up until his death. You can stay on the bus until it reaches London. 36 Up: (i) reaching a higher position - She climbed up the flight of steps. The village is further up the valley. (ii) along a road - We live just up the road, past the post office. They live up this street. 37 Upon: (i) depending on a person or thing - She depends upon you. The decision was based upon two considerations. (ii) a large amount of something spread - Mile upon mile there were no trees. 38 With: (i) together - She lives with her parents. I have a client with me right now. (ii) with a quality or characteristic - He looked at her with a heavy expression. They are both in bed with influenza. (iii) using a tool or instrument for a work - Cut it with a knife. It is treated with acid before being analysed. (iv) filling or covering something - The bag was stuffed with dirty clothes. Sprinkle the dish with salt. (v) about or concerning - Be careful with the glasses. Are you pleased with the result? Don't be angry with her. (vi) together with - She took the meal with wine. (vii) manner or process - He behaved with great dignity. She sleeps with the window open. (viii) cause or result - She blushed with embarrassment. His fingers were numb with cold. (ix) member of an institution or job - She acted with a touring company for three years. I bank with the HSBC. (x) although - With all her faults, I still love her. With all his mistakes, he has been accepted. (xi) material of making something - We make a house with brick. We can make cakes with eggs. (xii) helper - We are with you in your struggle. (xiii) After - The meeting came to a close with a vote of thanks. With these words, I declare the function open. 39 Within: (i) before a fixed time - You should receive a reply within seven days. Two elections were held within the space of time. (ii) not far from something - This is the house within a mile of the station. Is it within walking distance? (iii) within the limits of something - That question is not within the scope of this talk. We are now within range of enemy fire. 40 Without: (i) without getting or except something - They had passed two days without food. He found the place without difficulty. (ii) not with someone - Don't go without me. You cannot survive without her. (iii) not using or taking something - Can you see without your glasses? Don't go out without your coat. (iv) not doing a fixed work - He left without saying goodbye. You can't make an omelet without breaking eggs.

chunk_text: Lesson-05: Appropriate Prepositions - Why is Preposition Necessary? In our language we need to use a number of prepositions after certain words to show the relation between them. These prepositions are called Appropriate Prepositions. In other words, an Appropriate Preposition is a preposition which is appropriate to a word to express its meaning. There are no specific rules for learning Appropriate Prepositions; the only way is to learn them by heart. Example: Some animals are accustomed to eating grass. / Some animals are accustomed to eat grass. Here 'to' is the Appropriate Preposition after 'accustomed' and 'eating' is correct; 'eat' is wrong. Students should learn appropriate prepositions properly. chunk_text: Lesson-01: An Introduction to Conjunction. Read the passage and notice the underlined words: Dipu and Raj are good friends but they are not of the same age. They have been even together as neighbours. Many years back they thought they would settle about but after their higher study overseas they decided to buy land in the same area. When they found it together, Raj said to Dipu, "Let's buy it now or never." They had to face some adverse situations, yet they have maintained their friendship. The words and, but, or, yet are Conjunctions; their main work is to join words, phrases and clauses. Definition: the words used as a link between two or more words, phrases or clauses are called Conjunction. Examples: Rahim and Ram are good friends. Biplob or Sohel will help you. He is poor but honest. Words used as Conjunction: after, and, as, as well as, because, before, but, either, if, in order that, neither, or, since, so that, so, that, unless, until, whether, yet.

chunk_text: Lesson-02: Classifications of Conjunctions. Conjunctions are of four kinds: 1. Co-ordinating Conjunctions (Co-ordinators); 2. Correlative Conjunctions (Correlatives); 3. Subordinating Conjunctions (Subordinators); 4. Sentence Connectors. 1. Co-ordinating Conjunctions: join words, phrases and clauses of the same kind; also called Co-ordinators: and, but, or, nor, neither, for, yet, still, so. Examples: Meena and Raju are going to visit the zoo. The train has arrived but there is no sign of Sheema. 2. Correlative Conjunctions: used in pairs, before the same kinds of Parts of Speech only: both ..... and, not only ..... but also, either ..... or, neither ..... nor, so ..... that, hardly ..... when, scarcely ..... when, no sooner ..... than, as ..... so ..... as, the same ..... as, whether ..... or, no/ not/ never ..... or. Examples: The shoes are not only expensive but also of poor quality. I want to buy both vegetables and milk. He has no car or motorbike. I have never made a film or directed one. 3. Subordinating Conjunctions: join one or more Subordinate clauses to a Principal clause or Main clause; three kinds: (i) Simple Subordinating Conjunctions: after, as, because, before, however, if, once, since, than, that, though/ although, till/ until, unless, when, where, whether, while. Examples: He came after I had left. I will not go out if it rains. (ii) Compound Subordinating Conjunctions: as long as, as far as, as soon as, so long as, so far as, just as, in as much as, so that, in order that, provided (that), considering (that), as if, as though, in case. Examples: She welcomed him as soon as he arrived. You can go there provided you are well. Take extra money in case you need it. (iii) Correlative Subordinating Conjunctions: as ..... as, so ..... as, such ..... that, so ..... that, no sooner ..... than, hardly ..... when, whether ..... or, though ..... yet, if ..... then. Examples: No sooner had he gone to bed than he fell asleep. If I don't return in an hour then call the police. Note: Relative Pronouns and Relative Adverbs can also be used as Subordinating Conjunctions; had, should and similar verbs can be used as Subordinating Conjunctions in Conditional Clauses. 4. Sentence Connectors: join an idea in a previous sentence to an idea in a later sentence; they always point to an already stated idea and build a logical relation between the earlier and later ideas; a sentence connector without a previous sentence is meaningless. Example: On the contrary, he opposed me (needs a previous sentence: I supported). List: also, besides, equally, hence, however, likewise, moreover, on the contrary, on the other hand, only, otherwise, similarly, so, still, then, though, thus, too, yet. Examples: Take the umbrella, otherwise you will get wet. The offer was good, still he refused. He is tired. Or, at least he looks tired. He can't sing. He can't dance either. Difference between Sentence Connectors and Typical Conjunctions: 1. A conjunction joins words, phrases and clauses; a sentence connector builds a logical relation between one idea and the next and usually introduces a new sentence, ending with a full stop/ dash/ comma. Examples: He will buy a car or a bike ('or' is a conjunction). He is tired. Or, at least he looks tired ('Or' is a sentence connector). 2. A sentence connector usually sits at the beginning or end of a sentence; a conjunction usually sits in the middle. Examples: She will either watch TV or listen to the radio ('either' is a conjunction). She can't sing. She can't dance either ('either' is a sentence connector).

chunk_text: Lesson-03: Use of Conjunctions. 1. Co-ordinating conjunctions: And: joins two or more words or sentences. Examples: Sabiha and Saima are good friends. Be attentive and you will succeed. He went to London and joined the seminar. The sun rises in the east and sets in the west. But: joins words or sentences of opposite meaning. Examples: He is poor but honest. He tried his best but failed. Raihan is physically weak but Rakib is healthy. Or: joins words or sentences to express more than one possibility, in an alternative sense. Examples: Move or you will die. Sumi or Rumi will come here. Roney or his father will sow the seeds. Walk fast or you will be late. 2. Subordinating conjunctions: If: two clauses are joined by 'if' to express a condition. Examples: We will not go out if it rains. You can learn more if you read. As/ Because: 'as' or 'because' can join two sentences/ clauses to express a reason. Examples: He was absent from the class because he was ill. He can carry the load easily as he is strong. Since: used to express reason. Examples: I couldn't meet him since I was busy. I helped the boy since he was in danger. N.B. 'since' is also used to express time: She has been living in London since 2000. Many years have passed since she has gone abroad. Though/ Although: Examples: Though he is poor, he is kind. Though he ran fast, he could not win the race. Although he was not invited, he joined the party. Before/ After: Past perfect tense sits before 'Before' and after 'After'. Examples: The patient had died before the doctor came. He reached the school after the bell had rung. When: Examples: I met him last when he was in class eight. Every student keeps silent when the lesson begins. While: Examples: He came to me while I was writing. I saw him while he was eating meals. Therefore: Examples: He has not got a job, therefore, he was unable to maintain his family. I was busy with my studies, therefore, I could not attend the party. That: Example: I said that I would go there. In order that, So that: Examples: Rana works hard so that he may succeed in life. I get up early in the morning in order that I may get enough time to work. We eat that we may live. Lest: Examples: Walk fast lest you should miss the train. Be sincere lest you should make a mistake. Than: used after an Adjective or Adverb in the Comparative Degree. Examples: Raju is taller than Rakib. Gold is more precious than any other metal. Unless: Examples: Unless he pays, they will not do his work. Unless you work hard, you will fail. Till/ Until: Examples: Wait till he returns. Find it until you get. As if: Examples: He speaks as if he were a millionaire. He behaves as if he were a leader. Whether: Example: It is all the same whether you go or not. As ..... as: Example: He is as intelligent as his sister. So .... that: Example: He was so tired that he could not walk. 3. Co-relative conjunction: Both .... and: Example: Both he and his brother are present in the party. Neither ..... nor: Example: Neither he nor his brother has done the work. Either .... or: Example: Either she or her brother has done this. N.B. If the two Subjects joined by Neither ..... nor or Either ..... or are of different Numbers, the Plural subject sits later and the verb is plural. Example: Neither he nor his classmates have met the teacher. No sooner ..... than/ Hardly ..... when/ scarcely ..... when: the first part of such a sentence is Past perfect tense and the second part Past indefinite tense. Examples: No sooner had the bell rung than the teacher entered the classroom. Hardly/ Scarcely had he reached the station when the train left. Not only .... but also: used to join words of the same kind. Example: He is not only healthy but also industrious.

chunk_text: Lesson-01: What is Article? The word which is used to indicate the definiteness or indefiniteness of a noun is called Article. Opening passage about Polan Sarker, a booklover of Bausa village in Rajshahi, with the articles a, an and the in bold: Rajshahi is an old city; it stands on the Padma; a man recognised as a booklover; an old man; he buys books with his own money; The villagers become delighted with books they borrowed from Sarker; reading is a good habit. Articles sit before a noun or noun-equivalent and show whether it is definite or indefinite. Why articles are used: though they work like adjectives, articles belong to Determiners; one article signals that a noun follows; they show whether the thing spoken of is known to both speaker and listener. Articles are used with nouns, but not every noun takes an article, so one must know which nouns need an article and which article to use. Correct article use is one of the hardest parts of English grammar, though dropping articles often still leaves a sentence understandable (e.g. 'Can you lend me book of English Grammar till end of week?' against the version with articles); correct use is still preferable.

chunk_text: Lesson-02: Classification of Articles. Two kinds. 1. Indefinite Article: A and An point to an indefinite person or thing, so they are Indefinite Articles (I see a bird; He is an honest man). 2. Definite Article: 'The' is used to point to a definite person or thing, so it is the Definite Article (The cow is a domestic animal; The Bengalees are freedom-loving nation).

chunk_text: Lesson-03: Rules on Use of Articles, 51 numbered rules in four groups. (i) Selection for 'A', rules 1-10: before a consonant-start countable noun; before vowel-start words pronounced 'You' (a European, a university); before 'o' pronounced 'owa' (a one-eyed man, a one-day cricket match); before number/measure words (a dozen oranges, a million people); for profession (a nurse, a physician); 'most' meaning 'very' (a most wonderful sight); before an unknown person's name or title (A Kamal Basu, A Mr. Jenkin); proper noun used as common noun (a Kalidas, a Shakespeare); 'a' as disguised preposition (went a (on) hunting); before few, little, good many, lot of, great many, good deal (a lot of money, a good deal of books). (ii) Selection for 'An', rules 11-13: before a vowel-start countable singular noun or noun phrase (an apple, an umbrella); before a consonant letter pronounced like a vowel (an M.P., an L.L.B.); before silent-'h' words (an honest officer, an honourable person). (iii) Selection for 'A'/'An', rules 14-24: after 'what' in exclamatory sentences (What a beautiful picture it is!); first mention a/an, later mention the; 'a/an' for one or quantity (a house, an idle boy); first mention of a countable noun; whole class or species (A cow is a domestic animal, An owl is ugly to look at); case in apposition (Tahmina Anam, a Bengali novelist); after such, quite, many, rather (such a busy night, quite a lot of books, Many a ship was wrecked); price, rate or ratio (50 taka a kilo, four times a day, ten miles an hour); each/per (50 taka a day); abstract noun used as common noun (a beauty); only the first of two adjectives takes a/an (a blue and white shirt). (iv) Selection for 'The', rules 25-51: definite person, thing or matter (The man standing in front of you; The water of this pond); whole class with singular common noun (The elephant is the largest land animal; The English are brave); rivers, mountain ranges, seas, gulfs, deserts, island groups (The Padma, the Atlantic Ocean, the Bay of Bengal, the Himalayas, the Sahara, the Andamans); famous buildings, places, political parties, communities (The Empire State Building, The Congress, the Hindus); races (The English, The Bangladeshis); epics, scriptures, newspapers (The Shahanama, the holy Quran, The Observer); ships, aircraft, trains (The Titanic, The Boeing-747, The Upakul Express); ordinals and dates (the first position, the 26th December, 2009); important historic events (the Second World War, The French Revolution); adjective marking a class (the rich, the poor, the brave); comparison with a famous person (the Dundee of Bangladesh, the Byron of Bangladesh); descriptive geographical names (The Punjab, The Deccan, the USA); superlatives (the cheapest dish, the bravest man); definite material or abstract nouns (The kindness of Mohsin, The gold of this ring); 'the ... the' comparatives (The more you read, the more you learn); special emphasis (the singer of the nation); directions (the south, the east); adjective before a proper noun (The great Omar); singular designations (The Headmaster); trades and professions (the army); possessive adjective replaced (struck me on the head, pulled the boy by the ear); comparative of two (the younger of the two brothers); unique things (the sun, the earth); musical instruments (the piano); choirs, orchestras, pop groups (the Miles); some collective nouns (The elite, The peasantry); number-words as units (eggs by the score).

chunk_text: Lesson-04: Omission of Articles, rules 52-70. No article is generally used: before uncountable nouns (fond of x tea, likes x milk); before material nouns (x Iron is a useful metal, x Gold is a precious metal); before abstract nouns (x Honesty is the best policy, x Forgiveness is a great virtue); before institutions used for their own purpose - place, park, building, road, school, college, university, hospital, market (goes to x college everyday, went to x university) - but 'the' when visited for another purpose (went to the college yesterday, went to the hospital to see his friend); before plural nouns in general sense (x Tigers are ferocious animals, x Cows are gentle animals); before meals in general sense (invite you to x dinner, to x lunch); before mankind, woman, children and family relations (x Man is mortal, x Woman is quarrelsome, x Children are fond of sweets); before languages (speaks x French, expert in x English); before some diseases, arts and sciences (x Cancer is a fatal disease, Honours degree in x Chemistry); before games (play x football, play x cricket); before days and months (x January is the first month, x Friday is a Government holiday); before festivals (x Eid-ul-Fitr, x Christmas); before idiomatic phrases (live x from hand to mouth, x bag and baggage, work x at once); before an adjective ending a clause or sentence (I am x innocent, He is x honest); before society, nature, space, night (live in society); fixed expressions keep their article (the same, in the morning, one of the, each of the, as a result, most of the, to the point, by/at the side, a number of, x little, a little, the few, a few, the number of, such a, on the contrary, A many, a must); before radio, television, cinema, theatre as profession or workplace no article, but as entertainment the radio/theatre/cinema take 'the' while television does not (worked in radio and television; listen to the radio; hardly watch television); between adjective and noun (a noble x virtue); before non-noun parts of speech (respected by x all, closely x resembled his father).

chunk_text: Lesson-05: Repetition of Articles. (1) When 'and' joins two or more nouns or adjectives for the SAME person or thing, the article sits only before the first (The Headmaster and Secretary is coming; He has a red and blue pencil). (2) When they mean DIFFERENT persons, animals or things, each noun or adjective takes its own article (The Headmaster and the Secretary are coming; He has a red and a blue pencil). (3) In comparison, if the two nouns are different persons each takes an article (a better poet than a thinker); if the same person, only the first (a better poet than thinker). (4) 'The' sits before a comparative used as adverb (The sooner, the better; The more, the merrier; The more we have, the more we want). Difference between Article and Adjective: articles usually sit before a noun like adjectives, but articles have no Degree of Comparison and no predicative use, while most adjectives have both. Position of Articles: normally before the noun (a pen, an orange, the book); before the adjective when one precedes the noun (a good boy, an intelligent girl, the red pen); before the adverb when one precedes the adjective (a very good boy, a very intelligent girl); after predeterminers many, such, what, much, rather, quite (What a man he is! Many a man was injured; She is quite a beauty); after the adjective when as, so, too, how, quite precede it (How nice a place it is! It is too absurd an answer).

chunk_text: Lesson-01: An Introduction to Sentence. What is a Sentence? A word or a group of words making a complete meaning in a given context is called a sentence. Formation of Sentences: Single-worded and Multi-worded. Single-worded: Yes. / No. / Come. / Go. / Stop. / Halt. / Thanks. etc. Multi-worded: With Verbs (Who's speaking? What's the time now? Have you taken any sweets? Will you take any? Here it is.) and Without Verbs (Mr. Rupom. Five minutes past seven. Not at all. Why not? Ok.). Basic sentence Pattern in English: Subject + Verb (tr. verb) + Object/Complement + Modifier/Preposition etc. Examples: Mr. Jalil cancelled our class yesterday. He drove the car very fast. Rupa and I played on guitar last week. It is very cold today. There were many students in the room.

chunk_text: Lesson-02: Elements of Sentence. Every sentence has two parts: (i) Subject and (ii) Predicate. Subject: the part of a sentence about which something is said; generally a noun or a noun-centred phrase. Predicate: the part that says something about the subject's work; built with a verb or with a verb plus the rest of the sentence. Subject and Predicate may each be one word or more. Examples: Birds (Subject) fly (Predicate). (You) Do your duty. The cow (Subject) gives us milk (Predicate). Five basic structures: 1. Subject + Verb (Horses run. They are playing. Something happened.) 2. Subject + Verb + Object (He loves her. Sumi is playing the flute.) 3. Subject + Verb + Complement (The flute is beautiful. He was a good teacher.) 4. Subject + Verb + Adverbial (The book is on the table. She sings sweetly.) 5. Subject + Verb + Indirect object + Direct object (Mr. Rahman teaches us English. She bought her brother a watch.) Direct object: thing; Indirect object: person.
