chunk_text: Lesson-03: Classification of Sentence According to Meaning. According to meaning a sentence is of five kinds: 1. Statement or Assertive Sentence 2. Question or Interrogative Sentence 3. Commands or Requests or Imperative Sentence 4. Wishes or Prayers or Optative Sentence 5. Exclamations or Exclamatory Sentence. 1. Assertive Sentence: a sentence by which a statement or description is expressed. Structures: Structure-1 Subject + Verb (intransitive) + Modifier (Birds sing at dawn. Roudiya smiles sweetly.) Structure-2 Subject + Verb (intransitive) + Complement (Rafsan is a good boy. The mango tastes sweet. Everything is fine.) Structure-3 Subject + Verb (tr.) + Object (Bithi likes sweets. Rupom bought a bicycle. People praised her.) Structure-4 Subject + Verb + Indirect object + Direct object (Mr. Mukaddes teaches us English. He gave me a book.) Structure-5 Subject + Verb + Object + Complement (The sun gives us light. They elected him captain.) Structure-6 Subject + Verb + Object + Complement + Modifier (The sun gives us light at day time. The police beat the thief severely.) Pattern: Assertive sentences are of three kinds: Affirmative, Negative and Emphatic. In simple present/past tense, do/does/did before the main verb makes Negative and Emphatic statements (I like fish. / I do not like fish. / I do like fish.). 2. Interrogative Sentence: a sentence by which a question is asked about a person or thing. 3. Imperative Sentence: order, request, advice, proposal (Do it. Please help me. Let us go.). 4. Optative Sentence: wish or prayer (May you be happy. Long live Bangladesh.). 5. Exclamatory Sentence: strong feeling or wonder (What a beautiful pen it is! How nice the flower is!).

chunk_text: Classification of Sentence According to Structure. According to structure a sentence is of three kinds: 1. Simple Sentence 2. Complex Sentence 3. Compound Sentence. 1. Simple Sentence: a sentence with one Principal clause only (one finite verb). Example: The boys are playing in the sun. 2. Compound Sentence: a sentence with two or more Principal clauses joined by Coordinating conjunctions (and, but, or). Key points: a compound sentence must have one or more Principal clauses; Principal clauses must be joined by a Coordinating conjunction; a Subordinate clause may or may not be present; two or more Finite verbs are present. Example: She came here and visited her grandfather who is a farmer. 3. Complex Sentence: a sentence with one Principal Clause and one or more Subordinate Clauses. Key points: a complex sentence must have one Principal clause; it must have one Subordinate clause; at least two Finite verbs are present. Example: He said that he bought a book. (Principal Clause: He said; Subordinate Clause: that he bought a book.) Example: He is a man whom everybody respects.

chunk_text: Lesson-01: What is Phrase? Look at the sentences: Mr. Rahman is a man of letters. He tried heart and soul. Tell us the matter in brief. In the sentences above, 'a man of letters', 'heart and soul' and 'in brief' each work like a part of speech; but these groups of words have no subject or finite verb, yet they express a definite meaning. Definition: when several words without a Subject and a Finite verb are used together, work like a part of speech and express a definite meaning, that is called a phrase. A group of words without a subject and a finite verb, especially one that works as a part of speech and has a particular meaning when used together is called Phrase. A Phrase works in a sentence as parts of speech; according to whichever part of speech it works like, the phrase is named after that part of speech.

chunk_text: Lesson-02: Classifications of Phrase. Phrase is generally of seven kinds: 1. Noun phrase; 2. Adjective phrase; 3. Verb phrase; 4. Adverb phrase; 5. Prepositional phrase; 6. Conjunctional phrase; 7. Interjectional phrase. Features of a Phrase: no Subject; no Finite verb; works as Parts of speech; expresses a definite meaning like a single word. 1. Noun phrase: the Phrase that does the work of a Noun is called a Noun Phrase. Examples: To rise early is beneficial to health. Everybody wishes to be happy. Weal and woe come by turns. In the first sentence 'To rise early' is used as the subject of the verb 'is' and does the work of a Noun; in the second 'To be happy' is used as the object of the verb 'wish' and does the work of a Noun; in the third 'Weal and woe' is used as the subject of the verb 'come' and does the work of a Noun - so these Phrases are Noun Phrases. The first two are formed with Noun Infinitive + Object and the third with two Nouns joined by 'and'. Also Adjective + Noun (a good deal, black mail, a narrow escape), Noun + Preposition + Object (a bed of roses, a man of letters, birds of a feather), Gerund + Object (walking in the morning, reading novels, watching TV) etc. work as Noun Phrases. 2. Adjective Phrase: the Phrase that works like an Adjective is called an Adjective Phrase. Examples: The boy standing in the corridor is a new-comer. The man sitting behind the stage knows it. 'standing in the corridor' and 'sitting behind the stage' qualify the nouns 'The boy' and 'The man' respectively, i.e. they work like Adjectives, so they are Adjective Phrases; both are formed with Present Participle + Preposition + Object. Also Preposition + Adjective + Noun (with black eyes, of tender age), Past Participle + Preposition + object (damaged by floods, absorbed in study), As + Adjective + As + Noun (as soft as feather, as red as blood), Adjective + Preposition + Object (second to none, out of fashion), Adjective + and/or/but + Adjective (null and void, slow and steady) etc. work as Adjective Phrases. 3. Verb Phrase: the Phrase that works like a verb in a sentence is called a Verb Phrase. Examples: He could not make out the theme of the poem. Do not run after money. 'make out' and 'run after' work like verbs, so they are verb phrases. 4. Adverb Phrase: the Phrase that does the work of an Adverb is called an Adverb Phrase. Examples: We faced problem at every step. I meet him now and then. 'at every step' and 'now and then' give extra information about the verbs 'faced' and 'meet', so they are Adverb Phrases. Also place (on the way, to a foreign land, in the field), time (once upon a time, all day long, in no time), manner (at any cost, in full swing, with great care) and Nominative absolute (The sun having set, they returned home) etc. work as Adverbial Phrases. 5. Prepositional Phrase: the Phrase that does the work of a Preposition is called a Prepositional Phrase. Examples: I was absent owing to my illness. Shammy took English instead of History. She succeeded by dint of perseverance. 'owing to', 'instead of' and 'by dint of' sit before the nouns illness, history and perseverance and connect those nouns with the other parts of the sentence, i.e. they work like Prepositions, so these Phrases are Prepositional Phrases. 6. Conjunctional Phrase: the Phrase that does the work of a Conjunction is called a Conjunctional Phrase. Examples: He as well as his friends attended the meeting. The students stood up as soon as the teacher entered the classroom. In the first sentence 'as well as' joins the two Subjects 'He' and 'his friends'; in the second 'as soon as' sits in the middle of the sentence and joins two clauses; both Phrases work like Conjunctions, so they are Conjunctional Phrases. 7. Interjectional Phrase: the Phrase that does the work of an Interjection is called an Interjection Phrase. Examples: By God! I shall help you. What a pity! You failed in the examination. 'By God' and 'What a pity' express emotion, sorrow etc., and work like Interjections, so they are Interjectional Phrases.

chunk_text: Lesson-03: What is Clause? Clause means a part of a sentence. Definition: the group of words that has a subject and a finite verb and is used like a part of speech, forming a sentence or working as a part of a bigger sentence, is called a Clause. A clause is a group of words which forms a sentence or a part of sentence and has a subject and a finite verb. Examples: I know the boy who is poor. He has a ring which is made of gold. In the two sentences above, 'who is poor' and 'which is made of gold' each have a subject and a finite verb, so we can call these two parts clauses.

chunk_text: Lesson-04: Classification of Clause. Clause is of three kinds: 1. Principal clause; 2. Sub-ordinate clause; 3. Co-ordinate clause. Features of a Clause: it has a Finite verb; it works like Parts of speech; it expresses meaning like a single word; it can be called a small sentence within a sentence. 1. Principal Clause: the Clause that can express complete meaning independently without depending on any other Clause is called a Principal Clause. A Principal Clause has a subject and a finite verb. Examples: He passed the exam since he worked hard. He is honest though he is poor. In the two sentences above, 'He passed the exam' and 'He is honest' express meaning independently without depending on the other part of the sentence; moreover, the clauses can each be used independently as a sentence - that is why they are Principal Clauses. 2. Sub-ordinate Clause: Sub-ordinate means dependent. The Clause that depends on the Principal Clause to express its meaning is called a Sub-ordinate Clause. Examples: I don't know when he will come. He could not attend the class because he was ill. In the two sentences, 'when he will come' and 'because he was ill' depend respectively on 'I don't know' and 'He could not attend the class' to express their meaning completely - so these two parts are Sub-ordinate Clauses. Sub-Ordinate Clause is of three kinds: i. Noun Clause; ii. Adjective Clause; iii. Adverbial Clause. i. Noun Clause: the Clause that does the work of a Noun in a sentence is called a Noun Clause. Examples: I know when he will arrive. Can you tell me how he finished it? Uses of Noun Clause: a. As Subject of a Verb: What he told is true. That he is a scholar is known to all. b. As Object of a Verb: He wrote that he might come. I know that he is brilliant. c. As object of a Preposition: It depends on how you take it. He knows nothing of what his brother has done. d. As Complement of a Verb: That is what I wanted. The fact is that I am tired. e. As Apposition of a Noun or Pronoun: It is true that he is honest. It is obvious that he will not attend the party. ii. Adjective Clause: the Clause that does the work of an Adjective in a sentence is called an Adjective Clause. Examples: This is the man who brought the bag. Tell me the way how you did it. The boy who came here yesterday is my friend. Note: an Adjective Clause is also called a Relative Clause; an Adjective Clause sits just after the qualifying noun it qualifies. Examples: The man who came here is poor. Tell me the reason why he did it. Table: Noun Clause 'Tell me when he will arrive.' / Adjective Clause 'Tell me the time when he will arrive.'; Noun Clause 'Tell me who bought it.' / Adjective Clause 'I know the man who bought it.' iii. Adverbial Clause: the Clause that does the work of an Adverb in a sentence is called an Adverbial Clause; an Adverbial Clause modifies an adjective, a verb or another adverb in a sentence like an Adverb. Adverbial clauses work as follows: A. Adverb Clause of Time: this Adverb Clause shows the time of the work; it starts with When, whenever, while, before, after, till, until, since etc. Examples: He came when he was a small boy. He came after we had left. B. Adverb Clause of Place: this Adverb Clause shows place; it starts with Where, wherever. Examples: We shall go where you live. You may travel wherever you like. C. Adverb Clause of Manner: this Adverb Clause shows the manner of a work; it generally starts with 'as'. Examples: He helped as we expected. Write down as you like. D. Adverb Clause of Reason: this Adverb Clause shows a reason; it answers questions like 'why', 'for what' or 'for which reason'; it starts with Because, that, as, since etc. Examples: Since he was busy, he could not join the meeting. Everybody likes him because he is cooperative. I am pleased that you have done it. E. Adverb Clause of Purpose: this Adverb Clause shows a purpose; it starts with That, so that, lest, in order that etc. Examples: We eat so that we may live. He works hard in order that he may prosper in life. F. Adverb Clause of Result: this Adverb Clause shows the result of a work; it starts with so .... that, such .... that etc. Examples: He is so weak that he cannot walk. You are such a fool that nobody can depend on you. G. Adverb Clause of Condition: this Clause shows a condition; it starts with If, unless, whether, in case, provided, on condition etc. Examples: If he works hard, he will succeed. I shall wait until you return. It is all the same whether you come or not. H. Adverb Clause of Concession: it starts with Though, although, even, even if etc. Examples: Though he is rich, he is honest. Even if you are in danger, I will help you. I. Adverb Clause of Comparison: this Adverb Clause shows comparison; it starts with As .... as, such .... as, so .... as, than etc. Examples: You are so clever as your brother. My friend is stronger than I. I am not as tall as my brother. 3. Co-ordinate Clause: when two or more clauses of the same kind are joined by a Co-ordinating Conjunction (and/ or/ but/ not only .... but also) and form a sentence, they are called Co-ordinate Clauses. Example: The sky was clear and the weather was fine. In the sentence above there are two Clauses: 'The sky was clear' and 'the weather was fine'; both Clauses express meaning independently, i.e. both are Principal Clauses joined by 'and' to form one sentence, and each clause can be used independently as a sentence - so each of them is a Co-ordinate Clause. More Examples: It was dark everywhere and we could not go out. He was poor but he was honest.

chunk_text: Lesson-01: An Introduction to Transformation of Sentences. Transformation of sentences, or changing the form of a sentence, is a very important and extensive subject in the practice and development of grammar-based language. The process of transforming one sentence into another structurally without changing the meaning is called Transformation of sentence. The transformation process is mainly sentence-centred, so it can be completed in different ways. Pattern-1: Interchange of Sentences - i. Affirmative to Negative; ii. Assertive to Interrogative; iii. Exclamatory to Assertive; iv. Assertive to Imperative; v. Assertive to Exclamatory. Pattern-2: Degrees of comparison (Interchange of Positive, Comparative & Superlative).

chunk_text: Lesson-02: Interchange of Sentences. Affirmative to Negative. Rule 1: if in an Affirmative sentence the word 'only' or 'alone' qualifies a person, to make it Negative without changing the meaning, 'None but' is used at the beginning of the sentence in place of 'only' or 'alone', with no other change. Examples: Affir.: Only he can do the sum. Neg.: None but he can do the sum. Affir.: Allah alone can save us from danger. Neg.: None but Allah can save us from danger. Note: here 'only' generally sits before the person or noun/ pronoun it indicates, and 'alone' sits after that noun/ pronoun. Note: for objects, ideas or subjects, 'nothing but' is used in place of 'only', and for age or number 'not more than/ not less than' is used in place of 'only', with no other change. Examples: Affir.: I have only some rice in my house. Neg.: I have nothing but some rice in my house. Affir.: My uncle was only twenty. Neg.: My uncle was not more than twenty. Affir.: Only virtue prevails in the long run. Neg.: Nothing but virtue prevails in the long run. Rule 2: if an Affirmative Sentence has must, have to/ can etc., to make it Negative, 'cannot but/ cannot help' is used in place of must; but after 'cannot help' the verb takes 'ing'. Examples: Affir.: I have to do the work. Neg.: I cannot but do the work. Affir.: They must obey the rules. Neg.: They cannot but obey the rules. Rule 3: to make a sentence with Every or all Negative, in place of Every or all first 'There is no' is used + the Noun after Every or all + 'but' + the rest of the given Sentence. Examples: Affir.: Every king has a crown. Neg.: There is no king but has a crown. Affir.: Everyone wants to be happy. Neg.: There is no one but wants to be happy. Affir.: Every rose has a thorn. Neg.: There is no rose but has a thorn. Affir.: All men are mortal. Neg.: There is no man but is mortal. Rule 4: to make 'As soon as' Negative, in place of 'As soon as' 'No sooner had' is used + the Subject of the sentence + the Past participle of the main Verb + the rest of the Sentence + 'than' + the second Clause. Example: Affir.: As soon as the thief saw the police, he ran away. Neg.: No sooner had the thief seen the police than he ran away. Rule 5: to make a sentence with a Superlative degree Negative, follow this Structure: No other + the part after the Superlative + Verb + so/ as + the positive form of the Superlative degree + as + the Subject of the given Sentence. Example: Affir.: Romeo is the best boy in the village. Neg.: No other boy in the village is as good as Romeo. Rule 6: when an Affirmative Sentence is changed to Negative, the Negative form of the Affirmative word in the sentence can be used, and in that case 'not' must sit before that Negative word. Examples: Affir.: Jasim is honest. Neg.: Jasim is not dishonest. Affir.: I found him happy. Neg.: I did not find him unhappy. Rule 7: to make an Affirmative Sentence with 'Always' Negative, 'never' is used in place of 'always' and the opposite word (Antonym) of the Affirmative (key word) is used. Examples: Affir.: I always remember you. Neg.: I never forget you. Affir.: Hira is always punctual. Neg.: Hira is never late. A list of Antonyms of some words very frequently used in Transformation is given: able-unable, agree-disagree, arrive-depart, bright-dark, correct-incorrect, doubtful-sure, fat-thin, friend-foe, grateful-ungrateful, healthy-unhealthy, import-export, love-hate, pleasant-unpleasant, present-absent, regular-irregular, rich-poor, sincere-insincere, top-bottom, wise-unwise/ foolish, active-inactive, always-never, believe-disbelieve, comfortable-uncomfortable, defend-attack, equal-inequal, freedom-bondage, good-bad, happy-unhappy, honesty-dishonesty, kind-unkind/ cruel, moral-immoral, please-displease, punctual-late, remember-forget, rise-fall, sorrow-joy, unity-diversity/ disunity, young-old. Rule 8: to make an Affirmative Sentence with 'Too....to' Negative, 'so....that' must be used. Examples: Affir.: He is too weak to walk. Neg.: He is so weak that he cannot walk. Affir.: He is too honest for us to disobey. Neg.: He is so honest that we cannot disobey him. Rule 9: to make an Affirmative Sentence with 'As...... as' Negative, 'not less' is used in place of the first 'As' and 'than' in place of the last 'As'. Examples: Affir.: Jim and Della were as wise as the Magi. Neg.: Jim and Della were not less wise than the Magi. Negative to Affirmative: changing a Negative Sentence to an Affirmative Sentence is mainly the reverse process of changing Affirmative to Negative; so if the rules of Affirmative to Negative transformation are practised, a Negative Sentence can easily be changed to an Affirmative Sentence. Examples: Neg.: I am never late in the office. Affir.: I am always punctual in the office. Neg.: He did not disagree with me. Affir.: He agreed with me. Neg.: They did not leave the place quickly. Affir.: They left the place slowly. Neg.: He is not a traitor. Affir.: He is a patriot. Neg.: They are too wise for anyone to deceive. Affir.: They are so wise that no one can deceive them. Assertive to Interrogative/ Question/ Statements to Questions. Rule 1: to change an Assertive Sentence with an auxiliary Verb to Interrogative without changing the meaning, if the Sentence is Affirmative or yes-meaning, use this rule: To be verb first + n't + Subject + the rest + the question mark (?). Examples: Asser.: Habib is working hard. Int.: Isn't Habib working hard? Asser.: Murad is going to buy a car. Int.: Isn't Murad going to buy a car? Rule 2: when a Negative-meaning Assertive Sentence is made Interrogative, the Negative word is dropped and the auxiliary Verb comes first. Examples: Neg.: You do not know me well. Int.: Do you know me well? Neg.: The boy doesn't play football. Int.: Does the boy play football? Neg.: He did not get the job. Int.: Did he get the job? Rule 3: i. Rule for making an Assertive Sentence in Present Indefinite Tense without an auxiliary verb Interrogative: first Don't/ Doesn't + the given Subject + the main Verb + the rest + the question mark (?). Examples: Asser.: You know me well. Int.: Don't you know me well? Asser.: The boy plays football. Int.: Doesn't the boy play football? ii. Rule for making an Assertive Sentence in Past Indefinite Tense without an auxiliary verb Interrogative: first Didn't + the given Subject + the Present form of the given main Verb + the rest + the question mark (?). Example: Asser.: They finished their duties. Int.: Didn't they finish their duties? Rule 4: if an Assertive sentence has 'Never', when it is made Interrogative it becomes 'Ever', and if it has 'Nothing' it becomes 'Anything', and if it has 'No' it becomes 'any'. Examples: Asser.: I have never been to Cox's Bazar. Int.: Have I ever been to Cox's Bazar? Asser.: They never went to Dhaka. Int.: Did they ever go to Dhaka? Asser.: I know nothing about it. Int.: Do I know anything about it? Asser.: There is no room in the bench. Int.: Is there any room in the bench? Rule 5: to make an assertive sentence with Everybody/ everyone/ all Interrogative, in place of them first 'Who' + don't/ doesn't/ didn't + the Present form of the main Verb + the part after the main Verb + the question mark (?). Examples: Asser.: Everybody likes an honest man. Int.: Who doesn't like an honest man? Asser.: Everybody loves her mother. Int.: Who does not love her mother? Asser.: Everybody wants to be rich. Int.: Who doesn't want to be rich? Asser.: Everyone joined the party. Int.: Who didn't join the party? Rule 6: to make Nobody/ None/ No one Interrogative, in place of them 'Who' + the rest + the question mark (?). Examples: Asser.: Nobody trusts a liar. Int.: Who trusts a liar? Asser.: Nobody loves a liar. Int.: Who loves a liar? Asser.: None can be successful without hard work. Int.: Who can be successful without hard work? NB: in some cases a Negative sentence is used to put emphasis on an affirmative statement; basically the sentence is Affirmative and such sentences are a combination of negative and interrogative/ question; such sentences express affirmative or positive emphasis. Example: Asser.: Rupom is talking to the girl. Neg-Int.: Isn't Rupom talking to the girl? Note: if the Subject of a Sentence is a noun, to make a Neg-Int the Auxiliary verb with 'not' sits before that Subject, and if the subject is a pronoun the Auxiliary verb can be used before the subject in contracted form too. Examples: Asser.: Asma goes to school. Neg-Int.: Does not Asma go to school? Asser.: He works hard. Neg-Int.: Doesn't he work hard? Exclamatory to Assertive. Rule 1: to make an Exclamatory Sentence with How, What etc. Assertive, first the Subject + Verb + very/ great + the rest. Examples: Excl.: What a fool he is! Asser.: He is a great fool. Excl.: How beautiful the bird/ flower is! Asser.: The bird/ flower is very beautiful. If the structure of the Exclamatory Sentence is what + adjective + uncountable/ plural noun, 'The' must sit before the noun when making it Assertive. Examples: Excl.: What beautiful weather! Asser.: The weather is very beautiful. Excl.: What lovely flowers! Asser.: The flowers are very lovely. Rule 2: i. To make an Exclamatory Sentence with 'Hurrah' assertive, in place of Hurrah 'It is a matter of joy that' + the rest. Example: Excl.: Hurrah! We have won the match. Asser.: It is a matter of joy that we have won the match. ii. If an Exclamatory Sentence begins with 'Alas', when making it Assertive, in place of Alas 'It is a matter of sorrow that' + the part after Alas. Example: Excl.: Alas! He is undone. Asser.: It is a matter of sorrow that he is undone. Rule 3: i. If an Exclamatory Sentence begins with 'If', first the subject + wish + the part after 'if'. Example: Excl.: If I were a bird! Asser.: I wish I were a bird. ii. If an Exclamatory Sentence begins with 'had', first the Subject + wish + the subject again + 'had' + the rest. Examples: Excl.: Had I the wings of a bird! Asser.: I wish I had the wings of a bird. Excl.: Had I been a king! Asser.: I wish I had been a king. Rule 4: if an Exclamatory Sentence begins with 'Would that', first the given Subject + wish + the part after 'would that'. Example: Excl.: Would that I were a child again! Asser.: I wish I were a child again. Assertive to Exclamatory. Rule 1: when an Assertive Sentence is changed to an Exclamatory Sentence, the Exclamatory Sentence is formed on the basis of the noun, adjective or adverb in the Assertive Sentence; the following structures can be followed. i. If the adjective in the Assertive Sentence expresses a favourable idea of the related noun, that adjective is placed in the sentence as a modifier when making it exclamatory; the structure is: What + modifier + noun + other word. Examples: Asser.: It is an excellent idea. Excl.: What an excellent idea it is! Asser.: Friday was a fine holiday. Excl.: What a fine holiday Friday was! ii. If the adjective in the Assertive Sentence expresses a derogatory meaning of the related noun, it is better not to mention the adjective when changing it to an Exclamatory Sentence; the structure is: What + noun + other word. Examples: Asser.: He is a peculiar man. Excl.: What a man he is! Asser.: It is a silly idea. Excl.: What an idea it is! iii. If in the Assertive Sentence the meaning of the adjective is predominantly felt (To be heightened the effect or meaning of adjective), the structure can be: How + adjective/ adverb + other word. Remember that such Exclamatory sentences mainly Intensify the meaning of the Adjective/ Adverb, so there is no need to put the intensifying adverb (very, completely, absolutely etc.) used in the Assertive Sentence into the Exclamatory Sentence. Examples: Asser.: He is very tall. Excl.: How tall he is! Asser.: The play was completely amusing. Excl.: How amusing the play was! Rule 2: when an Assertive sentence with 'Wish + were' is made Exclamatory, everything from the beginning up to 'wish' is dropped + 'If' + the rest + the exclamation mark (!). Examples: Asser.: I wish I were a child again. Excl.: If I were a child again! Asser.: I wish I were a bird. Excl.: If I were a bird! Rule 3: when an Assertive sentence with 'Wish + had' is made Exclamatory, everything from the beginning up to 'wish' is dropped + the given 'had' sits at the beginning of the sentence + the rest unchanged + the exclamation mark (!). Example: Asser.: I wish I had been a magician. Excl.: Had I been a magician! Rule 4: when an Assertive sentence with 'Wish + could' is made Exclamatory, everything from the beginning up to 'wish' is dropped + 'would that/ if' sits at the beginning of the sentence + the rest unchanged + the exclamation mark (!). Example: Asser.: We wish we could be champion. Excl.: Would that we could be champion! Assertive to Imperative. Rule 1: rule for changing an Assertive sentence that is yes-meaning or Affirmative to Imperative: Structure: the present form of the main verb of the given Sentence + the part after the given verb. Examples: Affir.: You should do the work. Imp.: Do the work. Affir.: You speak the truth. Imp.: Speak the truth. Rule 2: rule for changing an Assertive sentence that is no-meaning to Imperative: Structure: Do not/ Don't + the Present form of the main Verb of the given sentence + the part after the given verb. Examples: Asser.: You should not kill your time. Imp.: Do not kill your time. Asser.: You should not find fault with others. Imp.: Don't find fault with others. Rule 3: rule for making an Assertive sentence with 'Never' Imperative: Structure: the given 'Never' + the present form of the given main verb + the part after the verb. Example: Affir.: You should never speak ill of others. Imp.: Never speak ill of others. Rule 4: if the Subject of an Assertive sentence is First person or Third person, it must be made Imperative by this rule: Structure: Let + the Objective form of the given Subject + from the main verb of the given sentence to the end. Examples: Asser.: We should settle the dispute. Imp.: Let us settle the dispute. Asser.: He wants to go out. Imp.: Let him go out. Asser.: He plays cricket. Imp.: Let him play cricket. Asser.: We should go out. Imp.: Let us go out. Rule 5: rule for making an Assertive Sentence with First person or Third person that has 'not' Imperative: Structure: Let + the Objective form of the given subject + not + from the given verb to the end. Examples: Asser.: We do not hate the poor. Imp.: Let us not hate the poor. Asser.: They do not watch the film. Imp.: Let them not watch the film.

chunk_text: Lesson-03: Degrees of Comparison (Interchange of Positive, Comparative & Superlative). Superlative to Positive. Rule 1: rule for changing an ordinary Superlative Degree (with 'the') to Positive Degree: i. first 'No other' + ii. the part after the given Superlative + iii. the Singular form of the Verb + iv. 'as' + v. the Positive form of the Superlative degree + vi. 'as' + vii. the Subject of the given Sentence. Examples: Super.: Hira is the best girl in our locality. Positive: No other girl in our locality is as good as Hira. Super.: Panna is the most brilliant girl in the class. Positive: No other girl in the class is as brilliant as Panna. Note: if 'of all/ of any' sits after the Superlative Degree, it is dropped. Examples: Super.: Romeo is the best of all boys. Positive: No other boy is as good as Romeo. Super.: It burns the prettiest of any wood. Positive: No other wood burns as pretty as it. Rule 2: rule for changing a Superlative Degree with 'One of the' to Positive Degree: i. first 'Very few' + ii. the part after the Superlative degree + iii. the plural form of the Verb + iv. 'so' + vi. the Positive form of the Superlative degree + v. 'as' + vii. the Subject of the given Sentence. Note: after all other, few other, many other, most other, one of the, very few, the Plural form of the Noun/ Pronoun sits. Examples: Super.: Tahsin is one of the best boys in the class. Positive: Very few boys in the class are so good as Tahsin. Super.: Akbar was one of the greatest kings of India. Positive: Very few kings of India were so great as Akbar. Super.: Habib is one of the cleverest boys. Positive: Very few boys are so clever as Habib. Comparative to Positive. Rule 1: rule for changing a Comparative Degree with 'Than any other/ all other' to Positive Degree: i. first 'No other' + ii. the part after 'any other' or 'all other' + iii. verb + iv. 'as' + v. the positive form of the Comparative degree + vi. 'as' + vii. the Subject of the given Sentence. Examples: Comp.: Boby is taller than any other girl in the class. Positive: No other girl in the class is as tall as Boby. Comp.: Tanvir is more intelligent than all other boys. Positive: No other boy is as intelligent as Tanvir. Rule 2: rule for changing a Comparative Degree with two-sided comparison to Positive Degree: i. the part after 'than' of the given Sentence first + ii. verb + iii. if the main sentence is Affirmative, 'not' is used, and if the main sentence is Negative, 'not' is dropped + iv. if the changed sentence is affirmative, 'as' and if negative, 'so' + v. the Positive form of the Comparative degree + vi. + 'as' + vii. the first Subject of the given Sentence. Examples: Comp.: Panna is taller than Hira. Positive: Hira is not so tall as Panna. Comp.: Sumaya is more beautiful than Sadia. Positive: Sadia is not so beautiful as Sumaya. Comp.: Shawn is not cleverer than Romeo. Positive: Romeo is as clever as Shawn. Rule 3: rule for changing a Comparative Degree with 'Than most other/ than few other' to Positive Degree: i. first 'Very few' + ii. the part after 'few other/ most other' + iii. the Plural form of the Verb + iv. 'so' + v. the Positive form of the Comparative degree + vi. 'as' + vii. the Subject of the given Sentence. Examples: Comp.: Javed is stronger than most other boys. Positive: Very few boys are so strong as Javed. Comp.: Tito is more handsome than few other students. Positive: Very few students are so handsome as Tito. Rule 4: rule for changing a Comparative Degree with 'No less/ Not less....... than' to Positive Degree: in place of 'No less' or 'not less' 'as' is used and in place of 'than' 'as' is used at that place; apart from that, no change is made to the given Sentence. Examples: Comp.: Sabrina is no less wise than Sagupta. Positive: Sabrina is as wise as Sagupta. Comp.: Sadheen was no less active than Asad. Positive: Sadheen was as active as Asad. Note: if there is only 'less..... than', in that case in place of 'less' 'not so' is used and in place of 'than' 'as' is used; apart from that, no other change is made to the given Sentence. Examples: Comp.: He is less strong than his friend. Positive: He is not so strong as his friend. Superlative to Comparative. Rule 1: rule for changing a Superlative Degree with 'The' to a Comparative Degree: i. the Subject and Verb of the given Sentence + ii. 'the' is dropped + iii. the Comparative form of the Superlative + iv. 'than any other' + v. the rest of the given Sentence. Examples: Super.: He is the wisest man in the village. Comp.: He is wiser than any other man in the village. Super.: Dhaka is the biggest city in Bangladesh. Comp.: Dhaka is bigger than any other city in Bangladesh. Note: if there is 'of all', in place of 'of all' 'than all other' is used, and in place of 'of any' 'than any other' is used. Examples: Super.: Fahim is the best of all students. Comp.: Fahim is better than all other students. Super.: Asad is the wisest of any boy. Comp.: Asad is wiser than any other boy. Rule 2: rule for changing a Superlative Degree with 'One of the' to a Comparative Degree: i. the Subject and Verb of the given Sentence + ii. 'One of the' is dropped + iii. the Comparative form of the Superlative Degree + iv. 'than most other' + v. the rest of the given Sentence. Examples: Super.: Bhutan is one of the smallest states in Asia. Comp.: Bhutan is smaller than most other states in Asia. Super.: Hadiuzzaman is one of the best poets. Comp.: Hadiuzzaman is better than most other poets. Positive to Comparative. Rule 1: rule for changing a Positive Degree with 'No other' to a Comparative Degree: i. the last Subject of the given Sentence first + ii. the given Verb + iii. the Comparative form of the Positive degree + iv. 'than any other' + v. the part from after 'No other' to before the Verb. Examples: Positive: No other man in the village is so wise as he. Comp.: He is wiser than any other man in the village. Positive: No other spinner in Bangladesh is as perfect as Sakib. Comp.: Sakib is more perfect than any other spinner in Bangladesh. Rule 2: rule for changing a Positive Degree with 'Very few' to a Comparative Degree: i. the last Subject of the given Sentence first + ii. the Verb according to the changed Subject + iii. the Comparative form of the Positive Degree + iv. 'than most other' + v. the part from after 'very few' to before the Verb. Example: Positive: Very few animals are as ferocious as the tiger. Comp.: The tiger is more ferocious than most other animals. Positive: Very few metals are as costly as diamond. Comp.: Diamond is costlier than most other metals. Rule 3: rule for changing a Positive Degree with 'As.... as' to a Comparative Degree: i. the Subject at the end of the given Sentence + ii. Verb + iii. if the main Sentence is affirmative, 'not' is used; but if the main Sentence is Negative, 'not' is dropped + iv. the Comparative form of the Positive degree + v. 'than' + vi. the first Subject of the given Sentence. Example: Positive: He is as wise as his brother. Comp.: His brother is not wiser than he. Positive: Tanvir is not as intelligent as Tazim. Comp.: Tazim is more intelligent than Tanvir. Comparative to Superlative. Rule 1: rule for changing an ordinary Comparative Degree [than (any/ all) other] to a Superlative Degree: i. the Subject and Verb of the given Sentence + ii. 'the' + iii. the Superlative form of the Comparative degree + iv. the part after 'other'. Note: if a Plural Noun sits after 'other', after the Superlative and before that Noun 'of all' is used. Examples: Comp.: He is better than any other boy in the class. Super.: He is the best boy in the class. Comp.: He is taller than all other boys. Super.: He is the tallest of all boys. Rule 2: rule for changing a Comparative Degree with 'Than most other/ than few other' to a Superlative Degree: i. the Subject and Verb of the given Sentence + ii. 'one of the' + iii. the Superlative form of the Comparative Degree + iv. the part after 'most other/ few other'. Examples: Comp: Dhaka is bigger than most other cities in South Asia. Super: Dhaka is one of the biggest cities in South Asia. Comp: Riaz is more popular than few other poets. Super: Riaz is one of the most popular poets. Positive to Superlative. Rule 1: rule for changing a Positive Degree with 'No other' to a Superlative Degree: i. the last Subject of the given Sentence first + ii. Verb + iii. 'the' + iv. the Superlative form of the Positive degree + v. the part from after 'No other' to before the Verb. Example: Positive: No other girl in the class is as tall as Sumi. Super.: Sumi is the tallest girl in the class. Rule 2: rule for changing a Positive Degree with 'Very few' to a Superlative Degree: i. the last Subject of the given Sentence first + ii. Verb + iii. 'one of the' + iv. the Superlative form of the Positive Degree + v. the part from after 'Very few' to before the Verb. Example: Positive: Very few boys in the locality are as wise as Habib. Super.: Habib is one of the wisest boys in the locality. Positive: Very few things were so costly as the fob chain. Super.: The fob chain was one of the costlier things.

chunk_text: An introduction to Conditionals. 'Condition' means 'sorto' (condition). Therefore, the sentences in which a Subordinate clause imposes a condition on the Principal/ Independent Clause are called Conditionals or 'sortadhin bakko'. The part of a Conditional Sentence by which the Condition is expressed is generally preceded by 'if'; this is called the 'if clause'. But a conditional sentence can also be formed without 'if'. A Conditional Sentence with an If clause is called an Open Conditional Sentence, and a Conditional Sentence without an If clause is called a Closed Conditional Sentence. Kinds of Conditional Sentences: Conditional Sentence is of three kinds: (a) First Conditionals, (b) Second Conditionals, (c) Third Conditionals. Conditional sentences have two parts. The first part is called the If clause or Dependent clause, and the second part is called the Principal clause or Independent clause. But the Principal clause can be written at the beginning of the sentence and the dependent clause at the end of the sentence. Structures: First Conditional: If + present +, + future (imperative); Second Conditional: If + past +, + past conditional (subject + would/ might/ could + main form of the verb); Third Conditional: If + past perfect tense + perfect conditional (subject + would have/ might have/ could have + past participle form of verb). First Conditionals. Structure: If + present + future (Imperative). Example: If you invite me, I will attend the party. Analysis: In First conditional, the If-clause imposes such a condition which may or may not be fulfilled. There are two clauses in this structure. One is the principal clause and the other is the subordinate clause; of them the clause with 'if' is the subordinate clause and it is Present indefinite tense. The other clause is the Principal clause and it is future tense or imperative sentence. The If clause is used before or after the principal clause. If the Clause is placed before the principal clause, a comma is placed after it. In this structure, if the If + subordinate clause is given, the Principal clause must be added to it to complete the sentence. The principal clause is generally future indefinite tense/ imperative. Example: If you invite me........... Ans. If you invite me, I will attend the party. Explanation: The If + subordinate clause above is present indefinite tense. So its incomplete part, i.e. the Principal clause, is formed in future indefinite tense to complete the sentence. Worked examples (answers printed in the lesson): 1. If he wants ___. Ans. If he wants, I will help him. 2. If it rains. ___. Ans. If it rains, they will not go to school. 3. ___ if you want to catch the train. Ans. Walk fast if you want to catch the train. 4. If you want to prosper in life, ___. Ans. If you want to prosper in life, work hard. Note: In an Imperative sentence the subject is naturally hidden. An Imperative sentence generally begins with the base verb. Again, in this structure, if the principal clause is given, the incomplete sentence must be completed by adding If + present indefinite tense to it. Example: I will help you ___. Ans. I will help you if you want. Worked examples: 1. You will catch cold ___. Ans. You will catch cold if you play in the rain. 2. They will work ___. Ans. They will work if they get due wage. Possible Variations of This Form: i. If + present + must, should or any expression of command, request, advice. (order, request, advice) If you want to maintain a good health, eat less. If you want to maintain a good health, you must/ should obey the rules of health. If you want to maintain a good health, you had better eat less. ii. If + present + may/ might (possibility) - to express possibility: If the fog gets thicker, the train may/ might delay. iii. If + present continuous, to indicate a present action or a future arrangement. (present work or future arrangement) If you are waiting for the ticket (present action), you had better stand in queue. If you are looking for the clerk (present action), you will find him in the office room. iv. If + present + may/ can (permission/ ability) (permission/ ability) If it stops raining, we may start playing. If your papers are ready, you can apply for a visa. v. If + present perfect: If you have completed the work, I will pay you the wage.

chunk_text: Second Conditionals. In this kind of Conditionals there is mention of a future event, and the condition imposed on it is hinted as if it is impossible to fulfil or even if it is not fulfilled, it is as if it were fulfilled. In this kind of conditional clause there is past indefinite tense and in the principal clause past conditional + should/ would/ might + present form of the verb is used. Structure: If + Past Indefinite + Principal Clause. Or, Principal clause + If + Past Indefinite. Example: i. If he worked hard, he could succeed (in reality he did not work hard). If + conditional clause + Principal clause. ii. I would attend the party if you invited me. But after the Subject in the If clause, 'were' can be used as the verb. Example: 1. If I were you, I would not do the work. 2. If I were a bird, I would fly. Note: In this kind of Clause 'were' is used for all Persons. In this case, instead of 'If', 'were + subject' can be used at the beginning of the conditional. Example: Were I a bird, I would fly. Third Conditionals. In this kind of conditionals the condition imposed cannot be fulfilled because the work of this clause did not actually happen. In this case the conditional clause has past perfect conditional (subject + should have/ would have/ might have/ could have + past participle of verb). If you had worked hard, you could have succeeded. (In reality he did not work hard.) Explaining the above example, it means: if you had worked hard, then you would have succeeded. But in reality he did not work hard. Note: (i) Many times in this kind of Conditional, instead of the subordinate conjunction 'if', 'had' can be used at the beginning of the sentence. Example: Had I seen him, I would have told him the matter. (ii) Adverbial clause of condition often begins with a relative pronoun or Adverb. However diligently you work, you will not succeed. Don't disturb me whatever you do. Whichever systems you adopt, you will not be able to reach your goal. Whatever happens, attend the meeting. Mixed Conditionals (some exceptional conditionals): 1. To express a polite request, 'If you will/ If you would' is used. But 'If you would' is the more polite form. If you will/ would inform me of the matter, I shall be grateful to you. (please help) 2. Instead of 'If + want/ wish', a conditional clause can be formed using 'would like/ care'. If you want to join the party, I will wait for you. If you would like to participate the debate, I will enlist your name. 3. When the speaker assumes that the listener will keep his condition/ request, then this clause begins with 'If you could + verb present form'. But in this case the principal clause is hidden. If you would fill up this form (in an office). If you would fill up this form (in a classroom).

chunk_text: Lesson-01: An Introduction to Wh-Questions. In English, questions are generally asked in two ways: (i) by Auxiliary verb, (ii) by Wh-word. A question beginning with an Auxiliary verb can be answered with Yes or No. These are called Yes/ No Question or Verbal Question. On the other hand, if a question is formed with a Wh-word, it cannot be answered with Yes or No, because a question formed with a Wh-word wants to know some information. So its answer is also given in full. This kind of Ques. is called a Wh-question. Look: (i) Do you study? - Yes. (Auxiliary verb) (ii) What do you do? - I study. (Wh-word) By Wh-word we mean those words which begin or end with W and H (Who, What, Which, Whose, Whom, When, Where, Why and How). With these 9 words, sometimes the subject, sometimes the object, verb, adverb or adverbial is asked about. General meanings of the Wh-words: How (how/ in what manner - used to know how or what it is like); Who, Whom, Whose (used for a person); Which (used for a child, animal, person, thing etc.); When (time), Where (place), Why (reason) etc. are used to know; What (what, which, how much, how many etc. are used to know). Wh-words ask about the subject and the object. In asking about these, the words keep their basic Parts of speech character. The category of the Wh-word group is: Interrogative pronoun: Who/ Whom/ Which/ What/ Whose - used in place of a noun in the sentence; Interrogative adjectives: Which/ What/ Whose - modify a noun in the sentence; Interrogative adverbs: Where/ When/ Why/ How - modify an adjective, verb, preposition and conjunction in the sentence.

chunk_text: Lesson-02: Use of Wh-Words. 1. Who: If you want to know about the Subject of a Sentence (if it is a person), i.e. who or whom it means, you have to ask with 'who'. 'Who' is used in both Singular and Plural cases. Structure: Who + verb + extension + ? Examples: i. Kobita is happy. (Statement) - Who is happy? (Question) ii. Shakib and his friends are playing cricket. - Who are playing cricket? iii. Mou opened the door. - Who opened the door? iv. Sojol will do it. - Who will do it? Note: If the Subject is 1st person, the Wh-question becomes 2nd person. Example: v. My friend helped me. - Who helped you? 2. Whom: If you want to know about the Object of a Sentence (if it is a person), i.e. whom or to whom it means, you have to ask with 'whom' (singular and plural both cases). However, in Modern English the use of 'who' in place of 'whom' is more noticeable. Structure: (a) Whom/ Who + auxiliary verb + subject + main verb + extension + ? Examples: i. I want Shafiq. - Whom do you want?/ Who do you want? ii. Hasib helped the girl. - Whom did Hasib help?/ Who did Hasib help? Structure: (b) With/ To/ By + whom + auxiliary verb + subject + main verb + extension + ? Or, Whom/ Who + auxiliary verb + subject + main verb + extension + ? Examples: iii. She lives with her mother. - With whom does she live? Or, Whom/ Who does she live with? iv. The boy went to the Headmaster. - To whom did the boy go? Or, Whom/ Who did the boy go to? v. The work is done by the boy. - By whom is the work done? - Whom/ Who is the work done by? Note: With 'Who' a question can be formed about both subject and object. 3. Whose: If you want to know about Possession or ownership (if it is a person), i.e. whose, of whom or of which person it means, you have to ask with 'whose' (singular and plural both cases). 'Whose' is used in both Subject and Object cases. Structure: (a) Whose + noun + verb + extension + ? (Subject case) (b) Whose + noun + auxiliary verb + subject + main verb + extension + ? (Object case) Examples: i. This garden is mine. - Whose garden is this? (Subject) ii. Rishad's pen is lost. - Whose pen is lost? (Subject) iii. I took Fahim's pen. - Whose pen did you take? (Object) iv. She is driving her father's car. - Whose car is she driving? (Object) 4. Which: If you want to know 'which one' about the Subject and Object of a Sentence (child, animal, thing or person, both), you have to ask with 'which'. Structure: (a) Which + noun + verb + extension + ? (Subject case) (b) Which + noun + auxiliary verb + subject + main verb + extension + ? (Object case) Examples: i. That boy saw the accident. - Which boy saw the accident? (Subject) ii. The river Narasunda flows through Kishoreganj. - Which river flows through Kishoreganj? (Subject) iii. Rumi will learn Japanese language. - Which language will Rumi learn? (Object) iv. I like mangoes most. - Which fruit do you like most? (Object) 5. When: If you want to know when or at what time a work happened, has happened or will happen, you have to ask with 'when'. Structure: When + auxiliary verb + subject + main verb + extension + ? Examples: i. Paul visited Sundarpur last month. - When did Paul visit Sundarpur? ii. Helen Keller was born in 1880. - When was Helen keller born? iii. Mita gets up early in the morning. - When does Mita get up? iv. Nahian's school breaks up at 4 pm. - When does Nahian's school break up? 6. Where: If you want to know about a place or where a work happens, you have to ask with 'where'. Structure: Where + auxiliary verb + subject + main verb + extension + ? Examples: i. The boy lives in Rangpur. - Where does the boy live? ii. Meena put the book on the table. - Where did Meena put the book? iii. Munna is going to the book fair. - Where is Munna going? iv. Paul's mother keeps the dishes in the cupboard. - Where does Paul's mother keep the dishes? 7. Why: If you want to know why or for what reason a work happened, has happened or will happen, you have to ask with 'why'. Structure: Why + auxiliary verb + subject + main verb + extension + ? Examples: i. The man was rewarded for his honesty. - Why was the man rewarded? ii. We eat to live. - Why do we eat? iii. He could not come on account of his illness. - Why could he not come? iv. I did not go there because of the rain. - Why did you not go there? v. Dipu could not pass as he was lazy. - Why could Dipu not pass?

chunk_text: 8. What: If you want to know 'what' about a thing or event used as Subject or Object, you have to ask with 'what'. To ask a person what class or profession he belongs to, 'what' is also used. Structure-1: (a) What + verb + extension + ? (Subject case) (b) What + auxiliary verb + subject + main verb + extension + ? (Object case) Examples: i. His name is Faiaz. - What is his name? (Subject) ii. He is a doctor. - What is he? (Subject - profession) iii. The news made him laugh. - What made him laugh? (Subject) iv. Paul likes teaching. - What does Paul like? (Object) v. Siam plays cricket. - What does Siam play? (Object) vi. Milk is a nutritious food. - What/ Which is a nutritious food? (Subject) Note: To know about a specific person or thing as subject, 'which' is also used. Besides, to mean a thing, Structure: What + noun + verb + extension + ? Example: vii. This is an English text book. - What book is this? To know about different measurement, age, etc., you have to ask with 'what'. Structure-2: What + noun (measure word) + verb + extension + ? Examples: viii. The length of this room is 12 feet. - What length is the room? ix. It is 9.30 pm now. - What time is it now? Or, according to Structure (a), What is the length of the room? To know how something is/ to describe something, Structure: What + auxiliary verb + subject + extension + ? Example: x. The story was interesting. - What was the story like? xi. The sky is clear. - What is the sky like? 9. How: To know how a work is done, or how old someone is, or what someone's physical condition is like, etc., you have to ask with 'how'. Structure-1: How + auxiliary verb + subject + main verb + extension + ? Examples: i. I went to Saidpur by plane. - How did you go to Saidpur? ii. He became successful by dint of hard work. - How did he become successful? iii. Rubayet is 14 years old. - How old is Rubayet? iv. It was a lovely day. - How was the day? v. She was ill. - How was she? Besides, to know number (in case of plural noun), measurement (in case of uncountable noun) and how long, 'how' is used in different ways. Structure-2: (a) How many + plural noun + auxiliary verb + subject + main verb + extension + ? Or, How many + plural noun + verb + extension + ? Examples: i. He bought ten pens. - How many pens did he buy? ii. Thirty teachers teach in the school. - How many teachers teach in the school? Structure-3: (b) How much + uncountable noun + auxiliary verb + subject + main verb + extension + ? Examples: i. I need 2 litres of milk. - How much milk do you need? ii. It will cost him five hundred taka. - How much will it cost him? Structure-4: (c) How long + auxiliary verb + subject + main verb + extension + ? Examples: i. We have been living here for 22 years. - How long have you been living here? ii. It took an hour to reach there. - How long did it take to reach there?

chunk_text: Lesson-01: An Introduction to Verbals. I want to play cricket (to play is the object of finite verb 'want', doing noun and verb work at once); I started playing cricket (playing is the object of 'started', noun and verb work); I saw him playing cricket (playing qualifies 'him', adjective work, and verb work). A Verbal is a verb form not determined by any subject's person or number that does the work of a Noun, a Verb and an Adjective at the same time. Three kinds: i. Infinitive; ii. Gerund; iii. Participle.

chunk_text: Lesson-02: Infinitives. In the passage the underlined 'to' words are infinitives (To walk early in the morning is good for health; One can get rid of various diseases by walking regularly; It is better to walk on the riverside or in the garden; Many people walk early in the morning to keep body and mind healthy and fresh). Sometimes 'to' may be hidden before a verb's basic form: with 'to' it is a to-infinitive (He went to see the cricket match); without 'to' it is a bare infinitive (I let him (to) do the work). A bare infinitive is only a verb, takes no 'to' before it and no '-ing' after it (I saw him cross the road; He made us laugh); its form looks like a finite verb but it is not one. Use of Bare Infinitive: 1. After 'let' and 'help' (Please help me (to) do this homework; I will not let him (to) take this advantage). 2. After than, but, except, had better, had rather (You had better (to) change your elective subject; I had rather (to) stay here; He did everything except (to) carry out my order; He did nothing but (to) give me false promise; I think he will choose a job than (to) continue his studies). 3. After certain auxiliaries (can, may, must, shall, should, will, would) and often after 'do' (I can (am able to) swim; Do (to) show something new; I will (am determined to) be a teacher; He may (is allowed to) go; You must (are commanded to) obey the rules of our team; I shall (am determined to) join that ceremony; If you came here, I would (be interested to) take you to the sea beach). 4. In Active Voice after please, see, let, make, know, feel, hear, dare, bid, behold, watch, notice (I saw him (to) draw a picture; Make her (to) do the homework; He dared not (to) compete with me; He will not let me (to) live in peace; He bade me (to) go; You can hear me (to) sing a song; She felt the gentle breeze (to) ruffle her hair). In Passive voice these verbs take 'to' (I was made to prepare this lesson; He was seen to sit alone in a remote place), except 'let' (He was let (to) go). Infinitives are of two kinds: 1. Simple/Noun Infinitive; 2. Gerundial/ Qualifying Infinitive. Simple or Noun Infinitive uses: 1. As subject of a finite verb (To tell a lie is a great sin; To find fault with others is easy; better begun with 'It' subject: It is a great sin to tell a lie; It is easy to find fault with others). 2. As object of a verb (I do not like to watch movie; He does not fear to die). 3. As object of a preposition (The patient is about to die). 4. As complement of a verb (His hobby is to collect stamp). 5. As objective complement (We think him to be a fool). 6. To express emotion or ask a question (To think that he would do this! And now what to do?). Gerundial or Qualifying Infinitive expresses purpose, cause, condition or result and qualifies a verb, adjective, noun or sentence (We eat to live; Orange is good to eat; It is time to read; To tell the truth, I don't like that person). Its patterns: 1. Subject + Verb + to/ not to (infinitive) (I want to swim; She decided not to play). 2. Subject + Verb + (Pro)noun + to/ not to (infinitive) (I do not want anyone to show me sympathy; I told Mira not to do that). 3. Subject + Verb + (Pro)noun + bare infinitive (He saw me go out; They made me do it). 4. Subject + Verb + conjunctive (how, what, when, who, whom, whose, why, whether) + to-infinitive (I know how to swim; He doesn't know what to do; when no special skill or training is meant, conjunctive 'how' is not used: We must learn to live in peace). 5. Subject + Verb + (Pro)noun + Conjunctive + to-infinitive (I told Rahim where to go; I asked her where to go). 6. In order to + Verb (We live in houses in order to protect ourselves from rain; 'in order to' expresses a specific purpose and is not used after for + object: This is a gold chain for her to wear, not 'for her in order to wear'). 7. Have to/ has to + Verb (Man has to breathe if he wants to live). 8. Subject + be + infinitive + verb (You are to knock before you come in; You are to write on both sides of the paper).

chunk_text: Lesson-03: Gerund. In the swimming passage the underlined -ing words (Swimming is a good exercise; One must practice swimming to enjoy the sport; after eating; There is a chance of drowning; Floating on the water is an enjoyable game; learn swimming by taking help of a trainer) are Gerunds (swim + ing = swimming; float + ing = floating). A Gerund is the present participle form of a verb (verb + ing) that works like a noun in a sentence, so it is also called a Verbal Noun. Gerund vs Present Participle: they look the same but work differently; a Gerund works as a Noun (Verbal Noun), a Participle works as an Adjective (Verbal Adjective). Uses of Gerund: 1. As subject of a verb (Seeing is believing; Eating much is harmful; Driving too fast is dangerous; Her knitting is beautiful). 2. As object of a transitive verb (I like playing cricket; Start reading; She likes sleeping in the afternoon; I enjoyed reading and writing; I didn't mind joining the music competition; He finished playing at 9 o'clock). 3. As object of a preposition (He has been criticized for writing this novel; He is hard of hearing; I have no objection to walking; She is fond of shopping; after a preposition there is always a Gerund, never an infinitive). 4. As complement of a verb (His profession is driving). 5. As part of a compound noun (This is my reading-room; I have bought a new washing-machine). Note on possessive case with gerunds: I like your speaking in this way (not 'you speaking'); He insisted on my going there (not 'me going there'); I am happy to know about my friend's taking this position (not 'my friend taking this'). Gerund in a Complement: after an objective-case noun/pronoun or a possessive-case noun/pronoun (I don't like Tom/ him watching TV all the time - objective case; I don't like Tom's/ his watching TV all the time - possessive case). Some Important Structures of Gerund: 1. By + Gerund (By eating nutritious food we can be healthy; By being a doctor he wants to help people). 2. Without + Gerund (Without working hard you cannot expect a good result in the exam). 3. N/P + Vi + Gerund (She could not help crying). The Verbal Noun: The + Gerund + of (The reading of newspaper increases our knowledge; The hunting of migratory birds is not good at all). Infinitive and Gerund problems: 1. After some verbs (with no noun or pronoun between the two verbs) a Gerund sits, not an Infinitive: advise, avoid, confess, consider, delay, deny, drop, endure, enjoy, escape, excuse, fancy, finish, forbid, forgive, mind, miss, pardon, practice, prefer, present, stop, suggest (I could not avoid facing the problem; He enjoys watching English movies); but if a noun or pronoun comes between, an Infinitive may sit (Mother advises me to read attentively, not 'reading'; He stops the machine to run, not 'running'). 2. After some verbs an Infinitive sits, not a Gerund: dare, expect, decide, desire, want, wish (He promises to help me, not 'helping'; I want to read in English, not 'reading'). 3. After some verbs both Infinitive and Gerund sit: attempt, begin, continue, fear, forget, hate, learn, like, love, omit, regret, neglect, start, try (They began making the poster - gerund; They began to make the poster - infinitive; I forgot taking moneybag with me - gerund; I forgot to take moneybag with me - infinitive).

chunk_text: Lesson-04: Participles. In the peacock passage the underlined verb + -ing/ -ed words (dancing, gathered, displaying, dancing, charmed) are participles. A Participle is a verb form ending in -ing (present participle) or -ed, -d, -t, -en, -n (past participle). Participles can modify a noun as Adjectives, and with 'to be' or 'to have' they can work as Action verbs (The talking parrots entertained the crowd - present participle as adjective; The wrecked sailboat washed up on shore - past participle as adjective; She is thinking of the children - action verb). Is 'Verb + ing' a Gerund or a Present Participle? If the 'verb + ing' form can be turned into an adjective clause it is a Present Participle, otherwise a Gerund (He killed a flying bird = He killed a bird that was flying; Look at the flowing water = Look at the water that is flowing - both are Present Participles, not Gerunds). Three kinds: 1. Present Participle; 2. Past Participle; 3. Perfect Participle. 1. Present Participle: verb + -ing, generally showing an action going on at present (We saw a girl singing a song; A rolling stone gathers no moss). 2. Past Participle: verb + -d, -ed, -t, -n, -en or -ne, generally showing a completed action (Rotten fish is not good for health; Insulted by his people, the man left his country). 3. Perfect Participle: having + past participle, also called Compound Participle, a mix of Present and Past Participle (Having seen the dog, the fox ran away; Having received her birthday wish, I became very happy). Uses of Participle: 1. As a verb: a participle is always used as part of a finite verb; Present Participle forms continuous tense (Meena is/ was/ will be/ has been playing); Past Participle forms perfect tense (Meena has/ had/ will have done the work). 2. Be + Past Participle forms passive voice (Letters are being typed; The book is being printed). 3. As an adjective: a Present or Past Participle sits before a noun to modify it (He killed a flying bird - Present Participle; He is a retired teacher - Past Participle). 4. As complement of 'be' verb (The news is surprising - Present Participle; The school is closed - Past Participle). 5. To show state: a Present or Past Participle sits after an object and shows its state (I saw the baby crying - Present Participle; I found the house deserted - Past Participle). 6. As an adjective phrase: a Present/ Past Participle can work as an adjective phrase (The girl dancing on the stage is my sister - Present Participle; The eggs bought yesterday are rotten - Past Participle). 7. As an adverb: a participle can modify a verb as an adverb (She came dancing/ singing - Present Participle; She got back home tired/ displeased - Past Participle).

chunk_text: Lesson-01: What is Capitalization? In the passage about Musa Ibrahim, the underlined words begin with a Capital letter; the other words begin with a small letter. In English there are some rules for using Capital letters (big letters). The use of Capital letters is called Capitalization. Use of Capital Letters: 1. The first letter of any complete Sentence is capital. Example: We want to learn English capitalization rules. Dirty clothes give off bad smell and invite germs. 2. The first letter of a Proper noun (country, nation, language, book, newspaper, magazine, etc.) is always capital. Example: Bangladesh, Indian, Bengali, The Daily Star. Mr. Tarek asked if Ali would help. Uncle Billal took us to Dhaka. 3. The pronoun 'I' is always a capital letter. Example: I read in class four. Everyday I learn something new. Listen to what I say. 4. The first letter of every line of a rhyme/ poem is capital. Example: Happy the man, whose wish and care. Content to breathe his native air. A few paternal acres bound. In his own ground. 5. The name of Allah and the first letter of the Pronoun used in place of Him is always capital. Example: Allah had His mercy on us. 6. The first letter of a day, month, season, festival or any special moment is capital. Example: Eid Day, May Day, Xmas Day, April, Spring, etc. 7. The first letter of the name of a group of islands, river, mountain, historical event is a Capital Letter. Example: We go to Andamans. The Jamuna is a mighty river. The War of Independence, etc. 8. The first Letter of a quoted Sentence is Capital. Example: Teacher said, "Obey your parents." Teacher said, "Always speak the truth." 9. Capital Letter is used to express a name or title in abbreviated form. Example: B.A., M.A., A.K. Fazlul Haque. 10. The first letter of the name of a religious book is Capital. Example: The Holy Quran, The Vedus, The Bible. 11. The first Capital Letter is used in addressing a letter. Example: My dear Father. 12. If a person's title or designation is used before his name, it begins with a capital letter. Example: Dr. Rehana works in a govt hospital. 13. The posts of high-ranking government officials begin with a Capital letter. Example: President Bill Clinton. Attorney General Shahed. 14. The first and any important word of the title of a book, magazine, song, film or any creative work begins with a Capital letter. Example: Read the first chapter of Gulliver's Travels. I saw American Pie last year.

chunk_text: Lesson-02: Basic Discussion of Punctuation. Punctuation means pause or rest. While speaking we sometimes stop a little and take breath in the middle. Similarly, while reading or speaking we have to stop from time to time. This stopping is a natural process of the tongue or the breathing system. But if this pause is not used at will but meaningfully, on the one hand pronunciation does not become difficult, and on the other hand the language becomes sweet-sounding and clear. So to understand the meaning of a sentence clearly there is a rule about where and how much to stop in a sentence, and these rules are expressed with the help of some conventional signs; these are called Punctuation or pause signs. In the lion-fox-wolf passage the signs used with the words make the passage clearer and more definite. These signs are Punctuation marks. Without proper use of Punctuation the meaning of a sentence cannot be understood correctly and the sentence does not sound sweet. So it is essential to have a proper idea about Punctuation. Punctuation Marks used in English: 1. Full Stop (.) - generally a pause of 1 second. 2. Semi-Colon (;) - half the pause of a Full Stop. 3. Comma (,) - half the pause of a Semi Colon. 4. Question Mark (?) - generally a pause of 1 second. 5. Exclamation Mark (!) - generally a pause of 1 second. 6. Colon (:) - generally a pause of 1 second. 7. Dash (--) - generally a pause of 1 second. 8. Quotation Marks/ Inverted Commas (" ") - generally a pause of 1 second. 9. Apostrophe (') - no pause. 10. Hyphen (-) - no pause. Rules of Punctuation: 1. Full stop (.) or Period: Full stop (.) is used at the end of a sentence expressing a general statement, order-prohibition, proposal, prayer, etc. Example: Today is my birthday. Blow out the candle. He went to Khulna last week. Note: Full stop was used to mark the abbreviated form of a name and a word. Example: B. A = Bachelor of Arts; M. A = Master of Arts. Nowadays the use of these is being dropped and written as BA, MA. But, in writing Internet and E-mail addresses full stop is used. Example: www.omicongroup.com - a full stop used in this way is called dot. Note: In American English a Full stop is called Period. 2. Semi-colon (;): Semi-colon has two uses. i. If two independent clauses related to each other are not joined by a conjunction, semi-colon is used to separate them. Example: To err is human; to forgive is divine. She looks wise; she has bright eyes. ii. Semi-colon is used to separately understand the word-groups separated by Comma. Example: a. I took a holiday and played golf, which I love; read a lot, which I needed to do; and slept late; which I hadn't done for quite a while. b. They plan to study German, for their travels; chemistry, for their work; and literature, for their own enjoyment. Note: The next part is a part of the same sentence. So, Capital letter cannot be used after Semi-colon.

chunk_text: 3. Comma (,): i. If three or more words or clauses of the same kind are used side by side in a list, comma is used between each of them to separate them. Example: I ate rice, vegetable, and fish. I like reading, listening to music, taking long walks, and visiting my friends. ii. Comma is used to separate the Nominative Case in Apposition from the rest of the sentence. Example: Mr. Aziz, our teacher, is very clever. iii. Comma is used to separate two Independent Clauses joined by a Conjunction like 'but', 'and', etc. Example: They wanted to purchase a new car, but their financial situation would not allow it. I would really enjoy seeing a film this evening, and I'd like to go out for a walk. iv. Comma is used to separate phrases or clauses from the Principal clause. Example: In order to pass the exam, you need to study more. Although he wanted to come, he failed to do that. v. Comma is used to separately express Date, address, place, etc. Example: Mina was born on 15, 1928. Rupom lives in Muktagachha, Mymensingh. vi. If someone's speech is to be used in direct speech, comma is used before the speech. Example: He said, "I can do it." vii. If words like Hello, Yes, No, Well, But, Alright sit at the beginning of a sentence, a comma must be put after them. Example: Yes, I mailed it, Ms Huq. viii. If someone is addressed by name in a sentence, comma is used to separate the name. Example: Tanim, listen to this song. Neel, please turn on the radio. 4. Question Mark (?): If someone is asked a question directly, a Question mark (?) sits at its end. Example: When is she coming? Are you Pollobi Khisa? Where do the Royal Bengal Tigers live? What bird would you like? At the beginning of such interrogative sentences there are generally who, what, where, when, why, whom, how, etc. words. These words together are called Wh-word. Besides, do, does, did, etc. words are also used. 5. Exclamation Mark/ Point (!): If a sentence expresses sudden fear, wonder, joy or any emotion of the mind, an exclamation mark (!) sits at the end of the sentence. Example: What a wonderful day it is! That ride was fantastic! I can't believe he is going to marry her! You did a fantastic job! You look great! What a picture! 6. Colon (:): i. Colon is used to give an explanation on a subject. Example: He had many reasons for joining the club : to get in shape, to make new friends, to loose some weight, and to get out of the house. ii. Colon is also used to express a list. Example: I will need the folowing items : paper, scissors, glue, and paint. The job calls for skills in the following areas: proofing, editing, and database administration. iii. Colon is also used before a quotation or sometimes before a direct speech (in this case comma may also be used). Example: The headline read : "Taxi Driver Battles Gangsters." They shouted : Our families are starving! We need food! 7. Dash (--): Dash is used in case of an interrupted or unfinished speech. Example: I - er - I -, that is, I have failed. 8. Quotation Marks/ Inverted Commas (double " " or single ' '): i. Quotation Marks are used to quote the speaker's words or statement as it is. Example: President Bush said, "We will not tire, we will not falter, and we will not fail." "Have you seen an Igloo?" asked the teacher. ii. To quote another quotation inside a quotation, Inner Quotation Marks are used. Example: 'Dave said, "Good afternoon, Frank,"' recalled Frank. iii. Quotation Mark is used to specially understand a word or phrase related to the context. Example: Thousands were imprisoned in the name of 'national security'. iv. Quotation Marks are used to express the name of an article, book, poem, play, etc. Example: Keats' "Ode to Autumn". I was watching "Match of the Day". Note: (a) In British English single Quotation Marks are used; on the other hand in American English double Quotation Marks are used. (b) Punctuation Marks generally sit inside the quotation marks. But if the Punctuation Marks are logically related to the part outside the quotation, in that case Punctuation Marks sit outside the quotation marks. Example: "That", said Meena, "is all I know." 9. Apostrophe ('): i. Apostrophe (') is used to form the Possessive case of Noun-groups. Example: Adnan's mother took his grandmother to a hospital. Rahim's father is a teacher in Khulna. Aladin's mother was surprised. ii. Apostrophe must be used to mention time. Example: It is 4 o'clock. iii. Apostrophe (') is used to make a Contraction or to join two words. Example: Don't disturb him. (Don't = Do + not) She can't join the party. (cannot = can + not) I'm your uncle. (I'm = I + am) Similarly, Haven't = Have + not; Can't = Can + not; Hon'ble = Honourable; etc. 10. Hyphen (-): i. Hyphen, a smaller joining sign than dash, is used to break a word apart or to join two or more words. Example: I love home-made cakes. - it joins two words. Similarly, cap-seller, full-time, well-known, etc. Generally if a whole word cannot be written at the end of a sentence, it is broken by hyphen and written in the next line. ii. Hyphen is used to write all compound numbers from 21 to 99. Example: My grandfather is sixty-five. We need thirty-eight packets more.

chunk_text: Lesson-01: An Introduction to Speech. Narration means description or statement; from the word 'Narrate' comes 'Narration'. Describing a speaker's statement directly or indirectly is called Narration or Speech. Generally a subject is described in two ways: A. Direct Speech; B. Indirect Speech. In Direct speech the speaker's words are separated by Inverted comma (" ") at the beginning and end and repeated exactly in another's language. Structure of Direct speech: Reporting clause + reported clause (within inverted comma). Example: He said, "I am writing a report on woman empowerment." She said, "Thanks." Parts of Direct speech: 1. Reporting Verb - the verb that directly reports a statement is called the Reporting verb; it is also called the Introductory verb because it sits to introduce any statement. In the examples above 'said' is clearly the Reporting verb. 2. Reported Speech - the reported speech is called Reported speech; in Direct speech it is separated by inverted comma, but in Indirect Speech no Inverted Comma is used; the part inside the inverted comma is known as the Reported clause or speech. 3. Reporting Clause - the clause formed with Subject and Reporting Verb is called the Reporting Clause; 'He said' is the Reporting Clause in the sentences above. It can have different Structures: i. Subject + say (without to + object) - it can sit before or after the Reported speech. Examples: He said, "I worked hard to pass the exam." "I worked hard to pass the exam", he said. ii. Subject + verb (admit/ answer/ assure/ complain/ explain/ pray etc. without to + object) - this is generally placed after the Reported Speech. Examples: "I will lend you some money," he assured. "I feel too bored," he complained. iii. Subject + say + to + object (person object) - this sits after the Reported speech. Example: "You are fit for the post," he said to me. iv. Subject + tell + object (person object) - this also sits after the Reported speech. Example: "I salute you," he told me. v. Similarly the Reporting clause can also sit in the middle of the Reported speech. Example: "I see", he said, "You will shine in life." Indirect Speech is mainly formed as Reporting Clause + Reported Clause (without Inverted Comma). When changing Direct Speech to Indirect Speech, the words used in Direct Speech are not repeated exactly; their Meaning or Substance may sit instead. This change follows some rules, but following only the rules outside the implied meaning makes Indirect speech hard to read instead of easy; so understanding the speaker's implied purpose is very necessary when changing to Indirect Speech. Change or transformation in Indirect speech follows two kinds of rules: General Rules and Special Rules.
