chunk_text: Lesson-02: General Rules of Changing Speech. The General Rules of Speech Change can be applied to almost all kinds of Sentence; these general rules affect: 1. Change of tenses; 2. Change of pronouns; 3. Change of expressions of time/ place; 4. Change of vocative case/ parenthesis. 1. Change of Tenses with Exceptions: the change of tense mainly depends on the tense of the Reporting verb. If the reporting verb is in present or future tense, the tense of the Reported Speech does not change at all. Examples: Neela says, "I went to Singapore". / Neela says that she went to Singapore. He will say, "I have no money." / He will say that he has no money. But if the Reporting verb is in Past tense, the Reported clause also becomes the corresponding past tense. Table: Present Simple -> Past Simple (She said, "It's cold". / She said that it was cold.); Present continuous -> Past continuous; Present perfect -> Past perfect; Present perfect continuous -> Past perfect continuous; Past simple -> Past perfect; Past continuous -> Past perfect continuous; Past perfect -> (No change) Past perfect; Past perfect continuous -> (No change) Past perfect continuous. To remember these changes, a correct idea of tense structure is essential. Exceptions: (a) If Simple present tense is used to indicate future, do not make it Past Indefinite; change it with Future in the past, i.e. with 'would'. Example: He said, "I leave for London tomorrow." / He said that he would leave for London the next day (correct); He said he left for London the next day (Incorrect). (b) If Present continuous tense is used to indicate future, use 'would be + present participle' in Indirect tense, not Past continuous. Example: He said, "I am visiting Cox's Bazar next week." / He said that he would be visiting Cox's Bazar next week (Correct). (c) If several verbs' actions happen at the same time in the past and those verbs are in the same reported speech, the verb of the reported speech does not change even though the reporting verb is in past tense. Example: He said, "The children sang, danced and played". / He said that the children sang, danced and played (correct). (d) Past Indefinite and Past continuous used as Adverbial clause of time do not change to the corresponding Past tense. Example: He said, "When I lived/ was living in a village, I faced a lot of troubles". / He said that when he lived/ was living in a village, he faced a lot of troubles. (e) Wish/ it is time/ it is high time (subjunctive mood - condition, guess or possibility) - unreal past tense remains unchanged in Indirect speech. Examples: He said, "I wish I were the President." / He said that he wished he were the president. (Correct). He said "It is high time, we changed our food habits." / He said that it was high time they changed their food habits (Correct). (f) Would rather/ would sooner/ had better remain unchanged in Indirect speech. Example: He said, "I would rather starve than beg." / He said that he would rather starve than beg. (g) In a sentence with an improbable or impossible condition, the tense of the reported speech remains unchanged. Example: He said, "If I were a bird, I would fly to you." / He said if he were a bird he would fly to me. So the change of tense can depend on the nature of the Sentence, its basic meaning, and the auxiliary elements in the Sentence. Also, if the reported speech in Direct narration has an eternal truth or Universal truth (fundamental truths of science), Habitual fact, proverb or Saying, the tense of Indirect speech does not change. Examples: Teacher said, "The earth moves round the sun." / Teacher said that the earth moves round the sun. He said, "A bad workman always quarrels with his tools. / He said that a bad workman always quarrels with his tools. Change of Modal verb in Reported speech: will -> would (She said, "I'll teach English online tomorrow." / She said that she would teach English online the following day.); can -> could; must -> had to; shall -> would (She said, "What shall we learn in this lesson?" / She asked what they would learn in that lesson.); may -> might (She said, "May I open a new account?" / She asked if she might open a new account.). NB: (i) Could, would, should, might and ought to do not change. Example: "I might go to the cinema," he said. / He said that he might go to the cinema. (ii) In the case of eternal obligation or firm assumption, 'must' and 'had to' do not change. Example: He said, "Every child must respect its parents." / He said that every child must respect its parents. 2. Change of time and place Adverb: if any time is expressed in the Reported sentence, it must change keeping consistency with the time of the Reporting sentence. Example: "Today's lesson is on preposition," she said. [Today] / She said that yesterday's lesson was on preposition. [24 hours later]. Table of changes: (a week) Ago -> (a week) Before; Come -> Go; Here -> There; Hence -> Thence; Hither -> Thither; Now -> Then; Next (day/ month/ week/ year) -> Following (day/ week/ month/ year); Today -> (24 hrs later) Yesterday/ That day; Thus -> So/ In that way; These (days) -> Those (days); This/ it (evening/ morning/ noon etc.) -> That (evening/ morning/ noon etc.); This day -> That day; Tonight -> That night; Tomorrow -> The next/ following day; Last weekend -> The weekend before last/ The previous weekend; Last night -> The previous night; Last month/ year -> The previous month/ year, The month/ year before; Yesterday (morning/ afternoon/ evening) -> The previous (morning/ afternoon/ evening); Tomorrow (morning/ evening etc.) -> The following (morning/ evening, etc.). Exception: 'This' used as a Demonstrative Pronoun changes to 'the'. Example: He said, "I enter this room." / He said that he entered the room. If This + time expression, only 'this' changes to 'that'. Introductory 'It' does not change in Indirect. Example: He said, "It rained heavily yesterday. / He said that it had rained heavily the previous day. 3. Pronoun change: the pronoun of the Reported speech almost always changes: i. The First person (I, we etc.) in the Reported speech is always determined in Indirect speech according to the subject (number, person, gender) of the Reporting verb. Examples: She said, "I teach English online." / She said that she taught English online. He says, "I am well." / He says that he is well. Exceptions: (a) If 'We' means 'mankind', it remains unchanged in Indirect speech. Example: She said, "We shall leave this world soon." / She said that we would leave the world soon. (b) If 'We' means both the speaker and the person spoken to, it remains unchanged in Indirect speech. Example: He said to me, "We have to tackle the situation." / He told me that we had to tackle the situation. (c) Editorial 'we' changes to 'It' in Indirect Speech. Example: The Independent says, "We make the people aware of this fact." / The Independent says that it makes the people aware of the fact. ii. The 2nd person (you, your etc.) of the Reported speech is always determined according to the Object (number, person, gender) of the Reporting verb. Examples: Ruksana says to Rupom, "I am well and you are unwell." / Ruksana tells Rupom that she is well and he (Rupom) is unwell. They said to me, "You did the work." / They told me that I had done the work. iii. If there is no speaker and reporting verb in Direct speech, the speaker must be assumed to make Indirect speech. Examples: I will go there soon. / The speaker says that he/ she will go there soon. We have won the battle. / The soldiers (speakers) said that they had won the battle. 4. Change of vocative case/ parenthetic (= Comment) clause: if there is a Vocative case in the Reported clause, it generally sits as the object of the reporting verb. Example: He said, "Karim, come here." / He told Karim to go there. But if the Vocative case is used as a symbol of someone's rank or as recognition of a close relationship, the Vocative Case can change as follows: He said, "Sir, I have an urgent piece of business." / He said respectfully that he had an urgent piece of business. He said, to me "Friend, listen to me." / Addressing as his friend, he told me to listen to him. But if the Vocative case means a real relationship, this kind of expression is not used; instead the Vocative case sits as the object of the Reporting verb. Example: He said, "Mother, help me." / He told his mother to help him. If a parenthetic or comment clause is used in Direct speech, it can be dropped when changing to Indirect speech to avoid the complexity of the sentence. You see, as you know, to tell frankly etc. are comment clauses. Example: He said, "As you know I am not able to spend for the occasion. / He said that he was not able to spend for the occasion. Similarly, expressions used to start a sentence as a reference to a previous discussion are also dropped in Indirect speech. Examples: He said, "Now, listen to my children". / He told his children to listen to him. He said to me "Well, you are alright." / He told me that I was alright. Using Reporting Verbs: In Indirect Speech, generally said, told and ask are the three most used Reporting Verbs: 1. 'asked' is used to report a question. Example: I asked Lucy what time the lesson started. 2. 'Told' is used with an object. Example: Lucy told me she felt tired. (here the object is me). 3. Generally 'said' is not used with an object. Example: Lucy said she was going to teach online. If 'Said' is used with an object, 'to' must be added. Example: Lucy said to me that she'd never been to Kuakata. But generally in this case 'told' is used instead of 'said to'. Other verbs that can be used besides said, told and asked according to the form of the Sentence, shown in past form: accused, admitted, advised, alleged, agreed, apologized, begged, boasted, complained, denied, explained, implied, invited, offered, ordered, promised, replied, suggested, thought. Using these verbs makes the speaker's statement more attractive and meaningful. Example: He asked me to come to the party. - the 'asked' verb can be changed to bring variety: He invited me to the party. He begged me to go to the party. He requested me to go to the party. He advised me to go to the party. He suggested that I should go to the party. Use of "That" in Reported Speech: in Reported speech 'that' is often seen. Example: He told me that he lived in Kishoreganj. But such use of 'that' is optional; the sentence above can also be written: He told me he lived in Kishoreganj. NB: In a question 'that' is never used; instead 'if' or 'whether' is used. Example: He asked me if I would come to the party.

chunk_text: Lesson-03: Sentence-Based Rules on Changing Speech. 1. Changing Assertive Sentences: (a) If the Sentence inside the Reported Speech in Direct speech is Assertive, the Conjunction 'that' sits before the Reported Speech of Indirect Speech, and if the Reporting verb 'say' has a person object after it, in Indirect speech that 'say' changes to 'tell' verb, but after 'tell' verb there is no need to use 'to' as a preposition. Examples: He says to me, "I shall beat her." / He tells me that he will beat her. They said to me, "You have written the feature." / They told me that I had written the feature. Abir says, "I can help you." / Abir says that he can help me. (b) To change Direct Speech to Indirect speech, generally 'say' or 'tell' is used as the reporting verb, but sometimes other verbs can also be used for this purpose. Examples: Rahim said, "I expect, I shall gain success in life." / Rahim expected that he would gain success in life. She said, "I repent, I have lost him for ever." / She repented that she had lost him forever. 2. Changing Interrogative Sentences: if the Reported speech in Direct Speech is an Interrogative Sentence, follow these steps in order: (a) In Indirect Speech the Reporting verb changes to 'ask', 'enquire', 'demand', 'wonder' etc. and the Question turns into a statement. (b) If the answer to the Question can be given only with 'yes' or 'no', then in Indirect Speech the conjunction 'if' or 'whether' must sit before the Reported speech. (c) But if the answer to the Question cannot be given with 'yes' or 'no', in other words if the Reported speech starts with a question-word like who, whom, what, when, which, how, why, whose, where, then in Indirect speech no conjunction 'if' or 'whether' is used before the Reported speech; that question word itself is used. Examples: Arif said to me, "Do you want my help?" / Arif asked me if I wanted his help. He said to me, "Are you ill?" / He asked/ enquired of me if/ whether I was ill. You said to me, "Do you hear me?" / You asked me if I heard you. He said to me, "Are you sure of this?" / He asked me if I was sure of that. Shall I/ we questions: when Shall I/ shall we express a request, advice or instruction, the change happens like a Yes/ no question; 'should' is used to express advice. Example: She said, "Shall I switch on the fan?" / She said whether she should switch on the fan. Again, if a request or permission is expressed, 'would' sits. Example: She said, "Shall I ever get the job?" / She said if she would get the job ever. Tag Question: if there is a Tag Question in Direct speech, drop the statement part and expand only the Question part according to the Context to make Indirect Narration. Example: She said, "You do not like him, do you? / She asked me if I liked him. 3. Changing Imperative Sentences: (a) An Imperative Sentence generally expresses order, advice, request, prohibition, entreaty, prayer, humility etc. So if the Reported speech in Direct speech is an Imperative Sentence, the Imperative verb changes to Infinitive, i.e. to + verb form, and according to the meaning, the Reporting verb changes to tell, order, advise, command, beg, request, entreat etc. Examples: Mother said to me, "Do not run in the sun." / Mother advised me not to run in the sun. I said to him, "Excuse me, sir." / I begged him to excuse me. My friend said me, "Go home at once." / My friend told/ advised me to go home at once. (b) If there are vocatives in Direct speech, they must be dropped or changed in Indirect Speech as follows. Examples: He said, "Iqbal, go there." / He told Iqbal to go there. He said, "Friends, lend me your ears." / Addressing them as friends, he requested them to lend him their ears. 4. Changing Optative Sentences: an Optative Sentence expresses wish, desire, blessing, prayer etc. So if there is an Optative Sentence in Direct Speech, in Indirect speech the Reporting verb changes to wish, pray etc. and the Optative sentence turns into an Assertive Sentence form. Examples: He said to me, "May you be happy." / He wished that I might be happy. He said to you, "May God bless you." / He prayed that God might bless you. 5. Changing Exclamatory Sentences: an Exclamatory Sentence expresses wonder, grief, sorrow, joy, pain etc. So if the reported speech in Direct Speech is an exclamation, the Reported verb changes to 'exclaim', 'cry out' etc. On the other hand the Exclamatory Sentence turns into a statement; moreover, new words or phrases must be added to express the necessary meaning. Examples: He said, "Alas! I am undone." / He cried out in sorrow that he was undone. He said, "What a fool I am!" / He exclaimed with grief that he was a great fool. He said, "Good-bye, my friends." / He bade his friends good-bye./ He bade good-bye to his friends. "Bless his kind heart!" they cried. / They blessed him for his kind heart. "Bravo well done!" they cried. / They applauded him that/ saying that he had done well. NB: sometimes the reported speech starts with what, how or who and such sentences have at least one adjective or noun; when making such sentences indirect, instead of who, what, how, great, very, very much, greatly, completely etc. are placed before the adjective. Examples: He said to me, "How happy you are!" / He told me that I was very happy. He said, "What a nice thing it is!" / He said/ exclaimed with joy that it was a very nice thing. He said, "What was my joy to see the thing!" / He said that his joy to see the thing was very great. Some Incomplete exclamatory sentences must be made into Indirect Narration according to meaning. Examples: He said, "What a man!" / He exclaimed with surprise that he was a peculiar man. He said, "What an idea!" / He exclaimed that it was a nice idea. He said, "What a surprise!" / He exclaimed that it was a great surprise. Changing Imperative Sentences beginning with 'Let': 1. If the Reported speech in Direct speech expresses a proposal with 'Let', in Indirect speech the Reporting verb changes to 'propose' verb and the conjunction 'that' is placed before the Reported speech and it, i.e. the Reported speech, is turned into a statement with 'should'. Examples: They said to me, "Let us decide the matter ourselves." / They proposed to me that we should decide the matter ourselves. He said to me, "Let us go home." / He proposed to me that we should go home. 2. But if 'Let' does not indicate a proposal, in Indirect speech 'Let' changes to may, might, might be allowed to or some other verb; in this case the Reporting verb changes to tell, wish etc. according to the meaning of the Reported speech. Examples: He said, "Let him do whatever he likes." / He said that he might/ might be allowed to do whatever he liked. He said, "Let me come in." / He requested that he might be allowed to go in. N.B.: instead of 'Might be allowed to', only 'Might' may also be used. Must/ should/ ought to in Imperative sentences: You + must/ should/ ought to - if a sentence of this structure expresses advice, its Indirect speech becomes like an ordinary Imperative sentence: i. the reporting verb changes to advise + object; ii. must/ should/ ought to is dropped; iii. instead of bare infinitive, full infinitive (to + verb) sits. Example: He said, "You must take some exercise regularly. / He advised me to take some exercise regularly. Might (expressing request) in imperative sentences: Indirect speech changes like an ordinary Imperative sentence: i. reporting verb changes to request + object; ii. might is dropped; iii. instead of bare infinitive, full infinitive sits. Example: She said, "You might attend the meeting on behalf of me." / She requested me to attend the meeting on behalf of her. Question-form Imperative sentences: if the reporting speech starting with will you/ would you/ can you/ could you expresses a Command, request or invitation, Indirect speech changes according to this structure: i. the reporting verb changes to ask/ request; ii. object sits; iii. To + verb (Infinitive) sits; iv. please/ kindly is dropped. Example: She said, "Will you lend me the book please?" / She requested me to lend her the book. Note: these patterns are not used to ask for information like an ordinary question, so making them Indirect by the Interrogative sentence rule would be wrong. Imperative sentence with Tag Question: in this case drop the tag question and make Indirect by the rule of the main Imperative sentence. Example: Father said, "Shut the door, will you?" / Father told me to shut the door.

chunk_text: Lesson-01: An Introduction to Voice. The manner of expressing a verb is called voice. If the subject itself does the work of the verb, the verb is in Active voice; the form of a verb by which what is done to a person or thing is expressed is Passive voice. Active Voice: the form of a verb which is used when the subject is the doer of the action of the verb is called active voice. Passive Voice: the form of a verb which is used when the subject (= nominative) is affected by the action of the verb is called passive voice. Passive Structures (be + Past Participle): He sells computers. / Computers are sold by him. The teacher is teaching grammar. / Grammar is being taught by the teacher. Note: the object of the active verb becomes the subject of the passive verb, and the subject of the active verb becomes the object of the passive verb. Passive Verb Forms: using forms of 'be' before the Past Participle (V3) of the verb - Simple Present am/is/are + V3; Present Continuous am/is/are being + V3; Present Perfect have/has been + V3; Past Simple was/were + V3; Past Continuous was/were being + V3; Past Perfect had been + V3. Passive Verbs with two Objects: verbs like bring, buy, give, lend, make, pay, promise, send, show, tell, write have two objects - Indirect object (person) and Direct object (thing); either object can become the subject of the passive verb, but using the person-object as subject is better; when the thing-object becomes the subject, 'to' is placed before the person-object. Example: He gave me some money. / I was given some money by him. Or, Some money was given to me by him. Changing Voice - Structure for Passive Verbs (General Structure): Subject (object of the active voice) + am/is/are, am/is/are + being, have/has + been, was/were, was/were + being, had been, shall/will + be, shall/will + be + being, shall/will + have + been + Verb in Past Participle form + by + Object (subject of the active voice).

chunk_text: Lesson-02: Rules on Passive Voice. Tense-based rules: Rule 1 Present Indefinite - object becomes subjective form + am/is/are + main verb Past Participle + by + subject becomes objective form. Examples: We eat rice. / Rice is eaten by us. We play cricket. / Cricket is played by us. Rule 2 Present Continuous - am being/is being/are being + V3. Example: I am writing a letter. / A letter is being written by me. Note on 'going to': if a continuous sentence with 'going to' indicates the future, the passive structure is am/is/are/was/were going to be + V3. Example: He is going to take the decision. / The decision is going to be taken by him. Rule 3 Present Perfect - have been/has been + V3. Example: He has broken the glass. / The glass has been broken by him. Rule 4 Past Indefinite - was/were + V3. Example: Rupom broke the plate. / The plate was broken by Rupom. Rule 5 Past Continuous - was being/were being + V3. Rule 6 Past Perfect - had been + V3. Rule 7 Future Indefinite - shall be/will be + V3. Rule 8 Future Continuous - shall be being/will be being + V3. Rule 9 Future Perfect - shall have been/will have been + V3. Rule 10 Modal verbs (may, might, can, could, must, ought to, going to, should): after the modal, 'be' is placed and then the Past Participle of the main verb; passive structure: object becomes subject + modal auxiliary + be + V3 + by + subject becomes object. Examples: I can do the work. / The work can be done by me. She should love her husband. / Her husband should be loved by her. Tense Based Basic Active Structure table (Simple/Indefinite, Continuous, Perfect, Perfect Continuous across Present, Past, Future with verb patterns do/does, did, shall/will do, am/is/are doing, was/were doing, shall/will be doing, have/has done, had done, shall/will have done, have/has been doing, had been doing, shall/will have been doing) with Bengali meanings. N.B.: after Modals the Base form of the verb sits; after a modal, V1 is used for Indefinite and have + V3 for Perfect form. Sentence-based rules: Rule 11 Interrogative Sentence - first turn the interrogative into an assertive sentence, change it to passive, then place the auxiliary verb first and add a question mark; passive structure: Auxiliary verb (per Tense, Number and Person) + object becomes subject + V3 + by + subject becomes object + ? Examples: Have you done the work? / Has the work been done by you? Rule 12 Interrogative with 'Who' - first 'By whom', then auxiliary verb, object in subjective form, be/being/been as per tense, main verb Past Participle, '?'. Examples: Who did the work? / By whom was the work done? Rule 13 Interrogative with 'Whom' - first 'who', then auxiliary verb, main verb Past Participle, by, subject in objective form, '?'. Examples: Whom do you want? / Who is wanted by you? Rule 14 Interrogative with 'What' - first 'What', auxiliary verb, main verb Past Participle, by, subject in objective form, '?'. Examples: What did you buy? / What was bought by you?

chunk_text: Lesson-03: Some other Rules of Voice Change. Rule 15 Imperative Sentence (affirmative, starting with the main verb) - first 'Let' + object in subjective form + be + main verb Past Participle. Examples: Buy me a pen. / Let a pen be bought for me. Do the sum. / Let the sum be done (by you). Rule 16 Imperative with 'Do not' (negative) - first 'Let not' + object in subjective form + be + Past Participle. Example: Do not miss the train. / Let not the train be missed (by you). Rule 17 'Let' + person object (me, us, you, them, him, her) imperative - first 'Let' + object in subjective form + be + Past Participle + by + the given person object. Example: Let him help the poor. / Let the poor be helped by him. Rule 18 Imperative with 'Never' - first 'Let not' + object in subjective form + ever be + Past Participle. Example: Never tell a lie. / Let not a lie ever be told. Rule 19 Present Participle - Subject + Verb + Object + Present Participle active becomes: object in subjective form + auxiliary verb per subject + main verb Past Participle + the Present Participle part + by + subject in objective form. Example: I saw him reading a book. / He was seen reading a book by me. Rule 20 Reflexive Object (myself, ourselves, yourself, yourselves, themselves, himself, herself) - the subject of the active voice sits unchanged as the subject of the passive voice + auxiliary verb per subject + main verb Past Participle + by + the reflexive object. Example: The woman fans herself. / The woman is fanned by herself. Rule 21 Factitive/ Double Object - the given pronominal object (me, us, you, them, him, her) becomes subjective form + auxiliary verb per tense and person + main verb Past Participle + factitive object + subject in objective form. Examples: We made him captain. / He was made captain by us. They elected me chairman. / I was elected chairman by them. Rule 22 Complex/ Compound Sentence - both clauses must be made passive; sometimes introductory Principal and Subordinate 'It' are used as subject. Examples: They invited me and I accepted the invitation. / I was invited by them and the invitation was accepted by me. I saw that he was reading a book. / It was seen by me that a book was being read by him. Rule 23 Silent 'to' - after Need, dare, make, hear, feel, let, know, behold, watch, 'to' is silent in active voice but 'to' is placed after them in passive voice; except for 'Let', where 'to' is not placed after the verb in passive. Examples: It made the wind blow. / The wind was made to blow by it. Rule 24 Other Prepositions - in many cases, when making the subject of the active voice the object, a preposition other than 'by' (to, at, in, with etc.) is used. Examples: I knew the writer. / The writer was known to me. The bad news shocked me. / I was shocked at the bad news. Rule 25 have/has to, had to, is going to, was going to, ought to, used to, have got to in active voice - 'be' is used with those verbs in passive. Examples: I have to write a report. / A report has to be written by me. We ought to love our country. / Our country ought to be loved by us. Rule 26 Quasi-Passive Verb + no Complement - from the subject to before the main verb + being + main verb Past Participle form. Examples: The books are printing. / The books are being printed. The palace is building. / The palace is being built. Rule 27 Quasi-Passive Verb + Complement - Subject + auxiliary verb per Tense, Number and Person + complement + When/ If + it/they per the number of the subject + Be verb per Tense, Number and Person + main verb Past Participle. Examples: The mangoes taste sour. / The mangoes are sour when/ if they are tasted. The bed feels soft. / The bed is soft if/ when it is felt. Note: a quasi passive verb in active voice can also be changed to passive another way: Honey tastes sweet. / Honey is tasted sweet. The bed feels soft. / The bed is felt soft. Complement: the word or phrase used after a Linking Verb that describes the sentence is called a Complement. Linking Verbs (be, seem, feel, smell, taste, look, sound etc.) take complements that are adjectives, noun phrases or prepositional phrases. Rule 28 Passive to Active - (i) if a passive voice has no object (whose subject is essential), a suitable subject must be placed according to the subject matter; (ii) in a complex sentence both parts change voice. Examples: The criminal was arrested. / The police arrested the criminal. The houses have been washed away. / Flood has washed away the houses. Note: They are gone., He is arrived., He is come. are not passive voice, because go, arrive, come are intransitive verbs and cannot be used in passive voice; they are alternatives of They have gone. He has arrived. He has come. - the first form stresses the state of the agent, the second stresses the time of the action. Intransitive verbs (appear, belong, comprise, disappear, despair, occur, ensure, result, wonder, perish, refer, issue, indulge etc.) have no passive voice. Passive Sentences with Objective Complements: some verbs have a noun or adjective after the object describing the object; these are called object complements. Examples: The teacher considered him a genius. / He was considered a genius (by the teacher). They elected him captain. / He was elected captain. Passive Adverbs: if an active sentence has an adverb, in the passive sentence it generally sits just before the past participle of the verb. Examples: I know him well. / He is well known to me. The police beat the man severely. / The man was severely beaten by the police. Sachin played the ball beautifully. / The ball was beautifully played by Sachin.

chunk_text: Lesson-04: Tense-Based Voice Change. Verbs that cannot be used in the Passive: not all verbs are used in passive form; only transitive verbs (verbs that have an object) can have a passive form, and not even all transitive verbs do. State verbs like has, fit, resemble express a state or condition and generally have no continuous form, so they cannot be used in Passive Voice: He has a camera. / A camera is had by him. (wrong). My shoes do not fit me. / I am not fitted by my shoes. (wrong). She resembles her mother. / Her mother is resembled by her. (wrong). When do we use The Passive? We use passive form in both speech and writing, but most in writing, especially in textbooks and reports, factory operations, science and technology, and official laws: Jute and jute goods are exported to foreign countries. The water is heated to boiling point. The gate will be shut at 10.00 pm. Payment can be made at any bank. In these cases what is done matters more than who did it, or who did it is hard to say; newspaper reports also often use passive form: A number of political leaders have been released. Talks will be held in Geneva next week. Tense-based items: 1. Present Simple: am/is/are + past participle. Example: Somebody cleans this room everyday. / This room is cleaned everyday. Football is played all over the world. A lot of tea is drunk in France. No sound is heard. Honest people are honoured in society. 2. Past Simple: was/were + past participle. Example: Somebody broke the glass yesterday. / The glass was broken yesterday. Mini was plucking flowers. / Flowers were being plucked by Mini. Many people were killed in the Liberation War. Crops were damaged in yesterday's storm. This book was published many years ago. The building was painted many years ago. 3. Present Continuous: am/is/are being + past participle. Example: Somebody is cleaning the room. / The room is being cleaned. The book is being printed. The house is being whitewashed. The land is being prepared for gardening. Look! A big stage is being constructed. 4. Past Continuous: was/were being + Past Participle. Example: Somebody was cleaning the room. / The room was being cleaned. I am going to open a bank account. / A bank account is going to be opened by me. 5. Present Perfect: have/has been + Past Participle. Example: Somebody has stolen the car. / The car has been stolen. 6. Past Perfect: had been + Past Participle. Example: The room looked much better. Somebody had cleaned it. / The room looked much better. It had been cleaned. Tense Based Basic Passive Structure table: Subject + 'Be' verb + V3 + by + object; Simple/Indefinite (Present am/are/is, Past was/were, Future shall/will be), Continuous (Present am/are/is + being, Past was/were + being, Future shall/will be + being), Perfect (Present have/has been, Past had been, Future shall/will have been), each with examples (I am helped by my elder brother. etc.) and Bengali meanings. N.B.: after Modals (can, could, may, might, must, ought to etc.) the 'Be' verb sits; after the modal, be, be being and have been are used for Indefinite, Continuous and Perfect forms respectively, and then V3 sits.

chunk_text: Completing a Story: in the exam the beginning (a few lines or clues) of a story is given; complete it logically following the given idea. Length, fluency and acceptability of the description matter most, along with grammatical accuracy, presentation style and use of quotation. Sentences should link logically with a smooth flow of ideas; the plot is somewhat unclear, so read the beginning again and again to decide the ending. Imaginary or well-known situations may be given; keep the subject, environment and style of language consistent with the given situation. Length 100 to 250 words, never below 100 words; use quotation marks where the description needs them. The language of a story must be colloquial; quotation and contraction are very necessary. Exclusive Story Writing Technique: read the given beginning or outline again and again; for a known story or fable write the answer from memory understanding its context; for an imaginary subject understand what to write from the given beginning or clue and fix a logical plot; use past tense; give a suitable title according to the plot; for a moral story the moral may be written at the end; always use direct speech for quotation; one or two extra points may be added for the story; write in 2/3 paragraphs as needed; use the given beginning and other points fully.

chunk_text: Completing a Story, model stories 1-30: 1. An Ant And a Dove - a thirsty ant swept away by a wave is saved by a dove's branch, then saves the dove from a hunter by biting him; moral: helping others selflessly never goes unrewarded. 2. Failure is The Pillar of Success - a king defeated six times takes courage from a spider that succeeds at the seventh attempt and wins. 3. Who Will Bell the Cat? / Easier said than done - mice agree to bell the cat but none will do it; they migrate. 4. A Witty Crow / Where there is a will there is a way - a thirsty crow drops pebbles into a jar to raise the water. 5. The Prudence of The Judge - the judge gives each servant a stick; the thief shortens his, so he is detected. 6. The Nobility of a Landlord - a landlord helps a farmer lift a fallen sack of wheat and asks him to help others in difficulty. 7. A Foolish Crocodile & a Cunning Fox - the fox eats the crocodile's four children one by one under the pretence of educating them. 8. The More Man Gets, the More he Wants - King Midas's golden touch turns his daughter to gold; he repents and the god takes the power away. 9. Happiness Lies in Contentment - a happy cobbler who lives from hand to mouth teaches a rich banker that happiness is relative. 10. Look Before You Leap - a fox trapped in a well tricks a goat into jumping in, climbs out on the goat's back and warns him to look before he leaps. 11. Story of a Cap-Seller and Some Monkeys - the cap-seller throws down his own cap and the imitating monkeys throw theirs; moral: an imitator is easily befooled. 12. A Liar Shepherd / Nobody believes a liar - the boy who cried wolf for fun is not believed when wolves really come; they kill his sheep and tear him to pieces. 13. An Honest Woodcutter and the Beautiful Fairy / Honesty is the best policy - the woodcutter refuses the gold and silver axes, gets his own iron axe and all three as a reward. 14. Slow and Steady Wins the Race - the hare naps while the tortoise toils on and wins. 15. What is Sport to one is Death to Another - boys throwing stones at frogs stop when an old frog tells them their sport is death to the frogs. 16. The Reward of an Honest Rickshaw Puller - Asif finds five lac taka in a bag on his rickshaw and returns it to the owner. 17. Outward Appearance is not all / Witty Saadi - Sheikh Saadi, ill-treated in simple dress, puts rich food into his pockets saying the food is for his dress. 18. A Friend in Need is a Friend Indeed - one friend climbs a tree while the other pretends to be dead; the bear whispers not to trust a friend who leaves a friend in danger. 19. The Wolf and The Crane - the crane pulls a bone from the wolf's throat; the wolf says not swallowing the crane's head is fee enough. 20. Bayazid's Love for His Mother - Bayazid fetches water from a fountain at night and stands by his sleeping mother's bed till morning. 21. Even a Small Creature Can Help a Large One - the mouse freed by the lion later cuts the net and frees the lion. 22. The Golden Touch - King Midas, granted the golden touch by god Mercury, loses his daughter to gold and prays for the boon to be taken back; moral: greed leads to ruin. 23. A Greedy Dog - the dog barks at its own reflection for a second piece of meat and loses its own; moral: grasp all, lose all. 24. King Solomon's Wisdom - Solomon opens the windows so bees sit on the real garland and picks it; moral: you may do a hard task by common sense. 25. Two Rats and the Monkey - the cunning monkey eats the whole loaf while 'dividing' it equally for two rats. 26. Unity is Strength - three quarrelling sons cannot break a bundle of sticks but break single sticks easily. 27. Greed Loses All - the farmer kills the goose that lays golden eggs and finds no egg inside. 28. A Fox Without a Tail - a fox whose tail was cut off in a trap advises all foxes to cut off their tails; an old fox reveals the trick; moral: none can befool all. 29. Grapes are Sour - a hungry fox jumps several times for ripe grapes hanging too high, fails, and consoles himself that the grapes are sour. 30. The Foolish Crow & a Sly Jackal - a sly fox flatters a crow into singing; the crow opens its beak, the stolen meat falls, and the fox takes it.

chunk_text: Writing Short Dialogues: in the exam full instructions for writing one dialogue are given; present the whole subject in at least 7-8 pairs following the given subject matter. In a dialogue informal English (colloquial language), contraction, notion/function are very important; also pay special attention to minor sentence, question tag and regular interruption. Exclusive Dialogue Writing Technique: in informal English the contracted form of the helping verb is mostly used. While exchanging ideas follow the rules of notions/functions and master the skill of expressing attitudes like greeting, apology, regret, gratitude, liking, disliking, agreement, disagreement. Contractions: I am -> I'm; I should -> I'd; You will -> You'll; We have -> We've; We will/shall -> We'll; They would/should -> They'd; Am not -> Aren't; Are not -> Aren't; Were not -> Weren't; Cannot -> Can't; Ought not -> Oughtn't; Will not -> Won't, etc. Attitudes/notions/functions: 1. Greetings - Hello/Hallo, Hi (friends, telephone), Good morning (till noon), Good afternoon (after noon till 4 p.m.), Good night (at night before sleep, on parting), Goodbye (formal parting), Bye/ Tata/Cheerio (informal parting), See you, Be seeing you/Cheerio, Assalamu alaikum (Muslim greeting for all), Nameste/Namesker (Hindu greeting), Adab (Hindu-Muslim mutual greeting), How are you? (known persons), How do you do? (unknown persons, both sides use it on introduction). 2. Request - Give me a pen (please) (ordinary); Will you lend me a pen? (polite); Could you lend me a pen? (polite); Do you think you could lend me some money? (more polite); I wonder if you could help me; Would you mind giving me the pen? 3. Gratitude - Thank you (ordinary); Thanks/many thanks/ thanks a lot (among friends, informal); Thank you very much (always usable); This is kind/good/nice of you (to unknown and respected persons); I am really grateful to you (formal, in writing). 4. Apology - 'Sorry' for small matters; I'm sorry mostly used; I'm very sorry/really sorry/ever so sorry for emphasis; I can't tell you how sorry I am (special situation, formal). 5. To accept apology - That's alright. Forget it. Don't worry/Not to worry etc. 6. Obligation/Necessity - You've to/must do it. We should/ought to love our country. You have got to take care of your health. You needn't go to college today. You mustn't touch the books on the shelf. 7. Preference - Do you like coffee? No, thanks. Would you prefer tea to coffee? Yes, I prefer tea. But I would rather have coffee than tea. 8. Suggestions/proposal - (a) Let's go out now, shall we? (b) Go out now. (c) Why don't we go out now? (d) We could go out now. (e) It might be a good idea to go out now etc. 9. Surprise - Surprising!/amazing!/astonishing! Good heavens!/What a surprise!/I can't believe it! What a pleasant surprise! 10. Opinion - Shall we go to the stadium? I don't think it's possible. I also think so. As far as I am concerned it's impossible. 11. To draw attention - Excuse me! Sorry to interrupt you. 12. Emphasis/Insistence/persuasion - Do sit down, please. Do have at least a cup of tea, please. 13. Agreeing - Ques. Do you agree with me? Ans. (a) Yes, it is. (b) Of course, quite so./exactly etc. (c) I agree entirely./I couldn't agree more. (d) That's just what I'm thinking. 14. Disagreeing - Ques. Do you agree with me? Ans. (a) No, surely not/certainly not. (b) I disagree / I don't agree with you. (c) Sorry; but I don't agree with you. (d) I'm not sure, I wonder. (e) I'm afraid, I can't agree. (f) I really don't think so. 15. Sounds expressing relevant attitudes - Um (hesitation); Mm/Hmm (doubt, difference of opinion); Err (making a mistake); Wow! (surprise/praise); Woah! Yeah/Yep (comment on someone's statement); Of/Ooof (oh); Hey (to draw someone's attention). Points to Ponder Over: use colloquial form of language; use minor sentences if necessary (e.g. Sorry? Cheerio, No kidding! Excuse me! etc.); use contracted forms (e.g. cannot = can't); use question tags (e.g. It's fine, isn't it?); use standard interruptions (e.g. Um...., Er.... etc.); use simple sentences.

chunk_text: Writing Short Dialogues, model dialogues 1-25: 1. Fahim and Asif on the lockdown situation of their locality due to coronavirus pandemic: lockdown for 21 days, offices and business centres closed, grocery and pharmacies open, transport suspended, police on guard round the clock, COVID-19 tests and isolation arranged. 2. Nahid and Neela on plans after the exam: Neela will go to her native village and try to make some people literate; Nahid teaches his maid at home. 3. Bristi and Dipti at a book fair: Dipti bought a set of Satyajit Roy; Bristi will visit stalls and go to Kashban Prokashan; favourite author Zafar Iqbal. 4. Habib and Nibir on the benefits of morning walk: Nibir feels tired and sleepy and goes to a doctor; morning walk from tomorrow will make him hale and hearty. 5. Saheen and Keya on games and sports they like: Keya plays basket ball at school and can swim; Saheen plays cricket and football, can swim, will learn cycling in the winter vacation. 6. Selim/Selima and Dipak/Dipika on favourite hobby: Dipika's hobbies are fishing and gardening; Myself's hobby is reading story books. 7. Raka and Riya on how to make a good result in the examination: regular in classes and studies, make notes, understand the subject matter, revise and write frequently; practice makes a man perfect; never memorise without understanding. 8. Myself and a fireman (telephone conversation, 100 words): fire broke out in the next door at 30 RM Das Road, Sutrapur; neighbours trying to extinguish it with water; fire brigades coming. 9. Sami/Safiq and a doctor: fever for five days, severe pain all over the body, everything tastes bitter, no appetite; viral fever, prescription for a week. 10. Anis/Anutosh and Abid/Animesh on the problems of frequent load shedding: cannot study even for an hour, exam knocking at the door; they will place an application to the TNO. 11. Customer and book-seller: JSC English Model Questions published by Lecture Publications Ltd., taka 220. 12. Suman and a stranger whose pocket has been picked: the stranger lost all his money, wanted to go to Cox's Bazar, now wants to return home; Suman gives him Tk. 100. 13. Sami/Samia and Rafi/Rafiq on the merits and demerits of using mobile phone: merits - communicate in the twinkling of an eye, timetable, date, internet, knowledge, plays, movies, games, admission, jobs; demerits - cancer, lessened eye-sight, inspiring criminals. 14. Upom/Upoma and Rana/Runa on the importance of learning English: international language, higher education, more than 80% of the world's computer information in English, global trade and commerce, culture, jobs, handsome salary. 15. Myself and younger brother on smoking: friends instigated him; smoking causes cancer, asthma, bronchitis, blood pressure, stroke, heart attack, loss of smell and taste, tooth decay, stomach ulcer, decreased appetite; harms non-smokers too; he will never do so. 16. Jamil/Jamila and Saad/Sadia on aim in life: Saad will try to be a doctor and build a charitable hospital in his village; Jamil will try to be a teacher and serve the country. 17. Durjoy and Bijoy on the necessity and importance of planting trees: trees supply oxygen and receive carbon dioxide, keep ecological balance, protect from natural disasters, provide food and shelter. 18. Rana/Rani and Rakib/Rakiba on early rising: Rakib's bad result because he gets up late; early rising is good for health and lessons; from tomorrow he will get up early every day. 19. Helal and the Headmaster on his mother's illness: mother has a fever and feels very weak, none to look after her; Helal asks for the day off; father will bring a doctor in the afternoon; Headmaster allows him to go home. 20. Ripon (class VIII) and the librarian on a library card: Ripon needs English grammar books; the card is the rule of the school; he will show the admission receipt tomorrow and get a card. 21. Khalid/Khalida and Hasan/Hasina on the importance of reading newspaper: current affairs, games and sports, trade and commerce, education, literature, art and culture, film, weather forecast; false news sometimes misleads, but reading newspaper daily is essential. 22. Siam/Sabiha and Fabiha/Fardin on the importance of taking physical exercise: feel hale and hearty, fresh mind, body free from diseases, desire for work increases; by walking, swimming or playing games and sports. 23. chunk_text: Writing Paragraphs by Answering Questions: A paragraph is a group of related sentences dealing with a central idea. Paragraph Structure: a well-organised paragraph has three main parts starting from Paragraph Introducer (PI), also called Topic Sentence, which gives an idea of the topic or main idea of the paragraph; the second part is Paragraph Developers (PD), which develop the Paragraph Introducer, i.e. explain or prove it; the paragraph ends with Paragraph Terminator (PT). PI: the main idea (main idea) is expressed here; in a good paragraph one sentence expresses the main idea and that sentence is called the Topic Sentence. PD: the main idea is described in detail in this part, also called Body; the sentences of this part are also called Supporting Sentences. PT: the conclusion, which presents the summary of the whole paragraph; in a good paragraph it is also one sentence and is called the Concluding sentence. Example-1 'Sentence functions in paragraph development': (1) sentences in most well written paragraphs may be analysed into four general functions; (2) first, there are paragraph introducers, which establish the topic focus of the paragraph as a whole; (3) second, there are paragraph developers, which present examples or details of various kinds that support the ideas set forth by the paragraph introducers; (4) third, there are viewpoint or context modulators, which provide a smooth transition between different sets of ideas; (5) fourth, there are paragraph terminators, which logically conclude the ideas discussed in the paragraph in a psychologically satisfying manner; (6) not all pieces of writing will conform to this analysis, however, most successful paragraphs usually contain some combination of these four sentence types. Steps: PI -> Sentence no. 1; PD -> Sentence no. 2-5; PT -> Sentence no. 6. Example-2 'A Small Town' (a small town by Lesley Coleman of Grand Valley Community High School, Kellerton, Iowa): (1) What is small town? (2) It sits on four city blocks: its inhabitants are friendly; it operates on one grocery store, one gas station, one post office, one beauty shop, one cafe, one bar, one car wash, and four different prayer hall. (3) On any given day, the band marches through town, and a three-car train chugs by. (4) Traffic is light; you can make U-turn in the middle of Main Street. (5) Conversation is easy. (6) If you smile at people, they smile back. (7) The only things more abundant than kids are stray animals - and the whole town takes care of both. (8) The folks who live here would not live anywhere else. Steps: (1) Main idea: a small town; (2) Size, residents, buildings; (3) Bands and trains; (4) Driving; (5), (6) Friendliness; (7) Kids, pets, caring; (8) A nice place to live in. Paragraph: Unity & Coherence - while writing a paragraph one should be careful about Unity and Coherence; the description of the subject matter of a paragraph will be unbroken only when the thoughts of the sentences used are confined to one subject; keeping Unity is very difficult and skill is needed. Model paragraph 'Edison': No other inventor has had more impact on modern life than Thomas Alva Edison; Edison invented the light bulb, the light switch, the light socket and the three-wire system of electrical wiring; his inventions ranged from ore-crushing machines and underground electric mains to storage batteries and electric pens; the electric railway car, the electric rail-road signal, the radio vacuum tube, the phonograph and phonograph record, the motion-picture camera, the first mimeograph and dictating machines, and wax paper. Unity: the role of the Topic sentence (PI) is the most important; in the model the Body (PD) collects information relying on the Topic sentence; note that sentences about Edison like 'Edison favoured the use of direct current (DC) electricity, for he considered alternating current (AC) dangerous', 'Thomas Edison never completed grade school' and 'When Edison publicly stated his intention to devise durable filaments for lamps, gas company stocks fell sharply on the New York Stock Exchange' are NOT added, otherwise the paragraph would lose its fluency. Next to Unity, the most important subject is Coherence, i.e. clarity and easy understanding; to hold the idea of PI in PD, three things must be kept: i. repetition of nouns and use of reference words (determiners, pronouns etc.); ii. conjunctions and adverbs; iii. transitional words and phrases.

chunk_text: Writing Compositions: in the exam a composition must be written according to the given Situation. Compositions are about the student's personal experience, familiar events, recent events or future plans. Whatever the subject, a composition must have Introduction, Body and Conclusion. Composition in Detail: like a paragraph, a composition has three components - Introduction, Body and Conclusion. Introduction: as a paragraph has a paragraph introducer (PI), the introduction of a composition also has a (PI), but more must be done here: show interest in the Topic and make it enjoyable to the reader; tell the reader - the Topic, the Definition of any unfamiliar term in the Title, the writer's outlook on the Topic, special aspects of the Topic, and the different area or part of the aspect of the Essay. Body: presents the main speech of the Topic, through any one of Listing, analyzing, narrating, describing, exemplifying, comparing, contrasting, or several of them together. Conclusion: presents the concluding idea of the Essay in a limited range; a big Summary; never introduce a completely new idea. Characteristics of a Model Short Composition: 1. Unity - present the subject keeping its relevance; irrelevant matter destroys Unity. 2. Order - present the subject in an orderly chain so the writing reaches a definite goal; disorderly speech destroys order. 3. Brevity - length limited to 250 words; though the length depends on the subject and no definite limit can be given, stay aware for brevity. 4. Style - the style of writing should be elevated and literary; never use colloquial language; follow an easy, simple and natural style in language and sentence structure.

chunk_text: Writing Informal Letters/E-mails: in the exam one item on informal letter or e-mail is given. Except for the medium (paper and pen for a letter, internet for an e-mail) there is no content difference between a letter and an e-mail. In an informal letter the content matters most, though the format should be of one kind: British style - indent each paragraph, writer's full address and date at the top right, name at the bottom right; American style - no indent, all parts start at the left range. Drawing an envelope or stamp in the answer script is not compulsory, so better not to draw it. For an e-mail the E-mail Id, Subject and Content must be shown. Follow either British or American style in the exam; never mix the two. Exclusive Letter/E-mail Writing Technique. Presentation: use social, colloquial language; choose the salutation according to the relation with the person; use the name and address given in the question properly (be careful with names and addresses in letters to foreign friends); the body may have several paragraphs but the whole letter should fit one page; drawing the envelope is not compulsory. Style: choose either British or American style; never mix them; the examples in this book follow American style - all parts at the left range, no indent in any paragraph. Exam Strategy: follow the question word by word; names and addresses must be exact. chunk_text: Writing Formal Letters/E-mails: between a Formal Letter and a Formal E-mail there is no special difference except the medium - paper and pen for a letter, computer for an e-mail; in the exam both are presented on paper. American Style formats: Formal Letter (Academic) - first the date (22 August 2024), then the recipient's designation and address (The Headteacher, .... School, Dhaka), then Subject (Request for Transfer certificate); Formal E-mail (Academic) - first the recipient's E-mail ID (To: zaman_2024@yahoo.com), then Subject (Request for Transfer certificate); from Subject onwards all parts are the same. Sample: Formal Letter (Academic Applications), Full Block Style - 7 parts: 1. The date, 2. Recipient's designation & address, 3. Subject, 4. Salutation, 5. Body, 6. Subscription, 7. Applicant's signature, Name & Identity (example: prayer for leave of absence, Aly Zaker (Reza), Class XI (Science Group), Roll No.-01). Points to Ponder Over: write the application in left range with enough space between parts; keep proper margin at the top and left of the answer script; the date may be written 23 April 2024, April 23, 2024 or 23/04/2024 (the last form is rare); do not abbreviate April as Apr. or any other month, nor Subject as Sub.; write the letter in easy language according to the main idea, in one page, with no extra information; never use contractions in a formal letter; better not to use comma or full stop in the recipient's designation and address, Subject, Salutation, Subscription and Signature parts - or use them in all places.
